title: PanoPed: Beyond Bounding Boxes for Sim-to-Real Panoramic Pedestrian Tracking
summary: Full-sphere panoramic cameras let fixed monitoring systems and mobile robots track people in every direction, but a planar bounding box does not fully describe where a person is on the sphere. We introduce PanoPed, a sim-to-real benchmark for pedestrian tracking on the full sphere. PanoPed-S contains 108,000 frames from fixed, quadruped-mounted, and drone-mounted cameras, with synchronized masks, depth, camera poses, and 3D pedestrian states. PanoPed-R adds 28,002 real frames from fixed cameras, 16,247 of them densely annotated. We find that an ERP rectangle cannot uniquely determine the spherical center and angular extent of the visible person, while the detector's visual query still carries information about them. Inspired by the sextant's use of angular measurements to locate objects, we propose Sextant, a plug-and-play angular localization head with only about 0.035M parameters. It reuses a frozen detector, keeps track identities unchanged, and needs no extra image encoder. Sextant gives the best result in our PanoPed-S test comparison, raising the strongest baseline, MOTIP, from 47.30 to 49.49 HOTA, with gains on all eight test sequences. Without fine-tuning on real data, the same synthetic-trained heads improve MOTIP and HAT by 0.96-1.14 HOTA on real video, and both seeds improve every real sequence. HAT+Sextant scores best among the compared systems that add no localization image encoder.

Introduction sec:intro Fixed cameras and robots that move through crowds see people on all sides, not only in front. Full-sphere cameras capture this whole scene, usually in the equirectangular projection (ERP), whose left and right borders are the same meridian and whose distortion grows toward the poles. A pedestrian can leave the image on one side and reappear on the other while staying in view, and a person near the lower pole appears as a wide, curved shape. A moving camera adds viewpoint changes and platform motion. This setting poses two problems: suitable data are missing, and a tracker's box output does not determine where the visible person is on the sphere. The first problem is data. Existing datasets cover only parts of this setting: JRDB-PanoTrack omits the poles le2024jrdbpanotrack , QuadTrack and EmboTrack cover the sphere partly or unevenly luo2025omnitrack,luo2025omnitrackpp , and 360VOT tracks a single object huang2023vot . None scores multi-person tracks on the sphere or offers dense masks, depth, and 3D states across platforms. Such labels are costly on real video, so simulation is the natural source, but its value must be shown on real targets built the same way. The second problem lies in the tracker's output. Trackers report each person as an ERP box, which records how far the person extends but not which pixels inside it belong to them. A fixed rule then converts the box into a region on the sphere, so two people in different poses who share one box receive the same region, although their visible pixels have different centers on the sphere (Figure~ fig:teaser b). Box-based evaluation hides this error, because it compares boxes with boxes. We address the first problem with , a sim-to-real benchmark for pedestrian tracking on the full sphere (Figure~ fig:teaser a). contains 60 synthetic sequences from 30 fixed, 18 quadruped-mounted, and 12 drone-mounted cameras whose motion follows simulated platform dynamics, and every frame has synchronized masks, depth, camera poses, and 3D pedestrian states. contains five real recordings from fixed cameras, three of them densely annotated over 16,247 frames. Both parts compute targets on the sphere from visible pixels by the same rule, with automatic masks on real video, so a model trained in simulation can be tested on real video directly. We address the second problem with , which reads three quantities that the tracker already computes: the detector's visual query for the person, a starting region from the box, and the detection score. From them it predicts the center direction and angular extent of the visible person (Figure~ fig:teaser c). The tracker stays frozen, no image encoder is added, and identities and scores pass through unchanged. With only parameters, improves MOTIP, the strongest baseline in our comparison, by 2.17--2.19 test HOTA, with gains on all eight test sequences for both head seeds. Because both parts share one target rule, we can test whether this correction transfers. Without fine-tuning, heads trained only on improve MOTIP and HAT by 0.96--1.14 HOTA on all 16,247 real frames, with gains in HOTA and IDF1 on every sequence for both seeds and trackers. HAT+ scores highest among compared systems that add no localization image encoder. Our contributions are: (i) , a sim-to-real benchmark for full-sphere pedestrian tracking whose targets are defined on the sphere by one rule in simulation and on real video; (ii) evidence that a tracker's box output loses localization information, with the detector and identities held fixed; and (iii) , a -parameter plug-in that reads this information from detector queries and transfers from simulation to real video without a localization image encoder. Related Work sec:related Panoramic tracking benchmarks. MOTChallenge milan2016mot16,dendorfer2021motchallenge and DanceTrack sun2022dancetrack define multi-object tracking with planar boxes in perspective video. Panoramic datasets widen the view but cover only part of the sphere or the task. JRDB martinmartin2021jrdb and JRDB-PanoTrack le2024jrdbpanotrack use a stitched cylindrical panorama without the poles. QuadTrack luo2025omnitrack , released with OmniTrack, is recorded through an annular lens on a quadruped, and EmboTrack luo2025omnitrackpp adds dual-fisheye video from a wheel-legged robot, but its vertical coverage is uneven. 360VOT huang2023vot covers the full sphere and scores regions on it, but tracks one object. No existing resource combines multi-person tracking, full-sphere coverage, spherical targets, dense masks and depth, and several platforms (Table~ tab:resources ). Localization on the sphere. Panoramic perception is moving from distortion-aware engineering toward sphere-native models zhu2026panoramicsurvey,zhu2026so3uformer . Work on spherical detection follows two lines. One adapts the network to ERP distortion, with spherical convolutions coors2018spherenet or detectors trained on panoramic images chou2020indoor360 . The other changes what is predicted. PANDORA xu2022pandora uses oriented boxes on the sphere, and later work makes them easier to match and regress with an unbiased spherical IoU dai2022unbiasediou , Gaussian label distributions xu2023gldl , or a mapping to planar oriented boxes (Sph2Pob) liu2023sph2pob . Both lines train new single-image detectors. Neither examines trackers, which are usually trained with ERP boxes and output boxes, or how much spherical localization a tracker loses at its output. Multi-object tracking. Most progress in multi-object tracking concerns association. ByteTrack zhang2022bytetrack keeps low-confidence detections for matching, and OC-SORT cao2023ocsort corrects its motion model with recent observations. Transformer trackers extend DETR carion2020detr,zhu2021deformabledetr with track queries meinhardt2022trackformer,zeng2022motr . MOTIP gao2025motip predicts identities from a history of identity-tagged observations, and HAT gao2025hat transforms ReID features with track history on top of MASA pretraining li2024masa . All of these trackers report each person as an image box. On the full sphere, a fixed rule must still convert this box into a region, and better association does not reduce the error of that conversion. Synthetic data and sim-to-real transfer. Game engines supply pedestrian video with exact labels. JTA and MOTSynth render boxes, masks, depth, and pose fabbri2018jta,fabbri2021motsynth . SPEAR is a programmable Unreal Engine simulator roberts2022spear . WorldRover renders annotated exploration video xu2026worldrover , whereas Sekai2 collects real exploration video he2026sekai2 . None of them targets pedestrian tracking on the full sphere. Transfer to real video also requires both domains to define targets in the same way, since annotation mismatches already affect models trained across detection datasets liao2024labels . Consistent real targets need masks, which are costly to label by hand. Box-prompted segmenters such as SAM~2 ravi2025sam2 and SAM-HQ ke2023samhq produce masks automatically, but these are estimates rather than verified labels. The Benchmark sec:dataset Tracking on the sphere sec:task The input is an ERP image, and the output is one region per visible pedestrian, each with an identity that persists within the sequence. For pixel-center indices in an image of width and height , the spherical coordinates are The horizontal wrap-around comes from the image format, so a person who crosses the seam keeps one identity even when a box export splits them into two pieces. A native spherical region stores a center direction, an angular extent, and the frame and boundary convention of the rule that produced it, and native IoU is computed between these regions on the sphere. provides four linked annotation levels. L0 holds the source annotations: rendered instance masks in S and human boxes around the visible body in R. L1 holds regions on the sphere, L2 ERP boxes that may wrap around the seam, and L3 standard MOT rows in which both pieces of a seam-crossing box keep one identity. S regions summarize the visible pixels. R has two region layers: Box-fit, an oriented and possibly asymmetric region fitted to each human box, and Support-auto, which applies the construction of S to automatically estimated masks. Box-fit keeps the original scored set, and Support-auto treats observations without a usable mask by fixed rules (Appendix~ app:support_auto ). : synchronized truth from fixed and moving cameras sec:panopeds contains 30 fixed-camera, 18 quadruped-mounted, and 12 drone-mounted sequences, each 60 seconds at 30 fps, for frames and sequence-local identities: 56 sequences at and four fixed TEST sequences at . The environment is a reauthored multilevel city with plazas, stairs, railings, and street furniture, rendered in under HDRI lighting conditions and varied layouts. Five fixed sites span camera heights of 0.8--3.0\,m with 5--50 pedestrians and moving-camera sequences use 16--32, drawn from 57 adult models and 45 animation states that mix locomotion, stops, turns, and social interactions. Seam handling is exercised in every split rather than in a curated subset: tracks wrap around the seam for instance-frames. Platform motion and synchronized capture. Camera motion comes from the platforms. The quadruped's gait follows the distance it travels, its body attitude follows speed and terrain, and the camera sits on a damped top mast. The drone's attitude responds to acceleration, banking, gusts, and motor vibration; four sequences add a stabilizer that levels the camera using only past motion. The visible platform is masked in every frame instead of being cropped out. At each simulation step, a frame barrier freezes crowd, animation, platform, and camera while six cube faces record RGB, instance ID, and radial range, together with root states and 22 body joints. Each modality is resampled to ERP in its own way (Appendices~ app:capture -- app:embodied ). All evaluated trackers use RGB alone at inference. : dense real annotation on the full sphere sec:panopedr was recorded with a GoPro MAX on fixed supports in an indoor corridor, a corridor corner, a rooftop plaza, and two multilevel plazas with stairs, and released as gravity-aligned ERP video at 29.97\,fps: frames over \,s. Three recordings are densely annotated with frames, identities, and modal boxes, of which are scoreable. title: FlashNeRD: Performance-First Contact-Rich Neural Robot Dynamics
summary: Compared with analytical physics, learned dynamics models promise robot simulation that is faster, inherently differentiable, and easily adaptable to real data. Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) pursues this by keeping collision detection analytical and replacing a simulator's numerical dynamics for the robot with a learned model. Three limitations remain. NeRD offers little speedup over the simulator it learned from, accepts contact only at predefined points, and has no two-way coupling with objects it manipulates. FlashNeRD removes all three with a parallel streaming architecture that makes each prediction faster and more accurate, an encoder that accepts contacts wherever they occur, and two-way coupling with objects simulated by analytical solvers. Experiments across five robots show faster and more accurate dynamics, faster policy learning, and faster inference-time planning. Across three robots, FlashNeRD's dynamics model is up to $55\times$ faster than an optimized NeRD and more accurate over long rollouts. This speedup extends to policy learning, where PPO trains an ANYmal locomotion policy in 34 seconds, $3.8\times$ faster than the analytical simulator and $2.7\times$ faster than an optimized NeRD. With DIAL-MPC, a sampling-based MPC method, the robot climbs all six test platforms where fixed-contact NeRD manages one, at approximately half the analytical simulator's planning time. Cube-reorientation policies trained with FlashNeRD complete within 2% of the simulator-trained policy's target count.

Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) pursues this by keeping collision detection analytical and replacing a simulator's numerical dynamics for the robot with a learned model. Three limitations remain. NeRD offers little speedup over the simulator it learned from, accepts contact only at predefined points, and has no two-way coupling with objects it manipulates. Experiments across five robots show faster and more accurate dynamics, faster policy learning, and faster inference-time planning. Across three robots, FlashNeRD's dynamics model is up to faster than an optimized NeRD and more accurate over long rollouts. This speedup extends to policy learning, where PPO trains an ANYmal locomotion policy in 34 seconds, faster than the analytical simulator and faster than an optimized NeRD. With DIAL-MPC, a sampling-based MPC method, the robot climbs all six test platforms where fixed-contact NeRD manages one, at approximately half the analytical simulator's planning time. Cube-reorientation policies trained with FlashNeRD complete within 2 of the simulator-trained policy's target count. Introduction Robot learning and planning require many dynamics predictions, making simulation cost a practical bottleneck. Analytical simulators such as MuJoCo todorov2012mujoco and GPU-parallel platforms such as Isaac Lab mittal2025isaaclab and Newton mujocowarp , whose MuJoCo Warp (MJWarp) backend we use unless otherwise stated, meet this demand by stepping thousands of environments. Three limits persist. Calls to an iterative contact solver bound throughput per GPU, many simulators are not differentiable, and fitting a simulator to real-robot data means tuning a few physical parameters that cannot express unmodeled effects such as actuator dynamics. Neural robot dynamics learns the robot's transition function from data, addressing all three limits in principle. Batched network evaluation has fixed cost and can outpace iterative contact solves. The model is differentiable by construction. The model can also be fine-tuned on real trajectories without selecting physical parameters to adjust. Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) pmlr-v305-xu25g is the state of the art, using one transformer per robot, trained on randomized states and actuator commands such as position targets or motor torques, with collision detection left analytical. Because the data are task- and controller-independent, the model learns generic robot dynamics rather than task-specific dynamics and serves any controller on the robot. NeRD also showed zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on reach tasks. Three limitations remain. (i) NeRD re-encodes the full history window at every step, so inference cost is similar to the analytical simulator's and the throughput advantage goes unrealized. (ii) Contact enters through predefined probe points, which are insufficient for more complex tasks where contacts happen at edges or surfaces, such as climbing. (iii) NeRD assumes the environment surrounding the robot is fully static, ruling out manipulation. removes each limitation, and each fix unlocks a capability. A parallel architecture with streaming inference that processes only the newest frame per step. This gives up to the model-only throughput of an inference-optimized NeRD baseline (Optimized NeRD) with lower rollout error, and is fast enough that end-to-end policy training also runs faster than in the analytical simulator. A set-based contact encoder that accepts contacts wherever collisions are detected, so contact-rich tasks such as platform climbing need no hand-placed probes. Two-way coupling via hybrid simulation, in which predicts the robot's free motion while MJWarp analytically simulates the objects and resolves their contacts with the robot, so forces flow in both directions and learned dynamics extend to manipulation. We validate each capability across five robots, spanning policy learning and inference-time planning with the learned model. trains a locomotion policy faster than the analytical simulator. With sampling-based MPC, the robot climbs all six test platforms where NeRD manages one, and a cube-reorientation policy trained with completes within of the simulator-trained policy's target count. Related Work Neural simulation has been explored for fluids~ sanchezgonzalez2020gns , deformable bodies~ pfaff2021learning, bertiche2022cloth , and rigid bodies~ sanchez2018graph, li2025rwm, zhang2026nrd, dou2026rigidformerlearningrigiddynamics, andriluka2024neural, heiden2021neuralsim . Among neural simulators for articulated rigid bodies, NeRD~ pmlr-v305-xu25g learns robot-specific physics from robot-centric states, controls, and contact features independent of downstream tasks. FlashNeRD builds on it with higher inference speed, variable contacts, and two-way coupling. Three bodies of work inform the design. Efficient transformer inference, including parallel attention and feedforward branches~ chowdhery2023palm , multi-query attention~ shazeer2019fast , sliding-window attention~ jiang2023mistral , IO-aware kernels~ dao2022flashattention , and object-level attention in RigidFormer~ dou2026rigidformerlearningrigiddynamics , motivates the architecture of Secs.~ sec-arch and sec-cache . In place of contact representations such as implicit signed distance functions~ pmlr-v155-pfrommer21a , mesh-face graphs~ allen2023learning , and predicted binary contacts~ jing2026contactawareneuraldynamics , FlashNeRD pools the analytical detector's unordered contact set. Coupling schemes between solvers~ shinar2008twoway, chen2026divide or learned models~ dou2025cfc motivate the shared contact solve of Sec.~ sec-coupling-method . Method sec-method FlashNeRD has three components, one per limitation above, all built on the shared transition-learning problem of Sec.~ sec-transition . The first is a transformer that evaluates attention and feedforward branches in parallel within each block and caches past keys and values, so each rollout step encodes only the newest frame (Secs.~ sec-arch and sec-cache ). The second is a contact encoder that accepts contacts wherever the collision detector finds them (Sec.~ sec-variable-method ). The third is two-way coupling via hybrid simulation, in which analytically simulated objects push back on the learned robot (Sec.~ sec-coupling-method ). Learning a Robot Transition sec-transition A robot state contains joint positions and velocities plus, for floating-base robots, base orientation and linear and angular velocity. Each input frame adds control and gravity direction . Contact input is either an ordered, fixed-length vector from predefined link probes queried against collision geometry each step or a variable set of detected contacts. Fixed contact suits known locations such as feet on flat ground, while variable contact handles changing locations such as edges. The model predicts a state increment from frames, including the current frame, where hats denote predictions. We add the increment to and compose orientation increments as rotations. Expressing , , , and in the robot's base frame removes dependence on world position and heading. Following NeRD pmlr-v305-xu25g , we train on randomized physical states and actuator commands independently of any controller, retaining analytical collision detection. Each robot's model serves RL and planning with the same actuator model and timestep, provided training covers the relevant states and contacts. Figure~ fig-architecture gives an overview. An Architecture for Fast and Accurate Rollouts sec-arch Two considerations shape the design. First, autoregressive rollout time grows approximately with horizon times per-step latency. Kernel overhead and memory traffic can substantially affect this latency, especially at small batch sizes, motivating reductions in sequential operations and data movement alongside arithmetic cost. Second, a short history provides temporal context that can help the model distinguish consistent motion patterns from noise or small errors in individual frames. Combining information across recent frames can therefore make predictions less sensitive to fluctuations in any single input state. The design retains this temporal context while minimizing sequential work per step. Section~ sec-cache then removes NeRD's repeated encoding of the full history window. Each of blocks has two branches that read the same normalized input and run in parallel, following PaLM chowdhery2023palm rather than the serial attention-then-feedforward layout of a standard transformer vaswani2017attention . Attention reads the current and preceding frames and captures history-dependent effects, while the feedforward branch transforms the current hidden state. The embedding is , where is a linear map of the contact probe vector for fixed-contact models and a gated map of the pooled contact bank (Sec.~ sec-variable-method ) for variable-contact models. Block computes where square brackets denote concatenation, RMSNorm zhang2019rmsnorm normalizes the input, and the feedforward branch is a SwiGLU gate shazeer2020glu . Multi-query attention (MQA) shazeer2019fast uses one key/value head for all query heads, so the cache read per step stays small. Both branches are produced by one packed input projection and merged by one output projection, halving the sequential launches per block relative to the serial layout. Temporal order is encoded by a learned relative positional bias. A learned scalar indexed by lag is added to each query-key score before the softmax, with lag zero the current frame. Because the bias depends only on lag, it is unaffected by where a frame sits in the circular cache of Sec.~ sec-cache . Attention summarizes history, but the increment depends most on the current configuration, velocity, and control. To retain this information, the readout combines a nonlinear head with a direct affine path from the current frame, where and inject contact information into the hidden readout and the increment (Sec.~ sec-variable-method ) and are omitted for fixed-contact models. The affine path captures approximately linear local dynamics, and the nonlinear head adds state-dependent corrections. The direct terms are initialized to zero so training starts from the nonlinear predictor alone. Inputs, outputs, and contact rows are standardized with NeRD's normalization (omitted from the equations), and the model is trained by mean squared error on standardized one-step increments with invalid transitions and padding masked. Beyond reducing sequential work, the parallel form decouples temporal-context modeling from current-feature transformation: attention captures history-dependent effects, while the feedforward branch processes current features without first passing through the same block's attention. This decoupling, together with the direct current-frame readout, has been shown in our controlled experiments to improve prediction accuracy and reduce recursive rollout drift. Streaming Dynamics with Bounded KV Caching sec-cache A full-window transformer re-embeds and re-projects all frames at every step even though of them were processed at the previous step. In FlashNeRD only the newest frame is projected, and the keys and values of earlier frames are reused from a cache. The reuse is deliberately bounded. No block attends beyond its span in training, and lag biases exist only within the window, so an unbounded cache would renormalize attention over untrained key/value pairs and lags, and predictions would no longer be those of the trained model. title: World Models Dream of Success: Diagnosing and Repairing Failure Insensitivity in Robot World Models
summary: Robot world models support policy evaluation, planning, and synthetic data generation, but these applications require predictions that distinguish successful actions from failures. Across four released checkpoints from two architecture families, we observe weak sensitivity to action changes and success-like predictions on verified failures. Although recent work incorporates failures into model training, which data can repair released checkpoints without changing their architecture or training objective still remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce CureWM, which constructs alternative actions from successful demonstrations across a severity grid, verifies their outcomes through execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes alongside nominal demonstrations. This construction provides controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts. On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism falls from 80\% after fine-tuning on the official data to 30--43\% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38\% mean). In two separate evaluations on a physical robot arm, failure predictions scored as success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic decrease from 90\% after fine-tuning on successful demonstrations alone to 33\% with CureWM. With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures yield a success--failure value gap of 0.124, compared with 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures. These findings support execution-verified counterfactual replay for post-hoc repair and show why reduced optimism must be evaluated alongside success--failure discrimination. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CureWM.

Introduction sec:intro Robot world models learn to predict how environments evolve in response to actions, from latent dynamics models to generative video simulators~ dreamerv3,unisim,cosmos . In the robotic domain, their predictions support policy evaluation in imagination~ ctrlworld , action selection and planning~ cosmospolicy , and synthetic experience generation for policy learning~ unisim,ctrlworld . These applications require more than visually plausible futures: a model must distinguish actions that accomplish the task from those that fail. If failing actions receive high success values or generate success-like futures, decisions based on these predictions can favor actions that do not achieve the intended outcome. However, how to repair failure prediction in released robot world models still remains underexplored. MiraBench~ mirabench found optimism bias in action-conditioned predictions, but diagnosing such failure insensitivity does not tell us which training data could correct it. In particular, failed trajectories need not teach a model how alternative actions from the same context change the outcome. This distinction matters for released checkpoints: simply adding failures may lower predicted success across both successful and failing actions, reducing the optimism without improving discrimination. Therefore, the question is which kind of data enable post-hoc repair of action-conditioned predictions, and how to distinguish that repair from a general shift toward pessimism. Concurrent work, such as FACT~ fact , combines failed policy rollouts with action conditioning and failure-aware masking in a world-action model. However, it does not directly address how to repair released checkpoints while retaining their architecture and training objective, or which failure data are most effective under these constraints. To fill these knowledge gaps, we introduce CureWM, motivated by the observation that correctly predicting the outcome of an observed action does not imply knowing how a different action in the same context would change the outcome. CureWM perturbs successful demonstrations across a severity grid while preserving actions before intervention, verifies outcomes through execution, and retains failed and successful replays for post-training. The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. We evaluate four released checkpoints from two architecture families, which are Cosmos Policy~ cosmospolicy and Ctrl-World~ ctrlworld , and test CureWM in simulation and on a physical robot arm. The ALOHA checkpoint is evaluated for diagnosis only (Appendix~ app:aloha ). Experiments on LIBERO~ libero and a physical robot show improved success--failure discrimination. Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures over fresh policy failures, while ablations examine successful replays and verified outcome labels. These results also show why reduced optimism alone does not establish repair. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce CureWM, which repairs released world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective. We demonstrate repair in simulation and on a physical robot, including improved success--failure discrimination and failure detection. Matched LIBERO comparisons show stronger discrimination than training on fresh policy failures. We show that reduced optimism alone can overstate repair, and evaluate success--failure discrimination together with false alarms on successful actions. Related Work sec:related World models and action-conditioned reliability. Cosmos Policy~ cosmospolicy predicts actions, future observations, and values for control and planning, while Ctrl-World~ ctrlworld supports policy evaluation and synthetic trajectory generation through action-conditioned video prediction. MiraBench~ mirabench evaluates physics adherence, action following, and optimism bias, and provides the perturbation families used in our experiments. WorldArena~ worldarena likewise distinguishes perceptual quality from functional utility. We study post-hoc repair. Our support argument relates to causal confusion in imitation learning~ causalconfusion , but does not identify a causal mechanism inside the model. Failure and counterfactual supervision. Learning from unsuccessful behavior and constructed examples has been widely studied: Dex-Net~ dexnet2 learns grasp robustness from synthetic examples with analytic labels, HER~ her reuses unsuccessful attempts through goal relabeling, and CoDA~ coda constructs counterfactual transitions using locally factored dynamics. AHA~ aha synthesizes manipulation failures to train a vision-language model for failure detection and natural-language reasoning. Concurrent FACT~ fact incorporates failed rollouts into world-action model training. We do not claim novelty in adding failure examples. CureWM combines controlled perturbations, execution-verified outcomes, and successful replay partners to repair released checkpoints with their original architecture and objective. Furthermore, matched comparisons test which data choices improve repair. Conservative values, failure detection, and predictive repair. Offline RL addresses unreliable extrapolation through data-constrained action selection bcq , conservative value learning cql , and uncertainty-aware penalties or pessimistic dynamics mopo,morel . These methods motivate caution about unsupported actions, but conservative decision-making and accurate outcome discrimination are distinct objectives. Our label ablation illustrates that reduced optimism can accompany underestimated success predictions. It does not evaluate those offline RL algorithms. Foresight~ foresight instead learns failure detection from action-conditioned world-model representations. CureWM updates the world model's own predictions. We assess whether it better distinguishes successful from failing actions, rather than simply assigning lower success values to both. Method sec:method Failure Insensitivity sec:problem Let denote the observation history and task context, and let and denote action sequences that succeed and fail from the same starting context. We call a model failure-insensitive when its predictions fail to distinguish these outcomes. Figure~ fig:insensitivity illustrates this behavior. This differs from optimism alone: a model can assign similar values to successful and failing actions even when neither value is high. We therefore evaluate both predictions on failing actions and discrimination between successful and failing actions. Measuring Failure Sensitivity Value prediction. For a model predicting native value predictions , we measure the mean success--failure value gap over action pairs: A positive gap means successful actions receive higher values on average. We report both values to check whether improved discrimination comes at the cost of underestimating successful actions. We use 0.5 as a fixed diagnostic threshold for the native value prediction. We do not assume that this value is a calibrated success probability. False-positive rate measures successful replays labeled as failures by this threshold. title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have emerged as a promising framework for robot control. By mapping visual observations and language instructions to continuous actions, they unify visual grounding, language understanding, and control within a single policy. Recent models have achieved strong performance across diverse manipulation tasks brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,wang2025vlaadapter . Yet this unified formulation hides a difficult representational transition. The visual-language perception space and the action space are organized around fundamentally different semantics. The former describes the current world and the intended task, including scene content, object relations, and instruction-level intent. The latter specifies how the robot should act through temporally ordered, executable control. We refer to this semantic mismatch as the perception--action representation gap. Existing VLA policies learn to traverse this gap primarily through end-to-end action supervision. The final action loss specifies which action should be produced, while the representation that connects visual-language semantics to action semantics is left implicit. Action tokens must therefore discover within the policy both what information is relevant to control and how it should be reorganized into an action-ready representation. Recent work has sought to facilitate this transition by exposing control-relevant structure through visual traces, affordances, visual reasoning, and learned latent actions zheng2024tracevla,nasiriany2024rtaffordance,zhao2025cotvla,liu2026lara . These efforts show that making such structure explicit can facilitate action generation. Yet robot demonstrations already pair the two sides of the transition: visual--language context specifies what behavior is required, while expert actions reveal how that behavior is executed. This raises a central question: we learn the missing intermediate representation directly from perception and action---a bridge that carries task semantics from one space and executable structure from the other? We introduce , a framework for learning a Perception--Action Intermediate Representation directly from paired robot demonstrations. From the action side, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into Action Latent Tokens. Reconstructing the demonstrated actions requires these tokens to preserve the temporal and executable structure. From the perception side, a Bridge Module condenses the current visual-language representations into compact, task-relevant features. Aligning these features with the Action Latent Tokens transfers action structure into the perception-derived representation, forming Bridge Tokens that jointly encode task semantics and action information. Perception supplies the semantic content, expert actions supply the executable structure, and alignment integrates both into a unified bridge. then projects the Bridge Tokens into the action-token space and injects them at the beginning of action decoding. This early Bridge Injection primes the action tokens with task-aware and action-structured information, providing an explicit starting point for the perception-to-action transition. The policy can then refine this prior through its original action-decoding process rather than constructing an action-ready representation from the final action objective alone. Experiments on LIBERO liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus fei2025liberoplus , and CALVIN ABC D mees2022calvin demonstrate consistent gains across OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter. raises the average success rate of VLA-Adapter from 97.3 to 98.4 on LIBERO and from 59.1 to 64.2 on LIBERO-Plus. On CALVIN, it improves the average completed sequence length from 4.28 to 4.40 with OpenVLA-OFT and from 4.42 to 4.53 with VLA-Adapter. Across seven real-world tasks, further raises the average success rate of OpenVLA-OFT from 51.4 to 65.0 . These improvements span standard manipulation, zero-shot distribution shifts and long-horizon execution. Representation analyses further show that Bridge Tokens retain task context while exposing action structure before decoding, supporting their role as an explicit interface between perception and action. Contributions. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1.5em, labelsep=0.5em, topsep=3pt, itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt, partopsep=0pt] We characterize the perception--action representation gap in continuous-action VLAs as the implicit transition from visual--language semantics to executable action semantics under final action supervision. We introduce , which learns perception-derived Bridge Tokens whose task semantics are organized by expert-action structure, and uses early Bridge Injection to provide Action Tokens with an action-aware starting point for refinement. We demonstrate consistent gains across standard manipulation, zero-shot distribution shifts, long-horizon execution, and real-world control, together with representation-level evidence that Bridge Tokens retain task semantics while exposing action structure before Action Expert refinement. Related Work Intermediate representations for perception-to-action learning. Intermediate representations make control-relevant structure explicit before action prediction. Motion-oriented approaches encode trajectories, visual traces, or future scene changes~ niu2024llarva,zheng2024tracevla,zhang2025dreamvla . Spatial representations introduce geometric information into perception and action modeling~ qu2025spatialvla,li2025bridgevla , while affordance-based methods describe possible interactions or key robot configurations~ nasiriany2024rtaffordance,yu2026affordancevla . These approaches define the intermediate representation through a chosen physical abstraction, such as motion, geometry, or affordance. PAIR does not prescribe a particular physical meaning for the bridge. Its content is learned from the two spaces it is meant to connect: visual--language context provides task semantics, while expert actions organize the representation around executable structure. In this way, task context and action structure jointly determine what the intermediate representation retains. Latent action representations and tokenization. Latent action methods learn compact representations of robot behavior for pretraining, prediction, and control. LAPA derives discrete latent actions from visual transitions for VLA pretraining without robot action labels~ ye2024lapa , while UniVLA learns task-centric latent actions for policy learning~ bu2025univla . FAST and VQ-VLA tokenize continuous action chunks for token-based policies~ pertsch2025fast,wang2025vqvla . These approaches primarily structure how actions themselves are represented, tokenized, or predicted. LARA~ liu2026lara moves closer to the perception--action interface by aligning latent visual dynamics with intermediate Action Expert features during generation. PAIR targets a different object: a perception-derived intermediate representation that is shaped by expert-action structure during training and made available before Action Expert refinement begins. The VLA backbone encodes the observation and instruction into visual--language representations , which condition an Action Expert to predict continuous actions. A useful representation between perception and action should carry two complementary forms of information: the task semantics that determine what behavior is required, and the executable structure that determines how the behavior should unfold. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:pair-framework , learns these properties from the two sides of the transition. A Masked Action Autoencoder captures action structure from expert trajectories, while a Bridge Module extracts compact task-relevant information from the visual--language context. Aligning their horizon-wise representations forms Bridge Tokens, which are injected into Action Tokens at the beginning of the Action Expert. At inference, the Action Autoencoder is removed and the Bridge Module predicts the task-conditioned, horizon-wise tokens directly from the current observation and instruction. title: Beyond Reconstruction: What Matters in Action Tokenization for Robot Policies?
summary: Autoregressive action-token policies such as vision-language-action models require action tokenizers to translate discrete token sequences into precise control actions in continuous space. Many action tokenizers learn the mapping between tokens and actions via a reconstruction objective. However, as we show through extensive analysis, sufficiently accurate action reconstruction is only one part of what makes a downstream robot policy successful. It is also critical that the policy is able to predict the right tokens for new observations, and that unseen policy token predictions still decode into reasonable actions. These properties are downstream of tokenizer training and are not directly incentivized by a reconstruction objective alone. In this work, we introduce Predictable and Robust Action Tokenization (ProAct), a tokenizer training method that strategically augments reconstruction with the goal of improving downstream predictability and robustness. ProAct is policy-agnostic and uses only action datasets for training. Across the Robomimic, LIBERO, and RoboTwin benchmarks and a diverse set of tokenizer architectures, ProAct improves rollout success by an average of 11.3 percentage points. These improvements also translate to vision-language-action policies and real-world robotic manipulation, yielding average gains of 21.8 and 36.7 percentage points, respectively. These results suggest that effective action tokenization should be designed as a policy interface that balances fidelity, predictability, and robustness, rather than as a reconstruction problem alone.

Introduction sec:introduction Many robot policies predict continuous action chunks~ Zhao2023ACT,Chi2023DiffusionPolicy , whereas autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) generate discrete token sequences. Action tokenization bridges this gap by encoding action chunks as tokens and decoding them back to continuous control actions. RT-1~ Brohan2023RT1 discretizes robot actions, while RT-2~ Zitkovich2023RT2 explicitly connects action tokens to pretrained VLMs and introduces the vision-language-action (VLA) formulation. Action tokenization has since become standard in autoregressive VLAs~ Kim2024OpenVLA,Pertsch2025FAST,Wang2025VQVLA , in part because it preserves the native next-token interface of autoregressive VLMs. Discrete action tokens can represent multiple valid action modes, whereas regression objectives average across modes and yield an invalid intermediate action~ Florence2022ImplicitBC,Shafiullah2022BehaviorTransformer,Lee2024VQBeT . Moreover, action tokenization enables temporal compression~ Mete2024QueST,Pertsch2025FAST and language-model-style policy post-training~ Galaxea2026G05 . This growing adoption of action tokenization raises a more specific question: how should continuous actions be tokenized? Independent per-dimension, per-timestep binning~ Brohan2023RT1 ignores temporal redundancy within action chunks and is inefficient (Appendix~ app:analytical-tokenization ); FAST~ Pertsch2025FAST exploits such temporal structure through frequency-domain compression, but relies on a fixed analytical representation~ Dong2026ActionCodec and is tied to dataset-specific frequency statistics, making it less transferable across tasks or embodiments. Recent learned tokenizers report gains over these fixed tokenization schemes on selected benchmarks~ Dong2026ActionCodec,Kang2026XTokenizer,Liu2026OAT ; however, the principles for designing effective learned action tokenizers remain underexplored. Existing works often choose nominal bitrate, chunk size, and execution horizon empirically, while the properties of the resulting token space remain poorly understood. More concretely, tokenizer training and policy learning involve different aspects of the same discrete token space: the tokenizer focuses on reconstructing expert actions from encoded tokens, while the downstream autoregressive (AR) policy must predict and compose those tokens from observations. As a result, reconstruction quality alone does not characterize either how predictable the induced token targets are or how policy-generated token sequences decode into actions. These gaps expose a fundamental question: ``what matters in action tokenization for robot policies?'' Across 22 tokenizer configurations that span key design choices~ Lee2024VQBeT,Mete2024QueST,Wang2025VQVLA,Liu2025FASTer,Dong2026ActionCodec,Liu2026OAT,Kang2026XTokenizer , we find that tokenizer reconstruction error alone is not a reliable indicator of policy success. Specifically, a sufficiently low reconstruction error is necessary for successful control, but further reductions in error do not predict rollout performance. We further analyze how bitrate, chunk size, and the execution horizon affect downstream performance. Beyond reconstruction, our empirical and theoretical results identify an underexplored failure mode: autoregressive policies can produce token sequences that differ from the encoded targets, yet standard training objectives do not directly control the resulting action-space error. This observation motivates , a tokenizer-training method with two components. Token Balance Regularization makes the encoded targets easier for the downstream policy to predict. Token Perturbation improves robustness to token mismatches. Neither requires access to the downstream policy or the observations. Together, we show that improves downstream rollout performance across nearly all evaluated tokenizer configurations. Ablating each component shows that both interventions can improve rollout performance even when reconstruction and policy-validation metrics do not consistently explain the gains. Decoded-error diagnostics support the intended robustness effect of Token Perturbation. Together, these results suggest that effective action tokenization requires balancing fidelity, predictability, and robustness to the sequences that the downstream policy actually produces. Our contributions are threefold: [nosep,leftmargin=2em] We conduct a controlled study of 22 learned action tokenizers, characterizing the effects of reconstruction fidelity, nominal bitrate, chunk size, and execution horizon on downstream control. We find that sufficient reconstruction accuracy is necessary for successful rollouts, but that further improvements in reconstruction do not reliably predict better downstream performance. We show that AR policies routinely compose complete token sequences not observed in the encoded demonstrations, and develop a one-step error decomposition that distinguishes matched predictions from token mismatches, revealing that standard tokenizer and policy objectives do not control the action-space severity of mismatched predictions. Motivated by this analysis, we propose , which combines two complementary tokenizer-only training methods: Token Perturbation, which improves robustness to token mismatches, and Token Balance Regularization, which makes the encoded targets easier for the downstream policy to predict. We show that improves average success rate by up to percentage points on Robomimic, LIBERO, and RoboTwin, by points for a VLA policy on LIBERO, and by points on real-world manipulation tasks. Related Work sec:related-work Imitation Learning and Action Chunking Imitation learning trains policies from expert demonstrations, commonly by behavior cloning~ Ross2011DAgger . Action chunking extends this formulation by predicting a sequence of future actions and executing either the full chunk or a prefix before re-planning. It is used across transformer, diffusion, and VLA policies, including ACT~ Zhao2023ACT , Diffusion Policy~ Chi2023DiffusionPolicy , and OpenVLA-OFT~ Kim2025OpenVLAOFT . Alongside these empirical design choices, recent theory analyzes when open-loop chunk execution can mitigate compounding imitation error under stability assumptions~ Zhang2025ActionChunking,Lazzati2026ActionChunking . Action-Generation Paradigms in VLA Policies A primary distinction among VLA policies is their output representation. One family predicts continuous action chunks directly through an action head: ~ Black2025Pi0 , ~ PhysicalIntelligence2025Pi05 , and GR00T N1~ NVIDIA2025GR00TN1 use flow-matching or diffusion-based objectives, whereas OpenVLA-OFT uses an regression objective~ Kim2025OpenVLAOFT . These methods map VLM features directly to continuous actions without an intervening vocabulary. A second family predicts discrete action tokens that must be detokenized before execution; recent examples include VQ-VLA~ Wang2025VQVLA , FASTer~ Liu2025FASTer , and G0.5~ Galaxea2026G05 . This token-based formulation allows action prediction to retain the VLM's native autoregressive next-token interface. The increased adoption of action tokenization for robot policies raises the question that we aim to address in this work: how to best train the action tokenizer that determines the VLM prediction targets. Discrete Representation Learning and Tokenization Discrete representation learning maps continuous features to tokens using vector quantization (VQ)~ Oord2017VQVAE , residual VQ (RVQ)~ Lee2022RQ , normalized RVQ (NRVQ)~ Yu2022ImprovedVQGAN,kumar2023high , finite scalar quantization (FSQ)~ Mentzer2024FSQ , or reconstruction-conditioned codebooks such as QinCo~ Huijben2024QINCo,Vallaeys2025QINCo2 . These methods are used by tokenizers for vision~ Oord2017VQVAE,Yu2022ImprovedVQGAN,Qiu2025RobustLatent and audio~ Zeghidour2022SoundStream . For robot control, tokenization defines the prediction targets for the downstream policy. Analytical representations include per-dimension binning~ Brohan2023RT1 , FAST frequency-domain codes~ Pertsch2025FAST , and BEAST B-spline coefficients~ Zhou2025BEAST . Learned methods include VQ-BeT~ Lee2024VQBeT and QueST~ Mete2024QueST for discrete skills, OAT for prefix decodability~ Liu2026OAT , and VQ-VLA~ Wang2025VQVLA and FASTer~ Liu2025FASTer for autoregressive VLAs. Recent methods further incorporate vocabulary structure~ Dong2026ActionCodec , robot state~ Jiang2026SAVLA , or multimodal features~ Kang2026XTokenizer . While such auxiliary signals can improve alignment on source tasks, they tie the tokenizer to task- or observation-specific supervision and may require realignment under distribution changes. To avoid this, we instead train tokenizers on action chunks alone, treating auxiliary supervision as complementary. Unlike prior systems that tune reconstruction, bitrate, and temporal horizons individually, we jointly analyze these factors and policy-generated sequences across a controlled tokenizer design space. title: SPLATIFY: Reproduce, Discover, Innovate! From Papers and Ideas to Trainable 3DGS Code
summary: The rapid growth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) research demands significant effort to reimplement papers before building on them. We introduce SPLATIFY, a multi-agent framework that converts 3DGS papers into trainable gsplat-based implementations, where generic paper-to-code methods and frontier models fail. SPLATIFY achieves this through five innovations: (1) A context-free grammar for gsplat over a modular method template with extension points for losses, densification, rendering, and optimization, constraining synthesis so generated code satisfies gsplat's architectural invariants by construction. (2) Architectural elements for faithful reproduction: fork-aware citation recovery retrieving component-level code at function-level granularity, Graph-of-Thought synthesis in topological dependency order, RAG-guided in-context example selection from over 20 verified implementations, and visual feedback combining PSNR-guided regeneration, Gaussian-level structural checks, and VLM-driven patching. (3) Knowledge-driven compositional improvement that autonomously finds weaknesses and composes complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies to improve upon original results. (4) Interdisciplinary method discovery where agents retrieve physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature and compose them with rendering knowledge to produce methods for previously unaddressed scene types. (5) SPLATIFY-Bench, an evaluation framework across 30 diverse 3DGS papers. On papers without public code, SPLATIFY matches expert implementations while reducing development time from weeks to minutes, and through compositional discovery further improves PSNR by up to 2.4 dB. We additionally demonstrate novel methods for volumetric nebula rendering and other scientific domains, synthesized entirely by SPLATIFY.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting has triggered a fast-growing sub-field of neural rendering, yet the community publishes knowledge far faster than it can absorb. Since Kerbl et al.~ kerbl20233dgs introduced 3DGS in 2023, follow-up papers have grown to over 1,500 in under three years~ chen2024survey3dgs, fei20243dgsnewera , with tracking repositories recording roughly three new arXiv submissions per day~ kulhanek2024nerfbaselines . For a researcher who wants to use a recently published method, however, the path from paper to working code remains prohibitively slow. Existing infrastructure cannot keep pace with this growth. While over 40 of tracked 3DGS papers release no code~ awesome3dgs , others publish isolated forks with incompatible assumptions about attribute layouts, density control, rendering conventions~ kulhanek2024nerfbaselines , and CUDA kernels. Building on a recent method typically demands weeks of manual reimplementation and debugging. Generic pipelines like Paper2Code~ seo2025paper2code and AutoP2C~ lin2025autop2c produce code that do not compile against any rasterization backend, and frontier models generate Python that collapses at training time for lack of domain knowledge about Gaussian attribute coupling or adaptive density control. No existing paper-to-code system, in any domain, handles 3DGS's fork-dominated landscape, provides Gaussian-level structural verification, or moves beyond reproduction to compositional improvement. Even if reproduction were perfectly solved, the deeper bottleneck would persist: the knowledge across 2k+ papers is neither discoverable nor composable. There is no efficient way to determine whether combining a depth distortion loss from 2DGS~ huang20242dgs with stochastic splitting from 3DGS-MCMC~ kheradmand20243dgsmcmc and an opacity regularizer from AbsGS~ ye2024absgs would outperform any of them individually. With hundreds of published techniques, the number of valid compositions is enormous, and manual exploration covers a negligible fraction. Entire application domains where Gaussians are a natural geometric fit, from optically thin nebulae to fluorescence microscopy, remain untouched because the engineering barrier is too high. The field needs infrastructure for discovering, composing, and extending the knowledge its papers contain. We introduce (Fig.~ teaser ) , a multi-agent framework operating at three levels: faithful reproduction of 3DGS papers as trainable gsplat~ ye2025gsplat plugins, compositional improvement that autonomously combines complementary techniques, and cross-domain method invention for unaddressed scene types. Its design rests on five contributions: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=3pt] A context-free grammar for gsplat plugins over a modular template with nine extension points covering the full 3DGS modification space, ensuring generated code satisfies architectural invariants by construction (Sec.~ sec:method_template ). Faithful reproduction extending the multi-stage pipeline of~ jain2026nerfifymultiagentframeworkturning with fork-aware citation recovery at function-level granularity, Gaussian-specific smoke tests, and PSNR training-curve monitoring (Sec.~ methodproposed ). Compositional improvement through autonomous diagnosis of weaknesses in reproduced methods and composition of complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies from the knowledge base, yielding up to 2.4\,dB PSNR gain with no human guidance (Sec.~ sec:knowledge_discovery ). title: CAP: Codebook-Aligned Prediction for Tokenized Robot Policies
summary: Action tokenization converts continuous robot actions into discrete symbols that can be modeled autoregressively. However, existing tokenizer-based policies typically ignore the tokenizer's learned latent code structure: after tokenization, the policy treats tokens as unrelated class indices and learns a new classifier from scratch. We show that this discarded structure is valuable. We introduce Codebook-Aligned Prediction (CAP), a method that directly reuses the tokenizer's code vectors as policy class prototypes while leaving the tokenizer and policy backbone otherwise unchanged. Across four quantizer families, three simulation benchmarks, and two real-robot tasks, CAP consistently improves task success over standard token classification heads while holding the tokenizer (and therefore its reconstruction quality) fixed. Our analysis further shows that these gains are not explained by higher token accuracy or changes in the policy head alone. Instead, reusing the tokenizer codebook provides the policy with valuable information about the tokenizer's learned latent structure across tokens, making token prediction errors more benign in action space and improving the representations learned by the policy backbone. These results suggest that action tokenizers learn useful action-aware latent structure beyond discrete targets that should be preserved when training downstream policies.

Introduction sec:introduction Robot policies learned from demonstrations now range from task-specific visuomotor controllers~ Zhao2023ACT,Chi2023DiffusionPolicy to generalist vision--language--action (VLA) models~ Kim2024OpenVLA,intelligence2025pi05 . A critical design choice for robot policies is how to represent the action space. Common approaches include direct regression~ Haldar2024BAKU , continuous generative models~ Zhao2023ACT, Chi2023DiffusionPolicy, Chisari2025PointFlowMatch , and discrete autoregressive models~ Shafiullah2022BehaviorTransformer,yunis24a . Each formulation presents distinct challenges for robot policies, including differences in training objectives and inference procedures. In this work, we focus on the last formulation: action tokenizers that discretize continuous action chunks, followed by autoregressive policies that predict the resulting action tokens. Casting action prediction as categorical next-token prediction enables the policy to represent multimodal action distributions, provide explicit token likelihoods, and avoid iterative continuous-sample refinement at inference time. For VLA models, it allows the policy to generate actions using the same autoregressive framework employed for language~ Zitkovich2023RT2,Pertsch2025FAST,Wang2025VQVLA . The tokenizer does more than simply convert continuous actions into discrete tokens for the policy: it determines reconstruction fidelity, sequence length, and the target distribution that the policy must learn. Existing action tokenizers fall into two broad categories. Predefined tokenizers map actions to tokens using fixed coordinates or trajectory transforms, including per-dimension bins~ Brohan2023RT1 , frequency coefficients~ Pertsch2025FAST , and B-spline bases~ Zhou2025BEAST . In contrast, learned action tokenizers adapt the discrete representation to the action distribution. Among these approaches, VQ-BeT~ Lee2024VQBeT and QueST~ Mete2024QueST learn latent vocabularies; VQ-VLA~ Wang2025VQVLA and FASTer~ Liu2025FASTer emphasize reconstruction and compression for autoregressive VLA models; OAT~ Liu2026OAT imposes coarse-to-fine structure across tokens; and other methods further shape the vocabulary through optimization-oriented or multimodal objectives~ Dong2026ActionCodec,Kang2026XTokenizer . Once trained, action tokenizers are typically used only to provide discrete token labels for downstream policy learning, while their associated code representations are discarded. This creates a mismatch between the structure learned by the tokenizer and how its tokens are modeled by the policy. In multi-level tokenizers, for example, the same token index may correspond to different code representations across levels, yet standard policies commonly use a shared classifier across the token sequence. More generally, one-hot supervision penalizes all incorrect tokens equally, regardless of their similarity to the target action. Consequently, the policy prediction objective ignores information already encoded in the tokenizer's latent code space. This raises a natural question: can these learned representations be used to better inform downstream policy learning? Our work answers this question affirmatively. We propose Codebook-Aligned Prediction (CAP) for policy training, which reuses tokenizer code vectors as class prototypes in the policy classifier and scores output representations by their distance to these prototypes. CAP therefore inherently aligns the policy's prediction heads with the tokenizer's level-wise structure and retains information already learned by the tokenizer without changing the tokenizer, policy backbone, or autoregressive training objective. Our contributions are summarized below: 2pt 0.5pt 0pt 0pt We propose , a simple prediction mechanism that reuses rather than discards tokenizer code representations and that can be used with both learned-codebook and lookup-free quantizers. We find that CAP consistently improves task success across four quantizer families, three simulation benchmarks, and two real-world tasks. We perform thorough analysis and ablations to investigate the causes of CAP's effectiveness, attributing these gains to more benign action errors and improved policy representations. Related Work sec:related-work Quantization and Robot Action Tokenizers Quantization has long been used for discrete representation learning, from scalar and vector quantization~ Gray1984VectorQuantization to neural quantizers such as VQ-VAE~ Oord2017VQVAE , residual quantization~ Lee2022RQ , and structured designs like FSQ~ Mentzer2024FSQ and BSQ~ Zhao2024BSQ . Its applications span vision~ Esser2021VQGAN , audio~ Zeghidour2022SoundStream , and speech~ Hsu2021HuBERT . In robotics, action tokenizers use either predefined or learned representations. Predefined quantization schemes discretize action dimensions or transformed trajectories, as in RT-1~ Brohan2023RT1 , FAST~ Pertsch2025FAST , and related approaches~ Zhou2025BEAST . Frequency- and spline-based methods~ Pertsch2025FAST,Zhou2025BEAST alleviate the redundancy of simple binning methods with compact trajectory representations, but their underlying bases remain fixed by design rather than adapting to correlations or recurring patterns in the action data. Learned tokenizers instead adapt their representations to the action distribution: VQ-BeT and QueST learn latent action vocabularies~ Lee2024VQBeT,Mete2024QueST , VQ-VLA~ Wang2025VQVLA and FASTer~ Liu2025FASTer integrate learned tokens into autoregressive VLA models, and recent methods further structure the vocabulary through architectural and auxiliary objectives~ Dong2026ActionCodec,Liu2026OAT,Kang2026XTokenizer . These works improve how actions are tokenized, but the downstream policy only receives token index labels and has to learn a new categorical classifier from scratch, ignoring the prior knowledge in the tokenizer's learned latent structure. In this work, we study how this structure can instead be leveraged to improve the policy. Imitation Learning Imitation learning trains policies with expert demonstrations, typically through behavior cloning, and is widely used for robot manipulation~ Ross2011DAgger . Action chunking predicts a sequence of future actions rather than a single action, allowing policies to capture short-horizon temporal structure and reduce the frequency of policy queries. Among methods that use action chunking, different policy parameterizations model the action distribution in different ways. ACT~ Zhao2023ACT directly predicts continuous action chunks with a conditional VAE, Diffusion Policy~ Chi2023DiffusionPolicy learns a denoising process, and flow-matching policies~ Chisari2025PointFlowMatch regress a conditional vector field. For tokenized policies, the action chunks are instead represented as discrete token sequences and predicted autoregressively~ Shafiullah2022BehaviorTransformer,Lee2024VQBeT,Mete2024QueST . We focus on this formulation and study how token representation alignment affects policy behavior. Method sec:method We first formulate the standard two-stage training pipeline where a tokenizer first learns a mapping between continuous actions and discrete tokens and an autoregressive policy then learns to predict the appropriate action tokens. We then identify two structural mismatches at their interface: (1) the same token index may correspond to different code representations across levels in a tokenizer, yet standard policies predict all levels with a shared categorical head, and (2) policy training uses only the discrete token indices and ignores the latent structure learned by the tokenizer. To address these issues, we propose Codebook-Aligned Prediction (CAP) to structure the policy's prediction space by reusing tokenizer representations as class prototypes for policy training. The trained tokenizer is then frozen, and its token sequences serve as categorical targets for an autoregressive policy conditioned on observations.
