title: Co-Evolving Robot Orchestrators and Policies through Deployment
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained on large datasets are capable within their training domains, yet they still fail to generalize to the variety of situations a robot meets in real-world deployment. Agentic robot systems complement the policy with a vision-language model (VLM) orchestrator that learns when to call the policy, how to instruct it, and when to use scripted skills instead. However, because the harness is built around a frozen policy that has limited language steerability, the orchestrator can avoid the policy's failures but never overcome them. The policy becomes the bottleneck of the whole system. Fine-tuning the policy can remove this bottleneck, but updating it alone decouples it from an orchestrator tuned to its old behavior. We propose Robo-COP, in which the orchestrator and policy co-evolve during deployment. Robo-COP curates skill demonstrations from its own executions, fine-tunes the policy when this data can address recurring failures, and adopts each new policy only after it improves the skills it was trained for. Across ten simulated RoboLab tasks, Robo-COP raises mean held-out success from 64.8% to 73.8% over the same harness with a frozen policy, while fine-tuning on a fixed schedule without verification reaches only 65.8%. On three real-world tasks, Robo-COP raises held-out success from 38.3% to 50.0%. Robo-COP turns deployment into a self-improving flywheel in which robots learn by doing, with each improvement in execution producing better data for the next round of learning. Videos and code are available at https://robo-cop.pages.dev/.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Robot foundation models trained on large datasets now generalize to many new objects and scenes openvla, pi0, pi05, droid . Still, they degrade under distribution shift once deployed liberoplus, radar , and no dataset can cover every situation a robot will encounter. Language models offer another route: they generalize zero-shot and can write code that plans over motion primitives saycan,cap,robotool,zeroshotplanner , but they are limited by the fixed set of primitives they can call. Recent agentic systems combine the two, with a language model reasoning and orchestrating vision-language-action (VLA) policies for low-level control pigey,roboharness,harnessvla . Such systems also improve by reflecting on failures during deployment reflect,droc,aspire and learning when to delegate to a VLA policy pigey,roboharness,harnessvla . Over many episodes, the harness adapts to the current policy, learning which parts of a task to give the policy and which to handle with scripted skills. The orchestrator can rephrase instructions or add supporting motions, but VLAs have limited language steerability liberoplus,cover , so the harness can only route around the policy's failures rather than fix them, and the upper bound of performance remains dictated by the policy. Updating the policy from deployment experience could raise this ceiling eximo , but doing so during deployment is hard. We study a deployment setting in which the robot must learn while attempting its assigned tasks, without a separate exploration phase. The training data must therefore come from these task attempts. In a novel environment many of these attempts fail, yet a failed episode often contains correct steps, such as a block that was grasped correctly before it was dropped, so keeping only successful episodes wastes much of the little data available. Even with new training data, fine-tuning does not guarantee improvement: the new checkpoint may perform worse than the deployed policy. Testing it requires further task attempts, so a poor update can cost deployment successes. Finally, updating the policy alone leaves the orchestrator behind: its memory, such as advice to grasp a block with scripted motion because earlier VLA grasps failed, was formed around the old checkpoint and no longer matches the new policy. Prior harnesses assume a fixed policy pigey,roboharness and never face these problems. We therefore ask: how can the orchestrator and its policy co-evolve during deployment? We introduce (Co-evolving Orchestrator and Policy), a self-improving system whose orchestrator uses scripted motion primitives and a VLA policy as tools, and which updates the policy and adapts the orchestrator's memory together purely during deployment (Figure~ fig:nested_loops ). It turns its own deployment executions into new training data for the policy by splitting each episode into skills and keeping every skill that succeeded, even when the episode as a whole failed, and it decides when this data warrants training. After fine-tuning, it evaluates each candidate during deployment, checking its target skills, overall task success, and previously admitted skills before deciding whether to adopt it or retain the current policy. We call this adoption check policy verification. After policy selection, it revisits memory entries that discouraged using the VLA, such as recommendations to use scripted motion after repeated grasp failures, so the orchestrator can reassess whether that advice still applies. Unlike skill discovery methods that spend a separate budget on exploration aspire , learns entirely during deployment, so every trial is an attempt at the task. We evaluate on ten simulated tasks chosen to span three regimes: tasks the pretrained VLA solves alone, tasks that scripted primitives solve, and tasks that need both. We also test the full loop on three real-world tasks. r 0.48 fig:nested_loops Our contributions are fourfold: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] Co-evolving orchestrator and policy. We frame deployment-time learning as improving an agentic harness and its policy together. Agentic data curation. We turn deployment executions into skill demonstrations without manual labels, keeping successful skills even from failed episodes, and train only when the data warrants it. Skill verification and memory revision. We verify each policy candidate before adoption and revise policy-dependent memory after every update. Performance gains in simulation and the real world. is competitive on all three regimes, raising mean held-out success from 64.8 to 73.8 in RoboLab simulation and from 38.3 to 50.0 on the real-world DROID setup over a frozen-policy harness. Related Work sec:related Agentic robot orchestration. Language-model planners compose motion primitives and learned policies into task-solving programs zeroshotplanner,saycan,cap,voxposer,robotool . More recently developed frameworks also improve during deployment: they revise failed programs and retain reusable skills aspire,resync,graphaspolicy , or learn when to delegate to a policy rather than an analytic tool pigey,volo,roboharness,hivla,retriever . All of these adapt how a fixed set of capabilities is used, so the system can do no better on a skill than its policy allows. keeps this adaptive harness but also improves the policy it calls, and revises the harness's memory whenever that policy changes. Generating robot-policy data. Improving a policy requires data that covers the situations it fails on. Simulation provides scalable supervision scenesmith , but transferring learned behavior to physical robots remains difficult whatwentwrong,dynamicsprompts,simrlvla . Real-world datasets and collection interfaces avoid this gap at the cost of human effort droid,umi,dexumi , and demonstration-generation methods stretch a small set of human examples further mimicgen,momagen . Closer to our setting, agents and policies can collect and filter their own experience demoscore,soar,veritas,enpire . draws its data from deployment itself, where executions mix policy and scripted actions, and curates skill-level demonstrations from them, including correct skills performed within failed trials. Policy improvement during deployment. Planner distillation and autonomous collection turn robot executions into policy supervision scalingup,optimus,robocat,soar , real-world reinforcement learning updates policies from interaction and reward mark2024parl,wagenmaker2025dsrl,lei2025rl100 , and VLM-guided exploration and skill acquisition generate training data for adapting VLA policies eximo,wang2026insightselfguidedskillacquisition . These methods typically deploy each updated policy, while test-time verification selects instructions or actions for a policy that stays fixed cover,veritas . instead treats each update as a candidate: it decides when training is warranted, verifies the whole candidate policy before adoption, and revises the memory that the harness built around the previous policy. Method sec:method updates both the VLA policy and the adaptive harness that orchestrates its use (Figure~ fig:system ). The harness logs policy and scripted actions as one stream (Section~ sec:orch ), curates it into skill demonstrations (Section~ sec:learn ), and verifies each new policy before adoption, revising the memory tied to the old one (Section~ sec:update ). Adaptive policy orchestration sec:orch Acting and reflecting. is an embodied coding agent built on the CaP-X execution tools capx , extended with an execute vla tool that invokes the VLA policy on a language instruction. Its orchestrator writes a program that calls scripted motion primitives, perception functions, and the VLA policy, conditioned on the task goal, current observation, episode history, and task memory , as in prior harnesses pigey,volo,roboharness . A vision-language model (VLM) monitors execution and can interrupt a call or end the episode. Whenever execution stops, a visual judge checks the outcome and either ends the episode or asks for revised code. It credits the VLA and scripted actions separately, so a successful skill keeps its credit even if a later step fails. At the end of the episode, the orchestrator records what worked and what failed in , a form of episodic memory that lets agentic robot systems improve without changing any weights reflect,droc,aspire,roboharness . Action unification. Training data for the VLA has to come from executions itself, yet many useful motions are produced by scripted primitives rather than by the policy. Within one execution, the orchestrator may alternate between VLA calls and scripted primitives. For example, the robot may approach a red block with scripted primitives and then call the VLA to lower and close the gripper. We record the commanded joint targets, gripper commands, observations, and robot states at each step in execution order, which yields a continuous action stream in the VLA's training format. The recorded steps can then become a demonstration labeled grasp the red block, even though part of it was produced by scripted primitives. Experience curation and policy improvement sec:learn From execution to labeled skills. The unified action stream contains interleaved VLA and scripted actions, which curates into skill demonstrations , where is a contiguous trajectory and is its language instruction, and collects the accepted ones in a training set . Experience curation evaluates segments independently of the episode outcome, a successful pickup can remain a training example even if the block is later dropped, and a successful episode does not make every segment valid. For each execution segment, a text judge uses the executed code, console output, and episode feedback to identify each segment's intended skill and assess its outcome. For VLA calls, it keeps the instruction passed to the policy. For scripted primitives, it groups consecutive calls into a motion-level skill, such as the scripted approach above, and a segment labeled pick up the red block must also include the lift. A video judge then checks sampled frames against the proposed instruction summarized from textual judge, and a segment enters only when the text judge accepts it and the video judge confirms success or clear partial progress. Figure~ fig:curation_examples shows a retained pickup and two rejected segments, including a grasp accepted by the text judge but rejected by the video judge. We therefore expect fine-tuning to improve most on skills that recur across episodes, such as grasping, which the failure analysis in Section~ sec:results examines. Appendix~ app:curation gives the segmentation rules and judge outputs. Deciding when to train. Training on a fixed schedule causes two potential problems: it trains on tasks the harness already solves, where an update can only add risk, and it trains before enough demonstrations have accumulated to support a useful update. therefore lets a language-model controller decide when to train given the deployment data so far. It reviews the curated demonstrations alongside recent performance, task memory, failures, and earlier attempts, and returns or with the desired improvement or the evidence still needed. We expect the controller to skip training on tasks the harness already solves, and to wait on the others until the curated demonstrations cover the skills that keep failing (Section~ sec:results ). A decision names up to four target skill instructions , which guide verification. Training itself uses all curated data collected so far. We fine-tune a candidate from the pretrained checkpoint with LoRA lora and the policy's original flow-matching objective. Deployment on the task pauses while trains. Afterward, stays in service as the baseline against which is evaluated. Appendices~ app:controller and~ app:train give the controller and training details. title: RoboRender: Robot-Oriented Video Generation for Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer
summary: Simulation enables large-scale, low-cost robot data generation, but policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world due to the sim-to-real visual discrepancies. Existing approaches often rely on intermediate representations, which can discard rich semantic information or require additional perception modules at deployment. We address this visual sim-to-real gap with RoboRender, a framework that converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos for policy learning. RoboRender trains a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB mask videos, preserving simulator geometry, robot motion, and action labels while synthesizing realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors. The generated RGB videos are paired with simulator-provided states and actions to train policies for zero-shot real-world deployment. On robot video test sets, our video model outperforms depth-conditioned video generation baselines in generation quality. In real-world experiments across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation tasks, policies trained on RoboRender-generated data achieve a 71% average success rate, outperforming raw simulation renderings and conventional visual domain randomization by approximately 7.1x and 3.6x, respectively. We further show that policy performance improves with more generated videos per simulation trajectory, increasing opening-task success by 65 percentage points. These results demonstrate that generative video rendering mitigates the visual sim-to-real gap for zero-shot policy transfer. Project website: https://robo-render.github.io/.

Introduction Simulation provides privileged state information, supports large-scale parallel data generation, and enables low-cost and automatic environment reset, making it effective for robot policy learning. However, transferring simulation-trained policies to the real world remains challenging due to the sim-to-real gap, which includes both dynamics and visual discrepancies. For vision-based manipulation, the visual gap is particularly limiting, as policies must act from observations whose appearance can differ substantially between rendered and real scenes. Existing approaches reduce this gap by reconstructing realistic digital twins~ kerbl20233d,torne2024robot,yu2025real2render2real,dan2025x , replacing RGB with depth or object states~ yuan2025hermes,lum2025crossing,kedia2026simtoolreal , or applying visual domain randomization~ he2025viral,deshpande2026molmob0t , but can be scene-specific, semantically lossy, require additional perception modules, or remain visually mismatched to real observations. Video generation models encode rich priors over real-world appearance, semantics, and temporal dynamics. In light of this, we propose ~( ), a framework that renders simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB-action data for zero-shot visual sim-to-real policy transfer. At its core is a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB masks. Depth preserves scene geometry and object motion across views, enabling multi-view-consistent generation; language controls appearance, materials, lighting, and background semantics; and robot masks preserve robot motion and support generation for unseen embodiments. Together, these conditions allow to synthesize rich, diverse and realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors while retaining simulator geometry and action labels, making it efficient for generating visually diverse and physically grounded data. Policies are then trained on the resulting photorealistic RGB-action trajectories and deployed zero-shot in the real world. We evaluate on five pick-and-place tasks, two opening tasks, and one mobile manipulation task. Compared with policies trained on raw simulator RGB and with visual domain randomization, policies trained on -generated data achieve \(7.1 \) and \(3.6 \) higher real-world success rates, respectively. We further show that generating multiple visually diverse videos from each simulated trajectory with different language prompts improves performance by up to 65 percentage points on opening tasks and 10 points on pick-and-place tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of in mitigating the visual sim-to-real gap for policy transfer. In summary, our contributions are: [leftmargin=*] We introduce , a framework that converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB demonstrations for zero-shot visual sim-to-real policy transfer. We develop a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on depth, language, and robot masks for grounded, controllable, and embodiment-aware video synthesis. Real-robot experiments indicate that enables significantly stronger zero-shot sim-to-real transfer than policies trained on raw simulation or conventional visual domain randomization, across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation tasks. Related Work Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer Simulation enables scalable robot data generation, but policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer due to dynamics and visual discrepancies. While dynamics gaps can be mitigated through system identification, dynamics randomization, or adaptation~ peng2018simtoreal,muratore2022randomizedsimulations , vision-based manipulation remains particularly sensitive to the visual gap between simulation and real observations. Prior work addresses this gap through three main strategies. Real2sim2real methods reconstruct photorealistic digital twins using neural rendering or 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d,torne2024robot,yu2025real2render2real,dan2025x , but require per-scene capture, calibration, or asset preparation, and may struggle with accurate interactive geometry~ torne2024robot,yu2025real2render2real . Geometry- or object-centric methods avoid sim-to-real RGB gap by using depth, point clouds, object poses, or object states~ yuan2025hermes,qin2023dexpoint,lum2025crossing,kedia2026simtoolreal , but can discard semantic appearance cues and require additional perception modules. Visual domain randomization trains policies on randomized textures, lighting, cameras, and backgrounds~ tobin2017domainrandomization,he2025viral,deshpande2026molmob0t , but often requires careful tuning and may remain far from real observations. In contrast, retains the simulator as the source of geometry, dynamics, and action labels, while using a generative video prior to render simulated depth trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos. This approach combines the scalability and physical grounding of simulation with the rich semantic and visual priors of video generation models. Video Generation for Robot Data Synthesis Video generation models have emerged as synthetic data engines for robot learning. DreamGen~ dreamgen2025 generates robot videos from language-conditioned world models, but language alone provides limited physical grounding, and actions must be inferred through inverse dynamics or latent action models. RoboCurate~ kim2026robocurate improves generation quality through simulator-replay filtering; instead starts from simulator rollouts with known actions, preserving grounded dynamics and action labels. Other works add grounding through robot motion or simulator-derived cues: AnchorDream~ ye2025anchordreamrepurposingvideodiffusion conditions on language and robot motion videos but lacks grounded robot-object interactions, while EmbodieDreamer~ wang2025embodiedreameradvancingreal2sim2realtransfer and CRAFT~ chen2026craftvideodiffusionbimanual translate simulated observations using object masks or Canny edges, which provide 2D structure but lack explicit 3D information and multi-view consistency. instead conditions on multi-view depth videos, preserving 3D scene structure for physically grounded, multi-view-consistent generation. RoboTransfer~ liu2026robotransfercontrollablegeometryconsistentvideo also generates multi-view-consistent videos using depth, surface normals, and appearance exemplars such as background and object images, but reliance on pre-collected photorealistic conditions limits flexibility. uses language to control textures, materials, lighting, and background semantics, enabling diverse synthesis without appearance exemplars. Compared with GigaWorld-0~ gigaworld2025 , which studies video-model-based robot data generation across appearance, view, human-to-robot, and sim-to-real transfer, focuses on visual sim-to-real transfer from simulated depth trajectories and supports distractor insertion and unseen-embodiment generalization through robot-mask conditioning. Overall, complements prior work with capabilities specialized for robot learning: physically grounded dynamics, simulator-provided action labels, multi-view consistency, distractor insertion, and embodiment generalization, helping mitigate the visual sim-to-real gap. Method Video Generation Model ssec:video_gen RGB videos for robot learning must be photorealistic, physically grounded, cross-view consistent, and action-aligned. Existing text-to-video models~ wan, cosmos provide strong visual priors but often fail to capture accurate causal interactions~ sora . Depth-conditioned variants~ wanfuncontrol, cosmostransfer improve geometric control, yet usually generate views independently and lack robot-specific manipulation priors. We therefore adapt a variant of Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B~ wan into a robot-oriented video generation model for robot visual sim-to-real transfer. As shown in Fig.~ fig:video_model_pipeline , the model is conditioned on depth videos for scene geometry and object motion, robot-mask RGB videos for embodiment and robot motion, language prompts for appearance and scene semantics, and any available previous frame for autoregressive long-horizon generation. During training, the depth and robot-mask videos are VAE-encoded and channel-wise concatenated with the noised latent of the ground-truth RGB video, then stacked across views into a unified multi-view latent. A diffusion transformer then denoises this latent to synthesize photorealistic, multi-view-consistent videos while preserving simulator-provided structure and action labels for policy learning. We fine-tune the model with LoRA at a global batch size of for K iterations on K real-world data. Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B is a bidirectional diffusion model with a fixed 81-frame window, whereas robot demonstrations are variable-length and often longer. For long-horizon synthesis, we condition the model on the previous frame (purple in~ ) during training~ skyreels, cosmos . At inference, it generates autoregressively, conditioning each chunk on the previous chunk's last frame. We randomly drop this condition during training, enabling first-chunk synthesis without a previous frame and autoregressive continuation with one. During training, we additionally mask large random depth patches in each view, so the model learns to synthesize plausible, prompt-guided appearance where depth is absent rather than merely reproducing the input geometry. At inference, this enables a controllable scene edit: by dropping depth over a target region across all views and prompting for a new object, the model inserts a distractor that remains consistent across views. Used as data augment

title: LACE-CRAFT: Robot Co-Design with Actor Inheritance and Blackboard Collaboration
comment: 16 pages including appendix. Project website: https://deemostech.github.io/lace-craft/
summary: Robot co-design couples morphology search with policy learning, yet training every new design from scratch discards acquired control experience. We present LACE-CRAFT, which compares continued learning on the current robot with policy adaptation to new morphology-reward pairs. LACE resumes the incumbent's full learning state and initializes compatible challengers with its actor parameters and observation statistics. A fixed task metric selects among both branches and the frozen incumbent. CRAFT coordinates Feedback, Morphology, Reward, and Integration roles through shared experimental records and behavioral replays to generate and cross-review paired proposals. A generative extension converts generated meshes into editable articulated models with configured joints, actuator interfaces, and consistently updated simulation assets. Across five locomotion benchmarks, mean scores over three evaluation seeds are 6.4-91.9% higher than D2C. Both methods train 30 new morphology-reward pairs over five rounds; LACE additionally uses four continuation training units. Five-task ablations examine policy inheritance and replay-derived feedback. A fabricated prototype demonstrates indoor walking and illustrates the geometry-to-hardware workflow.

Both LACE branches independently start from the same round-start state. Continuation restores the full training state, while adaptation inherits policy weights and input normalization and initializes other states anew. With equal additional environment-step budgets, both branches produce candidates scored by a fixed task metric and compared against the retained incumbent's stored score. The winner initializes the next round, and recorded results update the blackboard. Solid arrows carry states and candidates. Dashed arrows carry proposals, reviews and evidence. Five-task ablations examine policy inheritance and replay-derived feedback. A fabricated prototype demonstrates indoor walking and illustrates the geometry-to-hardware workflow. Introduction Robot morphology determines the dynamics a controller must exploit, while the training reward shapes the behavior it learns. Co-design therefore couples body design, reward design, and policy optimization~ luck2020data,fang2025robomore . Large language models (LLMs) provide flexible operators for this search: Eureka generates executable rewards from training feedback~ ma2024eureka , and Debate2Create (D2C) uses multi-agent debate to refine morphology--reward pairs before simulation-based evaluation~ qiu2026debatecreate . The search must also decide how to use the control experience acquired during candidate evaluation. In our D2C reproduction, design records guide subsequent proposals, while each new policy is trained from scratch. Prior co-design methods already reuse experience or transfer controller parameters across morphologies~ luck2020data,wang2018neural . We focus on how to select between further training the current design and adapting its policy to a new body and reward. A learned policy can provide a useful initialization after a design change, whereas value estimates and stored transitions depend on the dynamics and reward under which they were obtained. LACE--CRAFT addresses this decision through two competing training branches (Fig.~ fig:lace-craft-overview ). LACE initializes new designs with the incumbent's actor parameters and observation statistics, while resetting other learner components. A continuation branch resumes the incumbent's complete learning state on its unchanged morphology and reward. A fixed external task metric compares both branches with the frozen incumbent, allowing search to select either further learning on the current design or adaptation to a new design. CRAFT uses the resulting experimental evidence to guide subsequent proposals. Its shared blackboard links tested morphology--reward pairs to checkpoints, scores, and behavioral replays. Feedback proposes diagnoses and improvements; Morphology and Reward independently draft and then cross-review changes; Integration constructs complete paired candidates. New evaluations update the blackboard for the next round, preserving the association between each result and the robot that produced it. We further extend the morphology representation from parameterized benchmark bodies to generated meshes. Following the geometry-to-hardware approach of Text2Robot~ ringel2025text2robot , we process generated shapes into editable links, configured joints, and actuator interfaces. Geometry edits update the articulated model and its simulation assets while preserving LACE's policy interface. Alongside the five-task benchmark study, we document this processing workflow and a fabricated walking prototype. Our contributions are: Continuation-aware co-design. LACE compares full-state continuation of the incumbent with actor-initialized morphology--reward challengers under a fixed task metric, while retaining the incumbent as a selection option. Evidence-informed proposal generation. CRAFT coordinates four specialist roles through shared experiment records, diagnostic feedback, reciprocal morphology--reward review, and integration. A generative morphology extension. Editable links, configured joints, and actuator interfaces connect generated geometry to the co-design representation; processing records and a walking prototype illustrate its use. Related Work Morphology--control co-design Evolutionary co-design spans simulated creatures~ sims2023evolving and fabricated robots~ lipson2000automatic . Later approaches optimize body parameters or design distributions alongside controllers~ ha2019reinforcement,schaff2019jointly,luck2020data . RoboGrammar constrains structural search~ zhao2020robogrammar , while Transform2Act combines design and control~ yuan2022transformact . DERL couples evolution with lifetime learning~ gupta2021embodied . Morphological innovation protection allows controllers to adapt before new bodies face selection~ cheney2018scalable , highlighting the interaction between design changes and learning progress. Controller transfer Hardware conditioning~ chen2018hardware , graph policies~ wang2018nervenet , and shared actuator modules~ huang2020one support cross-morphology control. Amorpheus examines morphological graph biases~ kurin2021my , whereas MetaMorph and ModuMorph use Transformer-based conditioning~ gupta2022metamorph,xiong2023universal . N-LIMB jointly learns designs and a universal controller~ schaff2022n . Neural Graph Evolution inherits parental policies~ wang2018neural , and controller archives retrieve policies for related body plans~ le2022morpho . LACE compares compatible actor transfer with continued learning of the retained robot. Language-guided design Language models provide proxy reward signals~ kwon2023reward , synthesize dense reward programs~ xie2024text2reward , and translate instructions into control objectives~ pmlr-v229-yu23a . Code as Policies instead generates executable policy programs~ liang2023code . Eureka iteratively refines rewards using training feedback~ ma2024eureka . RoboMorph explores morphology~ qiu2026robomorph , while RoboMoRe and D2C jointly propose morphology--reward changes~ fang2025robomore,qiu2026debatecreate . Agent collaboration ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions~ yao2023react . Reflexion retains verbal feedback~ shinn2023reflexion , and Self-Refine revises outputs through self-critique~ madaan2023self . AutoGen supports configurable conversations~ wu2024autogen , MetaGPT structures role-specific artifacts~ hong2024metagpt , and CAMEL organizes role-conditioned cooperation~ li2023camel . Multiagent debate enables reciprocal critique~ pmlr-v235-du24e . CRAFT combines role specialization with a blackboard-style shared record~ hayes1985blackboard , grounding proposals in experimental evidence. Generated geometry and deployment CLAY generates static 3D assets~ zhang2024clay , BANG decomposes parts~ zhang2025bang , and Text2Robot connects generated geometry to fabrication~ ringel2025text2robot . RoboGen generates simulation tasks and training supervision~ pmlr-v235-wang24cc . Our extension exposes generated bodies as editable articulated morphologies. GPU simulation~ makoviychuk2021isaac and parallel locomotion training~ rudin2022learning accelerate policy optimization. Actuator modeling and robust training support physical quadruped deployment~ Tan-RSS-18,hwangbo2019learning , while DrEureka automates reward and domain-randomization proposals~ Ma-RSS-24 . title: Predicted Futures Are Not Enough: Learning Executable Goals for Robot Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://claire0730.github.io/executable-goals/ Code and models: https://github.com/Claire0730/executable-goals
summary: Generative world models provide rich predictions of how manipulation scenes may evolve toward task objectives, yet those futures do not directly expose the compact task variables required by control. When training supervises future prediction alone, terminal goal accuracy is not an explicit learning objective, even when geometric recovery is available. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout, a learned prediction-to-execution interface that makes the executable terminal goal an explicit output of a 3D trace world model. It combines object-centric pose prediction with translation grounded in observed depth to produce a compact goal in SE(3). A shared Pose-Native Executor consumes this fixed goal with online object-pose feedback for closed-loop control without rerunning the world model. Across five manipulation tasks, the pipeline achieves a mean success rate of 79.69%. Goal diagnostics directly measure terminal goal accuracy, while controlled translation perturbations characterize how execution degrades under goal error. Zero-shot deployment on a Franka arm achieves 73.33% success on nominal StackCube, 66.67% with distractors, and 75.00% on PickPlate with a target unseen during policy training. These results support treating the prediction-to-execution interface as an explicit learned component of world-model planning rather than incidental post-processing in the control pipeline itself. full_text: Predicted Futures Are Not Enough: Learning Executable Goals for Robot Manipulation Tzu-Yu Chuang , Ching-Hsiang Chang , Yi-Hsiu Lee , Yi-Ting Chen , Min Sun , YuanFu Yang National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University National Tsing Hua University Generative world models provide rich predictions of how manipulation scenes may evolve toward task objectives, yet those futures do not directly expose the compact task variables required by control. When training supervises future prediction alone, terminal goal accuracy is not an explicit learning objective, even when geometric recovery is available. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout, a learned prediction-to-execution interface that makes the executable terminal goal an explicit output of a 3D trace world model. It combines object-centric pose prediction with translation grounded in observed depth to produce a compact goal in . A shared Pose-Native Executor consumes this fixed goal with online object-pose feedback for closed-loop control without rerunning the world model. Across five manipulation tasks, the pipeline achieves a mean success rate of . Goal diagnostics directly measure terminal goal accuracy, while controlled translation perturbations characterize how execution degrades under goal error. Zero-shot deployment on a Franka arm achieves success on nominal StackCube, with distractors, and on PickPlate with a target unseen during policy training. These results support treating the prediction-to-execution interface as an explicit learned component of world-model planning rather than incidental post-processing in the control pipeline itself. Project page: Introduction sec:intro Generative world models support robot manipulation by predicting how scenes can evolve toward task objectives. Yet rich future predictions do not by themselves expose the compact task variables required by control. Video, point trajectories, and scene geometry require a prediction-to-execution interface. Figure~ fig:teaser frames this gap between prediction and execution. Geometric fitting can convert predicted motion into a terminal goal, but future prediction training does not optimize recovered goal accuracy. Prediction errors can still produce inaccurate control targets. Figure~ fig:motivation illustrates inconsistencies in generated futures. Our comparisons show that terminal goal errors remain after predictor training losses converge. Converged prediction objectives do not guarantee accurate goals for control. The design question is not whether a conversion procedure exists, but whether the task variables consumed by control are explicitly learned and exposed. We make terminal goal prediction part of the learning objective through object-centric prediction and observed geometry. The prediction-to-execution interface is learned as part of the model rather than left to incidental post-processing. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout, a learned interface between a 3D trace world model and a Pose-Native Executor. Figure~ fig:pipeline traces this interface from the world-model representation to closed-loop execution. An entity branch predicts terminal object pose, while a map branch grounds translation in observed depth to construct a compact executable goal in . A shared executor combines this goal with pose feedback to correct execution error without rerunning the world model. This separates episodic planning from continuous control while preserving the task variables required by control. We evaluate the interface through goal accuracy, manipulation success, and sensitivity to goal error. Across five tasks, our pipeline achieves higher mean success than both rigid readout pipelines under shared executor weights, with the largest gains on PickCube and StackCube. Goal error distributions characterize the targets delivered by the planner, while controlled translation perturbations measure the fixed executor's response to imposed goal error. Real robot trials extend evaluation to distractors and a target unseen during policy training. Our contributions are threefold: A Learned Goal Interface. Entity-Level Goal Readout makes control-relevant terminal variables explicit learning targets by combining object-centric pose prediction with depth-grounded spatial readout to expose executable goals from the world-model representation. Execution Trained for Imperfect Goals. A shared Pose-Native Executor is trained under measured planner goal errors using privileged teachers and online pose feedback, without rerunning the planner or receiving privileged guidance during execution. An Empirical Account of Goal Usability. Goal diagnostics across prediction representations, shared-executor evaluations, controlled perturbations, and real robot trials provide an empirical account of how goal quality translates into closed-loop execution. Related Work sec:related Generative World Models. World model planners represent future motion as generated observations, point trajectories, or scene geometry. Dream2Flow~ dream2flow2025 and TesserAct~ tesseract2025 recover motion or object goals from generated observations. ATM~ atm2024 and Track2Act~ track2act2024 predict 2D point trajectories, with Track2Act recovering geometric poses for control. TraceGen~ tracegen2026 and ~ mu0_2026 predict 3D traces, PointWorld~ pointworld2026 predicts action-conditioned 3D motion, and Structured-4D~ structure4d2026 forecasts scene geometry. Across these representations, our focus is how predicted futures become task goals consumed by control. From Predicted Futures to Executable Goals. Geometric readouts recover control targets through pose estimation or rigid registration, including Kabsch fitting with random sample consensus (RANSAC)~ kabsch1976 ,~ ransac1981 . Dream2Flow~ dream2flow2025 connects video generation to control through 3D object flow. Such interfaces determine how predicted futures are exposed to control, but future prediction supervision alone does not directly optimize terminal goal accuracy. Our readout makes the terminal goal an explicit learning target and evaluates the resulting goal quality in Table~ tab:goalerr . Goal-Conditioned Control. Diffusion Policy~ diffusionpolicy2024 , DP3~ dp3_2024 , and vision language action models map rich observations to actions. Our Pose-Native Executor instead receives one fixed pose goal in per episode. Dataset aggregation and privileged teacher methods motivate its distillation strategy~ dagger2011 ,~ chen2020learningbycheating ,~ lee2020legged . This keeps the prediction-to-execution handoff compact while separating goal quality from closed-loop execution. Method sec:method Overview and Problem Statement sec:overview The Entity-Level Goal Readout provides a learned prediction-to-execution interface between a 3D trace world model and goal-conditioned control, as shown in Fig.~ fig:pipeline . The system separates planning once per episode from closed-loop execution. Given a single RGB-D observation and task instruction, the world model predicts future scene motion. From the shared world model representation, the interface explicitly predicts one executable goal relative to the initial object frame. Execution runs independently at \,Hz. An online perception module estimates the current object pose in the world frame. A compact Pose-Native Executor maps the current pose, fixed executable goal, robot proprioception, and previous action to commands for seven arm joint increments and a gripper position target. The planner communicates a compact seven-parameter representation of the goal rather than the full predicted future. The planner and rigid baseline are described in Sec.~ sec:planner , the readout in Sec.~ sec:readout , and the executor and its training in Sec.~ sec:executor . Task success is evaluated separately from goal accuracy, as described in Sec.~ sec:exp_protocol . Trace Planner and Rigid Readout sec:planner Backbone. We build on TraceGen~ tracegen2026 , which predicts sparse 3D point trajectories rather than rendered future frames. DINOv3~ dinov3_2025 and SigLIP~ siglip2023 features are arranged on a spatial grid and augmented with depth, while a frozen T5~ t5_2020 encoder embeds the task instruction. A flow matching decoder based on CogVideoX~ cogvideox2024 predicts trajectories for query points over future steps. The visual and language encoders remain frozen while planner layers adapted to each task are fine tuned on manipulation demonstrations. Evaluation uses the checkpoints and readout routes specified in Sec.~ sec:exp_interface . Rigid Readout. The conventional rigid readout recovers a terminal transform from predicted object tracks using weighted Kabsch~ kabsch1976 inside RANSAC~ ransac1981 . This provides a strong geometric baseline, but the underlying predictor is not directly trained for terminal goal accuracy, and the task goal must be recoverable as a single rigid transform. Here denotes the number of stochastic trace predictions. For , traces are averaged before rigid fitting rather than selecting or averaging solved poses. Entity-Level Goal Readout sec:readout Figure~ fig:readout details the two branches that explicitly predict task relevant quantities from the shared planner representation. Entity Branch. An object mask derived from motion selects the relevant support on the vision token grid. A learned query performs masked attention pooling to produce a single entity token. Cross attention to the scene tokens enriched with geometry yields an object representation from which we predict the terminal object pose, whose rotation is used for executable goal composition. Keyframe poses, contact point, and contact normal are predicted only as auxiliary supervision and are not passed to the executor. Map Branch. Terminal position is grounded directly in observed scene geometry. From the same spatial geometry tokens, a linear head predicts logits over a goal map. After softmax and upsampling, the distribution is masked by valid observed depth and reduced to an image centroid weighted by depth. Unprojection through the RGB-D camera model yields a camera frame point. The calibrated camera to world transform maps it to the world position . This readout also supports targets defined by regions that do not correspond to a unique rigid transform. Goal Composition. Eq.~ combines the map position with the entity rotation, both expressed in the world frame, to form the terminal object pose. The interface expresses this pose relative to the initial object frame as . Here maps initial object coordinates to world coordinates. Training Objective. The readout is trained jointly with the trace objective in Eq.~ . where supervises terminal pose and auxiliary interaction quantities and supervises the spatial goal distribution. These terms directly supervise executable goal prediction rather than relying on goals recovered from future traces after prediction. Executor and Distillation sec:executor The readout runs once at episode start. The executor reconstructs the fixed world goal as and compares it with the online world pose . Both use the same world frame. The goal remains fixed while pose feedback updates the current state, correcting execution without rerunning the world model. Online Perception. An initial object mask supplies tracking points in RGB-D observations. Frozen CoTracker3~ cotracker3_2025 maintains their image correspondences. Depth unprojection followed by Kabsch recovers , which is updated while the executable goal remains fixed. Policy. The compact 0.8M-parameter transformer receives the current object pose, executable goal, joint positions and velocities, tool center point pose, and previous action. Its eight dimensional output comprises seven arm joint increments and a gripper position target at \,Hz. The same student policy is used across all five tasks. Current pose feedback supports correction during execution, while the fixed goal decouples control updates from planner inference. Distillation. We use dataset

title: DIVA: Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically feed dense visual patch tokens into a language-action backbone, preserving scene context but offering no explicit mechanism to regulate how strongly different visual tokens influence policy computation. We introduce DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module with an anchor-then-attenuate design. DIVA combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors, then applies them in two complementary spaces: it reweights projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuates low-relevance visual states within the backbone. DIVA preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision. On LIBERO, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success and raises its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments further show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations, supporting the robustness of intent-aware visual attenuation beyond simulation.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies feed dense visual patch tokens to a language-action backbone, preserving scene context without explicitly regulating each token's influence on policy computation. We introduce DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module with an anchor-then-attenuate design. DIVA combines task intent with local visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors and applies them in two complementary spaces: reweighting projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuating low-relevance visual states within the backbone. DIVA preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision. On LIBERO, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6 to 98.0 average success and raises its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments further show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations, supporting the robustness of intent-aware visual attenuation beyond simulation. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising foundation for language-conditioned robot manipulation openx2024rtx,li2023roboflamingo . By adapting large vision-language backbones for robot action prediction, recent models can map visual observations and natural-language instructions to actions across diverse tasks zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,black2024pi0 . A common design is to encode one or more camera views into dense visual patch tokens, project them into a language-action backbone, and let the backbone transform visual-language representations into robot actions liu2024rdt,qu2025spatialvla . This dense-token interface preserves rich scene information, but offers no explicit mechanism for regulating how strongly each visual token contributes to policy computation. Consequently, task-irrelevant objects may exert undue influence on the policy and impair action prediction. This raises a central question: how can a VLA policy attenuate weakly relevant visual evidence while preserving the scene context needed for reliable manipulation? Soft attenuation offers a non-destructive way to meet this objective. Rather than removing weakly relevant tokens, it reduces their contribution while keeping the complete visual sequence available to the policy. This distinction matters because evidence peripheral to the current instruction may still support spatial reasoning, obstacle awareness, or safe interaction. The goal is therefore not a binary partition of the scene, but a graded allocation of influence across visual tokens. Soft attenuation provides the general strategy, but answering this question in practice requires resolving two challenges. The first is how to estimate visual-token relevance. High-level task intent indicates what the policy should seek, but remains spatially ambiguous. Low-level visual evidence identifies local structures such as handles, contact regions, object boundaries, and free space, but may emphasize salient yet task-irrelevant content. Human gaze is jointly guided by top-down task intent and bottom-up visual evidence wolfe1994guided,corbetta2002control . Inspired by this process, we combine high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to construct patch-wise relevance anchors. The second is where attenuation should act once the anchors are established. Input space provides a natural starting point: projected visual tokens retain explicit patch correspondence, allowing the anchors to set the initial strength of each token before backbone processing. However, this one-time adjustment may be diluted by subsequent attention, feed-forward transformations, and residual updates. Deeper in the backbone, visual hidden states lie closer to action computation, making them a natural place to sustain attenuation. These complementary roles motivate a dual-space design: input-space attenuation initializes patch-aligned representation strength, while latent-space attenuation maintains it throughout policy computation. These two answers lead directly to DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module for VLA policies. DIVA follows an anchor-then-attenuate design. It first combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors. It then applies the same anchors in both input and latent spaces, reweighting projected visual tokens before backbone entry and attenuating low-relevance visual hidden states across layers. This design preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding labels. We instantiate DIVA on OpenVLA-OFT and evaluate it on LIBERO, zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and real-world manipulation tasks kim2025oft,liu2023libero,fei2025liberoplus . DIVA improves the baseline across these settings, while controlled ablations validate the complementary roles of high- and low-level evidence in anchoring and of input- and latent-space attenuation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify a key limitation of dense-token VLA policies: they lack an explicit mechanism to control the influence of visual tokens according to task relevance. We introduce DIVA, an anchor-then-attenuate framework that combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to construct patch-wise relevance anchors and applies them in both input and latent spaces. We evaluate DIVA on LIBERO, zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent gains under standard and perturbed conditions. Controlled ablations verify the contributions of Grounded Text Pooling, intent-aware relevance anchoring, and dual-space attenuation. Related Work Explicit grounding and input-side localization. Explicit visual grounding supplies spatial cues before action prediction, commonly through external detectors, segmenters, masks, boxes, cropped regions, or visual prompts zheng2024tracevla . RoboGround uses grounding masks as intermediate observations huang2025roboground , while other grounding-oriented VLAs generate object boxes, end-effector states, or grasp cues before predicting actions zawalski2024ecot,deng2025graspvla . Such cues are interpretable and can reduce ambiguity in object-centric manipulation. However, they rely on external models, additional supervision, or generated spatial targets, and their effectiveness depends on localization quality. Incorrect masks or overly narrow crops may discard scene context needed for spatial reasoning and collision avoidance. DIVA avoids external grounding targets and derives relevance anchors from the policy's own language and visual representations. Implicit grounding and attention-side visual modulation. Related approaches guide visual focus through attention mechanisms or auxiliary supervision. ReconVLA reconstructs gaze regions for manipulated objects song2025reconvla , gaze-regularized VLAs align internal attention with gaze-derived distributions pani2026gazereg , and AVA-VLA and FocusVLA modulate attention using recurrent states or task-conditioned visual signals xiao2025avavla,zhang2026focusvla . Their control acts locally through attention and may be reshaped by subsequent feed-forward and residual updates, while gaze-supervised variants require additional annotations. In contrast, DIVA directly regulates representation strength by using patch-wise relevance anchors to reweight projected visual tokens before backbone entry and attenuate the corresponding visual hidden states across layers, thereby sustaining attenuation throughout policy computation. Visual token pruning and selection. Visual token pruning reduces redundancy by retaining only selected tokens ryoo2021tokenlearner . LightVLA uses differentiable pruning for efficient inference jiang2025lightvla , DTP removes distracting image tokens li2026dtp , and ADP and related sparsification methods introduce action-aware or text-guided selection inside VLA backbones pei2025adp,wang2026etavla . Although efficient, hard keep-or-remove decisions may discard weakly salient regions that still encode spatial layout, object relations, obstacles, or target context. DIVA therefore takes a non-destructive alternative: it preserves the full visual sequence and softly attenuates low-relevance representations rather than deleting them. Method sec:method Overview DIVA is designed to control the strength of visual evidence in a token-based vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Given an instruction and visual observations, the base policy encodes images into projected visual tokens and feeds them, together with instruction tokens, into a language-action backbone. Let denote the projected visual tokens and denote the instruction-token embeddings. DIVA operates on the projected visual-token sequence and preserves its token layout throughout the policy. Following its anchor-then-attenuate design, DIVA estimates each patch-wise relevance anchor from task intent and local visual evidence, reweights projected visual tokens before backbone entry, and reuses the anchors to attenuate low-relevance hidden states across layers. Grounded Text Pooling Intent-aware relevance anchoring requires a task representation that tells the policy what to seek in the current observation. Instruction tokens are heterogeneous: object names, target descriptions, and relation words specify the executable intent, whereas generic function words carry little visual specificity. Uniform mean pooling ignores this distinction and, because it is independent of the observation, cannot determine which instruction concepts are visually instantiated in the current scene. We therefore introduce Grounded Text Pooling (GTP), which uses localized visual evidence to determine how instruction tokens contribute to a compact, observation-conditioned representation of task intent. Given instruction-token embeddings and projected visual tokens , we first measure the compatibility between every instruction token and visual patch: For each instruction token , the vector forms a response map over visual patches. A visually instantiated concept need not match the image globally; instead, it should receive distinctive support from a subset of patches depicting its referent, target, or relation. Generic function words carry little task-specific semantics. Treating all instruction tokens equally would therefore dilute the compact task summary needed for relevance anchoring. We therefore assess each instruction token by its support from localized visual patches rather than by global image-level compatibility yao2021filip,mukhoti2023pacl . To summarize localized visual support, we compute a soft local response: where controls the sharpness of visual selection. The term emphasizes the patches most strongly aligned with instruction token . However, a high local response alone does not imply that a token provides discriminative visual evidence. A token that is broadly compatible with the entire image may also obtain a large response, even though it does not identify any particular part of the scene. We therefore contrast the soft local response with a uniform visual baseline: The score measures the gain from localized visual selection over global image-level compatibility. Diffuse responses produce little gain, whereas tokens supported by a distinctive subset of patches receive larger scores. Thus, captures whether an instruction token is selectively grounded in the current observation, rather than merely compatible with it overall. We then convert these grounded scores into pooling weights: where controls the sharpness of text-token pooling. The resulting vector emphasizes instruction semantics with localized, discriminative support in the current scene and serves as the high-level task-intent representation for relevance anchoring. Intent-Aware Visual Relevance Anchoring Intent-aware anchoring follows human goal-directed vision, where gaze combines top-down task intent with bottom-up visual evidence wolfe1994guided,corbetta2002control

full_text: IVG-UAV: An Intelligent Voice-Guided UAV System for Autonomous Ripe Fruit Harvesting with Vision-Based Classification and Adaptive Path Planning\\ In tropical regions, their agricultural sectors remain highly dependent on manual labor for fruit harvesting. On large-scale farms, this dependency often results in significant labor cost and logistic complexities. This project presents the development and simulation of a voice-controlled Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) system designed to automate harvesting tasks in extensive plantations. The proposed system integrates speech recognition using Whisper radford2023robust and LLM, computer vision–based ripeness classification, and adaptive path planning within a unified framework. The entire system is modeled and validated in a Gazebo simulation environment, allowing performance evaluation under controlled agricultural scenarios. Introduction In tropical nations, their agricultural sectors remain highly dependent on manual labor for fruit harvesting. On large-scale farms, this dependency often results in significant labor cost and logistic complexities. With recent developments, robots have been introduced to reduce this burden as well as improve the productivity. A diversity of harvesting robots have been significantly investigated ranging from ground-based mobile manipulators to aerial platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). These systems are mostly equipped with vision-assisted technologies, enabling fruit detection, ripeness classification, and localization through advanced computer vision and deep learning algorithms. However, the majority of existing robots depends on fully automated programming paradigms, where robots autonomously navigate and search for ripe fruits based solely on pre-defined algorithms and perception models. This leads to the lack of real-time human interaction and adaptability, particularly during the fruit-searching and decision-making stages. This functionality allows the robot to adapt its flight trajectory according to user instructions. Additionally, it enables the UAV to handle edge cases through human intervention. This project proposes the integration of voice-guided interaction into the robotic system. This human-in-the-loop approach allows adaptive decision-making during the harvesting process, which enhances operational flexibility. To address the existing challenges, this work introduces IVG-UAV, a unified voice-guided UAV harvesting pipeline that integrates speech recognition, LLM-based command interpretation, vision-based fruit detection using YOLOv8 and RGB-D sensing, and adaptive path planning for autonomous navigation in orchard environments. Figure 1 illustrates the overall functionality of the proposed voice-guided interactive harvesting system. The framework integrates aerial perception, obstacle-aware navigation, adaptive task planning, and human-in-the-loop voice interaction into a unified architecture for intelligent fruit harvesting. Initially, the UAV performs journey exploration of the orchard and scans fixed trees using vision system. Robot performs a thorough scan by applying row-following strategy, that ensures all the trees in the farm are scanned. Unlike fully autonomous harvesting systems, the proposed framework enables real-time human guidance through voice commands. The operator can issue high-level instructions such as “Harvest all the ripe fruits” or “Take ripe fruits from three trees.” These commands are processed by a speech recognition module and translated into structured task constraints that influence the target selection and planning modules. During visiting a tree, a drone system can use vision perception to classify the ripe fruits and can actually detach them from the tree. In a flight journey, UAV system can avoid obstacles to find a target tree and using RRT* karaman2011sampling algorithm to find the shortest path that leads to the next target tree. Related works Vision-assisted Avocado Harvesting UAV In order to harvest avocados, this paper developed a vision-assisted robotic harvesting system which utilizes an aerial robot with a bimanual manipulation mechanism. The device integrates a dual-arm UAV manipulator with a gripper arm and a fixer arm with computer vision for avocado detection and posture estimation. A motion planner uses the location and orientation of the avocados determined by the visual perception module to direct the robotic arms. The gripper arm rotates to effectively separate the avocado while the fixer arm holds the fruit stem in place during harvesting. The system can recognize and pick avocados on its own in outdoor settings, according to experimental data, demonstrating the promise of aerial robotic manipulation for agricultural automation. alaaudeen2024intelligent Deep learning–based computer vision with robotic manipulation This work suggested an intelligent robotic harvesting system that combines robotic manipulation and deep learning-based computer vision for automated fruit picking. In order to increase harvesting efficiency, the system focuses on forecasting the best fruit gripping locations. In order to accomplish this, the authors created an image processing pipeline based on deep learning that recognizes apples in pictures and determines the proper gripping area for robotic picking. For fruit recognition, a lightweight one-step object detection network is used, allowing the system to instantly recognize fruits from visual input. The robotic manipulator is then guided by the detected fruit attributes to identify appropriate grabbing places and carry out the harvesting process. liu2024vision Both studies focus on automating fruit harvesting using computer vision–based perception and robotic manipulation techniques. In particular, they utilize visual sensing to detect fruits, estimate their position, and guide robotic systems to perform harvesting tasks. Although both strategies significantly rely on computer vision technology, their system architectures are different: the latter focuses on vision-based grasp prediction utilizing lightweight deep learning models for robotic manipulators, whereas the former incorporates aerial robotics with bi-manual manipulation. Despite these differences, both works share similar limitations. The systems lack natural human–robot interaction mechanisms, such as voice-guided instructions, which could allow users to intuitively guide or supervise the harvesting process. This limitation reduces system usability in practical agricultural environments where human workers may need to interact with robotic systems dynamically. Methodology Motivated by the limitations of existing systems, the author proposes a unified framework that combines voice-guided commands with existing robotic harvesting technologies. This approach introduces human-in-the-loop interaction, enabling users to provide intuitive voice instructions and improving the overall efficiency of robotic harvesting systems. The solution contains two phases: exploration and mission execution. During the exploration phase, the UAV uses coverage-based navigation to look over the orchard and make a map of the area by finding the locations of the trees. In the next phase of the mission, the system uses the map it created to plan the best ways to harvest and detect the ripe fruits. Exploration Phase In the exploration phase, the UAV utilizes an RGB-D camera to observe the surrounding environment and detect trees within the orchard. The RGB-D sensor continuously captures both color and depth information, where the depth measurements are integrated into an OctoMap hornung13auro framework to generate a probabilistic voxel-based 3D map of the orchard. Each voxel stores occupancy information, allowing the system to model tree trunks in a consistent spatial representation. As it moves around the orchard, the UAV gradually updates the OctoMap row by row and tree by tree. The produced voxel map allows for dependable spatial knowledge from a variety of perspectives while maintaining the environment's geometric integrity. The system determines each tree's spatial location in the global coordinate frame based on the occupied voxel clusters that correspond to tree structures. Each detected tree 's spatial position is represented by a 3D coordinate \[ T_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i), \] where \(x_i\), \(y_i\), and \(z_i\) denote the spatial coordinates of the \(i\)-th tree center within the orchard map. Mission execution phase After obtaining the orchard map from the exploration phase, the system enters the mission execution state. The execution pipeline is divided into three major components: (1) command generation and task planning, (2) navigation module, and (3) detection module. Command generation and task planning The command generation and task planning module converts user instructions into structured executable UAV actions. In general, the system receives voice commands from the human operator and utilizes the Whisper radford2023robust speech recognition model to convert the spoken instructions into text-based commands. The generated textual input is subsequently processed by a multi-layer large language model (LLM) framework that integrates both Phi-3.3B abdin2024phi3technicalreporthighly and Gemini 2.5 Flash models. By incorporating current mission context and domain-specific knowledge, the framework performs semantic verification, edge-case analysis, and hierarchical task planning to generate a structured UAV action plan for autonomous mission execution. As illustrated in Figure fig:llm , the Edge Case layer is implemented using the Phi-3.3B model, which utilizes current mission context and domain-specific knowledge to identify ambiguous instructions, invalid targets, and handle unclear situations such as commands containing relative descriptions including “furthest”, “nearest” or “all”. The processed command is then forwarded to the Verification layer, which is also implemented using the Phi-3.3B model. In this step, the framework performs validation to recognize mismatches between the user command and the current mission context, including unavailable targets, inconsistent task sequences, invalid navigation requests, or conflicts with environmental constraints. After successful verification, the validated command is transmitted to the Action Planning layer, implemented using Gemini 2.5 Flash, which performs hierarchical task decomposition and converts the high-level mission objective into a structured sequence of executable UAV actions, including takeoff, navigation, harvesting, and landing operations. An example output generated by the planner is shown below: takeoff uav1 navigate uav1 to tree 1 harvest uav1 tree 1 navigate uav1 to tree 2 harvest uav1 tree 2 Following that, the created action plan is provided to the Dispatcher module, which translates the high-level task sequence into executable UAV control commands and coordinates the execution flow of navigation, perception, and harvesting activities during autonomous mission execution. Navigation module The navigation module is in charge of allowing the UAV to navigate autonomously around the orchard area. The resulting map incorporates spatial information about vacant space, inhabited regions, and surrounding impediments including tree trunks, branches, and canopy structures. Based on this environmental representation, the RRT* algorithm is utilized for global path planning. The planner incrementally explores the search space to generate an optimized collision-free trajectory from the current UAV position to the target tree location. During trajectory generation, collision checking is continuously performed to ensure that the generated path satisfies safety constraints and avoids environmental obstacles. Once a feasible trajectory is generated, the UAV autonomously follows the planned waypoints to reach the target tree : \[ T_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i), \]. Detection module After reaching the targe

title: TempoBridge: Language-Guided Tempo Control for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are effective at understanding what task to perform, but provide limited control over how it should be executed, such as moving quickly or slowly. We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that uses frozen VLA representations to modulate actions according to tempo cues in the instruction at each task phase, without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning. TempoBridge extracts tempo cues from contextual VLM representations, aligns them with task progress through a causal phase router, and modulates nominal motion commands during execution. Across LIBERO tasks, TempoBridge improves Tempo Success Rate from 52.6% to 89.7% under canonical tempo instructions while retaining high task success. It also preserves near-baseline performance when no tempo cue is present and generalizes to unseen tempo expressions without additional training. Experiments on a physical robot further demonstrate language-conditioned tempo modulation in real-world manipulation.
