TempoBridge reads tempo cues from the internal representations of a frozen VLA policy and aligns them with task progress to adjust execution speed according to the instruction. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are effective at understanding what task to perform, but provide limited control over how it should be executed, such as moving quickly or slowly. We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that uses frozen VLA representations to modulate actions according to tempo cues in the instruction at each task phase, without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning. TempoBridge extracts tempo cues from contextual VLM representations, aligns them with task progress through a causal phase router, and modulates nominal motion commands during execution. Across LIBERO tasks, TempoBridge improves Tempo Success Rate from 52.6 to 89.7 under canonical tempo instructions while retaining high task success. It also preserves near-baseline performance when no tempo cue is present and generalizes to unseen tempo expressions without additional training. Experiments on a physical robot further demonstrate language-conditioned tempo modulation in real-world manipulation. Project page: INTRODUCTION sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling a single policy to execute diverse tasks from natural-language instructions zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 . Existing VLAs increasingly understand what to do, but provide limited control over how to execute it jing2026tempovla,haon2025mechanistic . In many practical settings, however, execution manner is an important part of the user's intent shao2025langwbc,belkhale2024rth . For example, a robot may be asked to move quickly for efficiency or slowly for deliberate execution. These preferences may also vary as a task progresses, as in ``quickly pick up the object, then slowly place it on the target.'' In this work, we study this capability as language-conditioned tempo control. A straightforward approach is to train a policy on trajectories associating tempo instructions with execution speeds. However, collecting demonstrations at different speeds is costly and difficult to scale across tasks, objects, and environments khazatsky2024droid,o2024open,walke2023bridgedata . Temporal augmentation can reduce the cost of collecting additional demonstrations jing2026tempovla , but incorporating the augmented trajectories into the policy still requires computationally expensive fine-tuning kim2025fine . Pretrained VLA representations may already encode semantic distinctions associated with manner expressions such as quickly and slowly, and prior work has shown that internal features related to such concepts can be identified and manipulated to influence VLA behavior haon2025mechanistic . This raises the possibility of using semantic tempo information available in the frozen representation as an interface for execution control, rather than learning tempo interpretation entirely from newly collected robot trajectories. The key challenge is to connect these semantic tempo cues to an explicit execution-time control mechanism while accounting for task progress. We therefore ask: Can semantic tempo cues from a frozen VLA be connected to execution-time motion modulation, enabling language-conditioned tempo control without tempo-specific robot demonstrations or policy fine-tuning? To address this question, we introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that reads semantic tempo information from a frozen VLA’s internal language representations and connects it to phase-aware motion modulation. TempoBridge takes a frozen policy black2025pi05 as its base policy and uses a prototype-based tempo readout to extract a compact tempo sequence from the instruction. When the requested tempo varies within a task, a causal phase router aligns this sequence with task progress using visual features reused from the policy and robot-state history. The selected tempo then modulates the nominal motion commands during closed-loop execution. The base VLA continues to generate the nominal task actions, while TempoBridge modulates their execution according to the requested tempo and estimated task phase. This design keeps the pretrained policy fixed while separating tempo interpretation and phase estimation from nominal action generation. The tempo readout is constructed from text examples, whereas the phase router is trained on existing task demonstrations annotated with phase-transition intervals, without tempo labels. Consequently, TempoBridge requires neither tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations nor tempo-specific fine-tuning of the base policy. When no tempo cue is detected, the readout returns NORMAL and the nominal actions remain unchanged. Because the readout operates on contextual VLM representations, the same fixed readout can also be applied to previously unseen tempo expressions without retraining. We evaluate TempoBridge on 40 manipulation tasks across the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites of LIBERO liu2023libero . TempoBridge raises Tempo Success Rate from 52.6 to 89.7 under canonical quickly/slowly instructions, while preserving near-baseline performance without tempo cues and improving tempo compliance for unseen expressions. Real-robot experiments further validate language-conditioned tempo modulation. Our main contributions are: We formulate language-conditioned tempo control for frozen VLAs and investigate whether semantic tempo cues in their internal representations can serve as an interface for execution-time motion modulation, without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning. We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that combines prototype-based tempo readout, causal phase routing, and execution-time action modulation while keeping the entire base policy frozen. We evaluate physical tempo compliance, task competence under original instructions, and transfer to unseen tempo expressions across 40 LIBERO tasks, and further validate TempoBridge in real-world manipulation experiments with a physical robot. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transfer semantic and world knowledge from pretrained vision-language models into robotic control. RT-2 zitkovich2023rt2 established this paradigm by co-finetuning web-scale VLMs with robot trajectories in a shared token space, and subsequent generalist policies scaled language-conditioned manipulation across heterogeneous embodiments ghosh2024octo, kim2024openvla or coupled pretrained representations with continuous action experts for dexterous, long-horizon execution black2025pi0, black2025pi05 . Across these paradigms, however, language specifies what should be achieved, while how an action is executed remains implicit in the demonstration distribution. Temporal characteristics such as speed or caution, therefore, do not surface as explicit control variables, even though the corresponding linguistic concepts are plausibly already represented in the pretrained backbone. Controlling Execution in Pretrained VLAs Approaches to controlling how a policy executes differ mainly in what part of the system they modify, and therefore in what supervision they require. One line modifies data and weights. Language motions as an intermediate action representation, counterfactual relabeling, and semantically aligned action tokenizers belkhale2024rth, glossop2025cast, wenjie2026lost all learn how a linguistic modifier maps to physical execution from robot trajectories. TempoVLA jing2026tempovla conditions on an explicit speed scalar and re-times demonstrations by temporal augmentation, with a VLM scheduler dispatching per-chunk speeds at deployment. This still requires retraining the policy, and tempo arrives as a numeric input from an external module. A second line intervenes on a frozen policy's internal activations, differing in how the directions are identified haon2025mechanistic, buurmeijer2026observing, khan2025sparse and how the intervention is regulated once found babu2026ctrlsteer, khayatan2026dimas . H\"aon et al. haon2025mechanistic show that linguistic concepts such as slow survive VLA training in the backbone and remain causally linked to end-effector motion, though they identify features heuristically by token similarity and steer by overriding their activations with a selected coefficient rather than a physically interpretable execution variable. Buurmeijer et al. buurmeijer2026observing make such intervention systematic by training linear observers for robot states and actions and computing the minimal representation-space edit that places an observed feature inside a desired interval. In both cases, the target is an externally specified number rather than read from language, and identifying the directions requires either manual inspection or labeled robot data. CTRL-STEER babu2026ctrlsteer instead regulates the magnitude of the intervention online with a feedback controller, although the target concept is still supplied externally and the controller is fitted per task. In contrast, TempoBridge reads tempo cues from the language instruction through frozen VLA representations and connects them to phase-aware motion modulation, without tempo-conditioned demonstrations or tempo-specific VLA fine-tuning. Method Overview and Problem Formulation We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that interprets language-specified tempo using contextual representations from a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy and connects it to phase-aware motion modulation. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:figure2 , TempoBridge uses a frozen policy~ black2025pi05 as its base policy, consisting of a PaliGemma~ beyer2024paligemma VLM backbone and an action expert. We use tempo to denote the qualitative execution pace associated with a task event. At each replanning step, the base policy produces a nominal action chunk from the current observation and language instruction, while all of its parameters remain fixed. TempoBridge consists of three components: a prototype-based tempo readout, a causal phase router, and tempo-conditioned action modulation. The readout processes the instruction once and extracts a cached tempo sequence , where \[ = \ & [ ],\, [ ],\, [ ],\\ & [ , ],\, [ , ] \ . \] A single-entry sequence specifies one tempo throughout execution. A two-entry sequence specifies the requested tempo order over two successive task events, for which we assume a single forward transition between events. During closed-loop execution, the causal phase router tracks task progress and selects the active entry of the cached tempo sequence. The corresponding tempo is then used to modulate the nominal action chunk. For a single-entry sequence, the router is bypassed and the same tempo is applied throughout the rollout. The readout and router use different representations from the same frozen VLM backbone. The readout performs a language-only forward pass once per instruction, whereas the router reuses visual features from the multimodal policy forward pass at every replan. Prototype construction uses text instructions, while router training uses existing task trajectories with phase-transition annotations. Neither component requires tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or fine-tuning of the base VLA, and no external language model is used. Prototype-Based Tempo Readout Contextual Features and Tempo Prototypes For each instruction, we perform a language-only forward pass through the PaliGemma VLM backbone within the frozen policy. This pass uses the same VLM parameters as the multimodal policy pass but is executed only once per instruction. Valid language tokens attend bidirect

title: TMT: Runtime Backdoor Detection for Vision-Language-Action Policies on Unseen Tasks
summary: Backdoored vision-language-action (VLA) policies can preserve benign task performance while producing malicious actions when a trigger appears. Detecting such activation is difficult because malicious behavior can comprise individually plausible actions, while unfamiliar tasks introduce legitimate changes in observations and behavior. We introduce TMT, a runtime backdoor detector based on Token Manifold and latent Transition modeling. Trained on benign rollouts, its two branches assess input-token structure and prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. A suspicious rollout identified by the token manifold branch, once confirmed through latent deviations, guides transition selection for subsequent monitoring. We further explore policy purification through self-distillation: a frozen copy of the backdoored policy provides benign-input actions to supervise a student on paired benign and triggered observations, without requiring a separate clean reference policy. For evaluation, we adapt traditional backdoor detectors and repurpose anomaly and failure detection methods as VLA backdoor detectors. In a post-hoc comparison with ten baselines, TMT achieves state-of-the-art backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks. Our project page is available at https://zzr42.github.io/tmt/.

In a post-hoc comparison with ten baselines, TMT achieves state-of-the-art backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks. Our project page is available at . Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions~ kim2025fine,wang2026vla,intelligence2025pi_ . A compromised policy can retain its performance on benign inputs while changing its behavior when a trigger appears. Recent attacks demonstrate that backdoor activation can disrupt task execution, redirect the robot toward an attacker-specified goal, or induce an undesired low-level action~ zhou2026badvla,zhou2025goal,xu2025dropvla . For example, backdoor activation could cause a robot to suddenly drop a knife it is holding, posing a physical safety risk. This coupling between backdoor activation and physical execution motivates runtime backdoor detection in VLA policies. Existing inference-time backdoor detectors for classifiers assess suspicious inputs by examining how class predictions respond to input perturbations~ gao2019strip,liu2023detecting . VLA policies, however, generate task-conditioned control actions, and backdoor activation need not produce a fixed target output across states and timesteps. We consider four requirements for runtime backdoor detection in this setting. ~The detector must learn from benign rollouts without prior knowledge of the trigger pattern or access to the VLA policy's original training process. ~The detector must distinguish backdoor-induced behavior from benign execution even when both involve the same actions. This distinction depends on which goal the resulting sequence serves. ~The detector must generalize to unseen tasks without mistaking legitimate changes in observations and behavior for backdoor activation. ~The detector must identify backdoor activation with minimal delay after trigger onset. To address these challenges, we introduce TMT, an inference-time backdoor detector that combines Token Manifold and latent Transition modeling using internal representations of the deployed VLA policy (Figure~ fig:tmt-framework ). TMT examines both the structure of input-token representations and how these representations evolve across backbone layers. Our t-SNE visualizations show that the input-token representations of triggered queries are shifted relative to those of benign queries in the projected space, while the two groups still overlap (Figure~ fig:token-motivation ). This motivates examining layer-wise transitions alongside token structure. Trained on benign rollouts, the token manifold branch assesses token structure conditioned on the preceding policy query, while the latent transition branch scores prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. Both branches evaluate each policy query, and TMT raises an alarm when either score exceeds its calibrated threshold. In this paper, we focus on detecting backdoor activation on unseen manipulation tasks, with TMT fitted using benign rollouts from seen tasks. For comparison, we adapt traditional backdoor detectors~ gao2019strip,liu2023detecting,hou2025dede,hu2026dup and repurpose anomaly and failure detection methods~ ruff2018deep,burda2018exploration,he2024rediffuser,xu2025faildetect,romer2026failure for detecting backdoor activation (see Appendix~ sec:alternative-detection ). Detectors are fitted using benign rollouts from three LIBERO-10 tasks~ liu2023libero and evaluated on the remaining tasks under BadVLA~ zhou2026badvla , GoBA~ zhou2025goal , and DropVLA~ xu2025dropvla . In the post-hoc comparison, TMT achieves the highest or joint-highest trigger detection rates (TDRs) of , , and , respectively, with observed false-rejection rates (FRRs) of , , and . Branch ablations show that, for GoBA and DropVLA, the token manifold branch provides broader detection coverage on tasks represented during fitting, whereas the latent transition branch provides broader coverage on unseen tasks. We further examine detection in real-world robot execution, and observe that TMT achieves a TDR of with an observed FRR of . Beyond detection, we explore policy purification through self-distillation without a separate clean reference policy. A frozen copy of the backdoored policy serves as the teacher, and the student is initialized from the same checkpoint. We execute the teacher's benign-input actions in both benign and triggered environments, collecting paired observations under a shared action history. The student is trained to reproduce each benign-input action from both observations. Results show that original-task success rates under triggered inputs increase to -- , while benign-input success rates change by at most . Our contributions are threefold: We introduce TMT, an inference-time VLA backdoor detector that combines input-token structure and latent dynamics learned from benign rollouts. We propose policy purification through self-distillation without a separate clean reference policy, using the victim's benign-input actions to supervise paired benign and triggered observations. We adapt existing detection methods to VLA backdoor detection and evaluate them under three kinds of VLA backdoor attacks. Our post-hoc results show strong backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks. Related Work Backdoor Attacks on VLA. Backdoor attacks on VLA policies implant trigger-dependent control behaviors while preserving benign performance. BadVLA~ zhou2026badvla uses objective-decoupled optimization to separate triggered and benign visual representations and induce control deviations. GoBA~ zhou2025goal poisons demonstrations with physical-object triggers to redirect high-level goals, whereas DropVLA~ xu2025dropvla relabels selected action targets to induce low-level failures such as premature gripper opening. Attack demonstrations appear in Appendix~ app:attack-demonstration . These attacks expose the need for runtime detection across different malicious behaviors. TMT addresses this need by monitoring token manifolds and latent transitions without assuming a specific target action. Traditional Backdoor Detection. Existing detectors screen inputs through prediction responses or representation statistics. STRIP~ gao2019strip measures prediction entropy under perturbations, while TeCo~ liu2023detecting compares the corruption severity needed to change predicted labels across corruption types. DeDe~ hou2025dede uses decoder reconstruction errors to screen inputs to self-supervised encoders; DUP-MS~ hu2026dup combines class-agnostic Mahalanobis distances with spectral statistics of inter-layer feature differences. Concurrent work, TrustVLA~ fu2026trustvla , uses token- and layer-wise epistemic uncertainty for VLA detection. STRIP, TeCo, DeDe, and DUP-MS were originally developed for image or language models. We adapt them to VLA backdoor detection, but our post-hoc comparison shows limited detection on unseen tasks, whereas TMT achieves higher TDRs. Anomaly and Failure Detection. Learning a reference distribution from normal data provides a basis for detecting previously unseen deviations. Deep SVDD~ ruff2018deep scores learned representations by distance from a hypersphere center, while RND~ burda2018exploration measures prediction error against fixed random features. ReDiffuser~ he2024rediffuser uses RND confidence to guide diffusion-based planning. LogPZO~ xu2025faildetect models successful-rollout observations with a flow and scores their inferred latent noise. FIPER~ romer2026failure requires both embedding-space RND and action-chunk entropy to exceed calibrated thresholds over short windows. These methods struggle to distinguish benign execution on unseen tasks from trigger-induced execution. Our post-hoc results show that TMT distinguishes these cases more effectively. Problem Formulation sec:problem We study inference-time backdoor detection for a potentially backdoored VLA policy . At each query , the policy receives an observation and a language instruction , and produces an action chunk . Executing these actions changes the environment and determines subsequent observations, yielding a rollout of queries indexed by . A backdoor trigger may become active at any query and alter subsequent actions and the resulting trajectory. Defender Capability. The defender has access to trusted benign rollouts and can inspect the policy's internal representations during inference. Detector fitting and calibration use only benign rollouts, without access to triggered training examples, the trigger specification, or an uncompromised reference policy. Here, benign rollouts denote the absence of a backdoor trigger, regardless of whether the policy successfully completes the task. Defender Objective. The defender aims to detect backdoor activation online. Deployment may involve unseen tasks during detector training, requiring cross-task generalization. We aim to identify triggered rollouts with a high detection rate and low trigger-relative detection latency while controlling the rollout-level false-rejection rate (FRR), defined as the fraction of benign rollouts with at least one alarm. Backdoor Detection We introduce TMT, as shown in Figure~ fig:tmt-framework , a backdoor detector that examines each policy query through two complementary branches. The token manifold branch assesses whether input-token representations conform to the distribution learned from benign queries. The latent transition branch assesses whether observed adjacent-layer transitions agree with those learned from benign inference. Both branches are trained on benign rollouts collected by executing the victim policy without triggers, while the policy remains frozen. After training, we calibrate thresholds using held-out benign rollouts. During online detection, an alarm is raised when either branch's score exceeds its threshold. Motivation sec:motivation Benign Token Representation. Existing analyses~ hu2026dup,wang2025backdoor of backdoor attacks at the input-query level have shown that triggers can induce anomalous representation patterns. With privileged access to the labels of benign and malicious queries, the t-SNE visualization~ van2008visualizing in Figure~ fig:token-motivation shows that most benign queries cluster in similar regions. Motivated by these observations, we hypothesize that benign query representations possess a learnable manifold structure and that triggers can shift query representations away from this manifold. We therefore model the benign representation distribution, which we refer to as the benign token manifold, to identify trigger-induced deviations. Inference Dynamics Consistency. title: TileSkipper: Region-Adaptive Tile Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Tiled 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizers often use one scene-wide contribution cutoff for tile enumeration, although content differs in its sensitivity to support truncation. TileSkipper selects a static per-Gaussian cutoff policy for a frozen checkpoint. Calibration renders measure candidate pair savings and an isolated-removal distortion proxy that accounts for front transmittance and background color. The method allocates cutoffs across 64 Gaussian groups and accepts policies only after complete renders on disjoint selection views. The exported policy uses one byte per Gaussian, with no parameter updates, additional kernel, or per-frame policy inference. Across 13 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, a fixed-policy AccuTile sweep gives dataset-macro speedups of $1.088\times$ at standard resolution and $1.238\times$ at 3840 pixels wide, with $-0.007/-0.023$ dB mean PSNR change. Six integrations with existing opacity-aware bounds yield $1.009\times$--$1.121\times$ compiler-only speedups. For four ports from $3σ$ rasterizers, we separately attribute the prior exact-bound transition and our incremental gain. Matched-quality ablations show modest gains over scene-global calibration and parity with per-Gaussian control; the standalone comparison with AdaGScale is regime-dependent.

Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs has become a dominant representation for real-time novel view synthesis. While fast in absolute terms, this pipeline pays a per-frame cost that scales with the number of (Gaussian, tile) pairs: a Gaussian with a large projected footprint is replicated across many tiles, and the binning, sorting, and rasterization kernels must process every resulting pair. Reducing this work matters particularly for stereo rendering and for mobile or XR hardware with limited throughput. A natural way to shrink the work per frame is to test tile intersection against a tighter footprint than the one used for blending. AdR-Gaussian~ wang2024adrgaussian , Speedy-Splat~ hanson2025speedysplat , and FastGS~ ren2025fastgs use an opacity level set to replace a conservative projected footprint by a tighter bound. We borrow this level-set construction; the formula itself is not our contribution. Our question begins after the bound is available: how far can the cutoff be raised, differently for each frozen Gaussian, under a measured image-error budget? Raising removes low-contribution tails, but their cumulative image error is not guaranteed to be negligible and must be measured. Several threshold-based paths expose only a single global ; whether fixed by the implementation or tuned for a dataset, it cannot allocate an error budget among Gaussians. Flat backgrounds, distant geometry, and nearly opaque material patches tolerate aggressive tile skipping; sharp edges, fine textures, and specular highlights require a conservative threshold. A global rule is forced into a compromise that is too loose on the easy regions and too tight on the hard ones. We make this concrete in : on a single playroom view, the largest locally safe threshold spans the full tested range from to across regions of the same image. AdaGScale~ jo2026adagscale is the closest prior method to this operation. It also performs lossy, viewpoint-adaptive scaling only for tile intersection, uses offline parameter search and a depth lookup table, and retains the original Gaussian during color accumulation. Consequently, training-free operation, a lookup table, and sub-Gaussian support control are not distinctive claims of TileSkipper. The difference is the decision principle: AdaGScale derives a current-view peripheral score from local Gaussian contribution and depth, whereas TileSkipper measures candidate deletion residuals over calibration views using the transmittance in front of the Gaussian and the composited color behind it, allocates a discrete error budget across Gaussian groups, and rejects proposed policies by complete renders on disjoint training views. TileSkipper trades AdaGScale's runtime view adaptation for a scene-level, static one-byte policy with no per-frame policy inference. The policy is not indexed by precompiled camera poses: an arbitrary runtime camera is projected and rendered normally using the same level byte, so an interactive viewer requires no camera matching. The checkpoint-matched comparison in is dataset-dependent and does not establish broad runtime dominance. Figure~ fig:motivation motivates heterogeneous allocation. Calibration renders measure pair savings and a compositing-aware isolated-removal residual for each cutoff. selects one scene-wide value; allocates levels across risk-stratified spatial groups. Complete renders on disjoint training views validate every proposal. Regional allocation adds roughly -- over Global at matched native-resolution quality ( ). The output is one uint8 level per Gaussian plus a lookup table, with no checkpoint update or per-frame policy inference. evaluates the same exported policies across resolutions, while compares against fixed-threshold alternatives. The method is deliberately a post-training systems adapter. Its measurements are scene-specific, but the resulting decision is static and portable: policies compiled on AccuTile transfer unchanged into SeeLe~ huang2026seele and FlashGS~ feng2025flashgs . A measured cost model further separates the pair-dependent work the policy can reduce from fixed work it cannot, and predicts when a complementary geometric pre-culler pays. Contributions. Compositing-aware support allocation for frozen checkpoints. For each discrete cutoff, TileSkipper measures exact pair savings and an isolated-removal residual that accounts for front transmittance and the composited color behind the Gaussian, then allocates the image-error budget across risk-stratified, workload-balanced regions. Complete renders on disjoint training views reject proxy failures. The technical distinction from AdaGScale is this measured compositing residual and the resulting error allocation; static one-byte export with no per-frame policy inference is a deployment tradeoff, not the claimed novelty. Evidence across model and rasterizer families. Six integrations isolate the compiler on paths that already expose an opacity-aware tile bound. Four additional ports begin from released rasterizers; for these rows we report the deployment-facing total and separately attribute the prior exact-bound transition and the incremental TileSkipper gain. They use the same nine Mip-NeRF~360~ barron2022mipnerf360 , two Tanks~ ~Temples~ knapitsch2017tnt , and two Deep Blending~ hedman2018db scenes. A standalone comparison with AdaGScale fixes the renderer, checkpoint-matched calibration table, selection views, test views, and timing protocol. A Speedy-Splat sweep varies , the number of policy regions, from 1 to 1024 to separate scene calibration from regional allocation. A measured boundary on systems benefit. A latency model fitted from controlled sweeps predicts the pair-dependent ceiling and the complementary pre-culling regime. The optional pre-culler is image-bit-exact in all 52 measured runs, but is correctly disabled when its planning overhead exceeds the predicted saving. Related Work sec:related We distinguish primitive, tile-pair, and fragment reduction; Appendix~ app:related_table summarizes their control units. Per-Gaussian thresholds at the fragment level. Fragment Pruning~ ye2024fragmentpruning learns one truncation threshold per Gaussian via a sigmoid relaxation and controls per-pixel coverage after sorting. TileSkipper selects discrete tile-enumeration cutoffs without updating checkpoint parameters and acts before sorting, removing pairs from both sorting and blending. evaluates TileSkipper on the checkpoint families used by Fragment Pruning; it tests checkpoint compatibility, not composition with learned fragment pruning. System-level paths. SeeLe~ huang2026seele combines camera-cluster preprocessing with contribution-aware rasterization. Its tile-intersection test uses the support in with fixed at compile time. TileSkipper changes that cutoff policy, while our transfer experiment retains SeeLe's other components and does not claim to reproduce its full mobile deployment pipeline. Tile-pair reduction. AdR-Gaussian~ wang2024adrgaussian derives the opacity level set at the renderer's minimum splatting-opacity cutoff and bounds it with an adaptive radius and an axis-aligned box. We borrow that level-set construction rather than claim the support formula as new. Speedy-Splat~ hanson2025speedysplat introduces accurate tile pruning, FastGS~ ren2025fastgs combines it with a compact box, and FlashGS~ feng2025flashgs and QuadBox~ li2026quadbox further tighten geometric enumeration. These exact or fixed-threshold bounds are complementary to selecting heterogeneous lossy cutoffs. View-adaptive tile support. AdaGScale~ jo2026adagscale is the closest work in action space: it estimates a current-view peripheral contribution score, applies depth-dependent lookup-table calibration, and adjusts the scale used for tile intersection while retaining the original Gaussian for color accumulation. TileSkipper instead measures a compositing residual---including front transmittance and the composited color behind the Gaussian---for discrete candidate cutoffs over calibration views, allocates the resulting error budget across Gaussian groups, and accepts a static policy only after complete-image validation on disjoint training views. AdaGScale offers runtime view adaptation; TileSkipper incurs no per-frame policy inference and directly measures the compiled policy's complete-render error. compares the standalone methods inside AdaGScale's released renderer. Method sec:method TileSkipper takes a converged 3DGS checkpoint and a tile rasterizer whose tile-intersection test uses one scene-wide contribution cutoff , then replaces that constant with a static per-Gaussian cutoff policy. No checkpoint parameter is retrained. At runtime the rasterizer reads one byte per Gaussian and a lookup table, with no camera-conditioned policy inference. defines the cutoff and its geometric effect; measures pair savings and compositing risk, groups Gaussians into workload-balanced regions, selects one cutoff level per region, and validates complete candidate renders. Appendix~ app:systems_details provides the empirical cost model, optional pre-culler, and dispatch rule. summarizes the offline measurements, policy selection, and the one-byte runtime application. Official-Fixed uses the published cutoff for every Gaussian. selects one scene-specific multiplier shared by all Gaussians ( ), whereas selects levels for regions. Here is the number of independently selected policy regions, and denotes Gaussian 's multiplier on ; recovers Official-Fixed. Rendering pipeline. shows the four stages relevant here. (1)~Each visible Gaussian is projected to a screen-space footprint. (2)~Every intersecting tile is enumerated, creating one (Gaussian, tile) pair per overlap. (3)~Each tile's assigned Gaussians are sorted front-to-back. (4)~Pixels evaluate and alpha-blend the sorted Gaussians. Vanilla 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs uses a conservative box, whereas Speedy-Splat~ hanson2025speedysplat , FastGS~ ren2025fastgs , and SeeLe~ huang2026seele derive tile support from a fixed contribution cutoff. TileSkipper changes only stage~2; Gaussian parameters, depth sorting, and blending arithmetic remain unchanged. title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies. INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach for bringing foundation models into robot manipulation~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,intelligence2025pi_ . By integrating visual and language understanding with action generation, VLAs can translate high-level instructions into continuous robot control. Large-scale pretraining on heterogeneous robot and vision-language data has further enabled generalization across tasks, objects, environments, and robot embodiments~ oneill2023openx,gr00tn1_2025,gemini2025robotics . Despite this progress, VLAs still exhibit unreliable behaviors, including unstable or premature actions, long-horizon drift, failures to recover from execution errors, and infeasible actions~ gu2026safe,zhang2026safevla,fei2025liberoplus,zhou2025libero,zhang2025experiences,lin2025failsafe,soh2026actionhallucination . This is particularly concerning in physical robot execution, where erroneous actions directly affect the robot and its environment. Within this broader set of failures, we focus on a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues a manipulation sequence based on a robot-object state that has not actually been achieved. We refer to this behavioral pattern as state hallucination, because the policy acts as if an unrealized physical state were true. For example, a VLA may close its gripper before reaching an object and subsequently execute transport and place motions as though the object has been successfully grasped, as shown in Fig.~ fig:1_teaser . Such a mismatch can persist across subsequent actions, allowing a local execution error to propagate over multiple stages. This recurring and persistent behavior motivates us to investigate whether policy knowledge associated with state hallucination can be selectively removed while preserving successful manipulation capabilities. We first examine how the policy's internal representations differ between hallucinated and successful behaviors. Such hallucinated rollouts exhibit weakened attention to task-relevant regions, such as the gripper and target object, together with more spatially dispersed attention. Through a mechanistic analysis with sparse autoencoders, we also observe that sparse features exhibit distinct activation patterns during hallucinated and normal executions. To characterize these sparse feature activation patterns, we define a feature association score that contrasts activations across execution outcomes, such as failures with hallucination, failures without hallucination, and successful executions. Based on this score, we categorize sparse features according to whether they are more strongly associated with hallucinated failures or successful executions. Building on these observations, we propose (SOUL), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination, where sparse features identified from hallucinated failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. This feature-level policy unlearning objective suppresses activations of the forgetting targets while enhancing activations of the retention targets, thereby mitigating recurring hallucination behavior while minimizing interference with useful manipulation capabilities. We validate our approach with OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla and ~ intelligence2025pi_ on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , and a real-world Franka robot, achieving an average 21.7 p reduction in hallucination rate and a 22.1 p improvement in task success while preserving 89 of behaviors that were successful before unlearning. These results demonstrate that interpretable feature analysis can reveal internal representations associated with recurring policy failures, providing a practical basis for selectively unlearning such behaviors in embodied foundation models. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*] We characterize state hallucination as a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved. We analyze state hallucination through visual attention and sparse features, revealing weakened attention to task-relevant regions and distinct feature patterns associated with state hallucination. We introduce a sparse feature policy unlearning method that selectively unlearns recurring state hallucination behavior by suppressing hallucination features while enhancing features that support successful manipulation. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action models have become a major direction for generalist robot manipulation. Prior work has improved generalization through larger pretrained vision-language representations, heterogeneous robotic data, and stronger action generation architectures~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,intelligence2025pi_,oneill2023openx,gr00tn1_2025,gemini2025robotics,driess2023palme,octo2024,black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla . Deployment reliability has also been improved through intermediate reasoning~ zhao2025cotvla,lin2026onetwovla , failure detection and recovery~ lin2025failsafe,liu2026selfcorrectingvla , and test-time sampling or verification~ kwok2025robomonkey,jang2025mgselect . These approaches primarily focus on improving policy outputs during deployment, rather than directly modifying policy knowledge associated with recurring failures. Recent concurrent mechanistic interpretability studies have begun to analyze and steer VLA behavior at inference time by intervening on representations, such as feed-forward activation directions~ haon2025mechanistic and sparse features~ khan2025controlling . In contrast, we formulate the selective modification of undesirable policy behavior as a policy unlearning problem, where knowledge associated with recurring hallucinated behavior is removed while representations supporting successful execution are preserved. Encoding this modification in the pretrained policy parameters enables persistent behavior correction without repeated intervention at inference time. Machine Unlearning Machine unlearning aims to make a trained model forget knowledge associated with selected data without retraining the model from scratch~ cao2015unlearning,nguyen2025survey . Prior work has studied unlearning mainly in classification tasks, where the influence of selected training data is removed from trained models~ golatkar2020eternal,thudi2022unrolling , and in language tasks, where factual knowledge or undesired responses are suppressed~ yao2024large,maini2024tofu . A central challenge is balancing the removal of targeted knowledge with the preservation of useful model capabilities. This trade-off is particularly consequential for robot policies, where modifying one behavior can inadvertently disrupt multiple tightly coupled skills. Motivated by this, we introduce feature-level selective policy unlearning by explicitly identifying features for forgetting and retention to suppress undesirable behavior while preserving useful manipulation capabilities. Sparse Autoencoders Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense model activations into sparse latent representations, enabling individual features to be associated with more localized and interpretable patterns in model behavior~ huben2024sparse,gao2024scaling,bussmann2024batchtopk . They are trained to reconstruct the original activations under a sparsity constraint, such that only a small subset of latent features is active for each input. A commonly used variant is the Top- SAE, which imposes this sparsity constraint explicitly by retaining only the largest latent activations. In VLAs, SAE features have recently been used to interpret and repeatedly steer policy at test time~ khan2025controlling . In contrast, the proposed method identifies recurring internal patterns associated with unreliable behaviors using sparse features and translates these patterns into forgetting targets to guide targeted policy unlearning. Analysis of State Hallucination in VLAs sec:analysis What Is State Hallucination? We define state hallucination as a behavioral execution pattern in which a VLA continues to generate actions based on a robot-object state that has not actually been achieved. State hallucination can occur at different manipulation stages: [leftmargin=*] A grasp hallucination occurs when the gripper closes in free space without contacting the target object. Note that grasp failures involving object contact, such as inaccurate localization or slippage, are not considered hallucinations. A transport hallucination occurs when, after either a grasp failure or a grasp hallucination, the gripper remains closed and continues moving from the grasp location toward the destination while the object remains ungrasped. A place hallucination occurs when the gripper opens at the destination without holding the target object. We label these events by tracking ground-truth robot-object states in simulation and observable interaction states in the real world. Based on these criteria, we categorize each rollout as clean success (CS), hallucination failure (HF), or non-hallucination failure (NF). Here, HF denotes failed executions that exhibit at least one state hallucination event, whereas CS and NF denote successful and failed executions without state hallucination, respectively. Attention Analysis of Hallucinated and Normal Executions sec:attn_anal To examine how the policy behaves internally during state hallucination, we compare internal attention patterns between CS and HF executions. At each rollout step, we aggregate the attention from action tokens to visual tokens and project the resulting attention scores onto the input image, revealing which visual regions the policy attends to while generating actions. For visualization, we show representative time steps immediately preceding the corresponding manipulation event, such as grasping. As shown in Fig.~ fig:2_attention , CS executions exhibit attention concentrated on task-relevant regions, particularly the target object and gripper. In contrast, HF executions show weaker attention to these regions and increased attention to background regions. These differences suggest that state hallucination is accompanied by a distinct shift in the policy's visual attention. This motivates us to look beyond attention and examine whether hallucinated executions are also reflected in the internal representations of the policy. title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
summary: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. Through real-robot evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we show that under vision loss the success rate of the baseline policy drops substantially, whereas TMD sustains task execution. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.

Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. Through real-robot evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we show that under vision loss the success rate of the baseline policy drops substantially, whereas TMD sustains task execution. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss. INTRODUCTION In imitation learning, a manipulation policy is developed directly from demonstrations, without a tailored reward function or controller. A human operator teleoperates the robot to perform a task while the camera images, the robot's own state and the commanded actions are recorded. The policy is then trained via supervised learning to predict the actions from the observations. At run time the task is executed in a closed loop; thus, each step is driven by the sensor inputs available at that moment. Recent studies have increasingly adopted vision-language-action models, which encode images and language instructions using pretrained foundation models and generate actions from the resulting representation~ tvfdit2026, zhang2025tavla . In contact-rich manipulation, vision alone does not reveal how much force is applied or whether contact has been established; thus, integrating several modalities such as vision, language, and force is intuitive~ famil2026 . However, when a policy is trained by integrating multiple modalities, potential overreliance on a particular modality may lead to underuse of the others~ wu2022greedy . Vision, in particular, tends to become dominant because it is information-rich; consequently, vision loss at inference time can severely impair policy execution. Camera failures and occlusions do occur in real-world deployment, making overreliance on a particular modality a practical robustness concern, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Modality dropout can intervene in this bias by stochastically removing modalities during training~ neverova2016moddrop, liu2017sensordropout . Randomly removing modalities, however, does not account for which modality is dominant and thus does not correct the bias itself. In this study we propose Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), which estimates each modality's dependence from attention and drops the modality with the largest dependence as a target. We further introduce entropy regularization over the dependence distribution to alleviate concentration on any single modality. To date, robustness to missing modalities has been assessed mainly using multimodal classification benchmarks or simulated manipulation. Situations where vision is lost while a real robot executes a task, i.e., robustness in a closed loop, have rarely been examined. In this study we apply TMD to a real bimanual manipulator and evaluate whether task execution is sustained when vision is stochastically lost at inference time. We also examine the effect of dependence-based targeted selection by comparing TMD with a conventional dropout in which the dropped modality is selected at random, referred to as Random Modality Dropout (RMD). The contributions of this study are as follows: We propose Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), which drops the dominant modality as a target based on the dependence estimated from attention, together with entropy regularization. Through real-robot closed-loop evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we demonstrate that TMD sustains task execution under vision loss and that its action commands are disturbed less. We show that RMD, which replaces the targeted selection with a random one and omits the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss. RELATED WORK Multimodal Imitation Learning for Manipulation In manipulation, the modalities received by a policy carry different types of information. Images provide the position and orientation of the objects, and a language instruction specifies the task to be performed. Force or tactile signals report the contact that images cannot capture~ famil2026 . Transformer-based policies treat these inputs as a single token sequence to generate an action chunk~ zhao2023aloha . In vision-language-action models, pretrained encoders provide the visual and language tokens~ tvfdit2026, zhang2025tavla . These inputs substitute for one another only partially. Thus, losing one of them at inference time does not uniformly degrade the performance of the policy; only what that input alone was supplying is lost. Nevertheless, the extent to which a policy relies on each input is determined implicitly through training, and such policies are typically developed under the assumption that all inputs are available. Controlling Modality Reliance When a policy is trained on multiple modalities, it may over-rely on a dominant one and fail to use the others~ wu2022greedy . Several lines of research have addressed this issue. Fusion-mechanism design suppresses the dominance of a particular modality through architectural choices~ famil2026 ; however, this approach is closely tied to the specific policy architecture. Phase-dependent weighting dynamically adjusts the contribution of each modality according to the task phase~ ichiwara2023modality, msbot2024 , but presupposes that all modalities remain available. Visual degradation during training reduces the policy's reliance on vision~ liu2025factr but does not examine which modality is dominant. Gradient rebalancing modulates the gradient of each modality based on its contribution at each iteration~ peng2022ogm, li2023agm but does not train the policy to handle the absence of a modality. Modality dropout stochastically drops modalities during training~ neverova2016moddrop, liu2017sensordropout , but randomly selecting the dropped modality does not account for modality dominance. In a setting closer to ours, modality dropout has been used to keep a network from ignoring the weaker of two modalities in audiovisual facial animation~ abdelaziz2020modalitydropout , with the probability of dropping each modality tuned in advance based on prior knowledge of the dominant modality rather than on a quantity estimated during training. Because this study targets robustness to the loss of the dominant modality, we identify the dominant modality using attention and selectively drop it during training (Section~ sec:method ). Evaluation under Missing Modalities Most of the methods described above are evaluated under normal operating conditions that do not involve complete modality loss. Research on visuotactile fusion addresses vision-constrained conditions, but remains limited to situations where vision is only partially restricted~ gelfusion2025 . Robustness to missing modalities has been studied mainly outside real-robot closed-loop settings: on multimodal classification benchmarks~ ma2022missing or simulated manipulation~ retrieval2026 . The scenario in which vision is stochastically lost while a real robot executes a task in closed loop has rarely been examined. Unlike existing studies, this study focuses on evaluating real-robot task execution under inference-time vision loss. title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

Introduction sec:intro Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used to search for objects in large urban environments. In aerial object search, the UAV often receives an RGB-D view, its pose, and an instruction describing a target instance, then must find and stop at that target without an externally provided route. Unlike conventional indoor ObjectNav and short-horizon aerial navigation, outdoor search provides no target location and may contain many similar objects across a region much larger than the camera field of view. The agent must maintain what has been observed while deciding which future region is most useful to visit. Broad exploration wastes the step budget while following only the current target hypothesis can cause repeated visits and occlusion traps. Map-based agents mitigate partial observability with explicit spatial memory yamauchi1997frontier, chaplot2018active, chaplot2020semexp , but they are fundamentally reactive: they reason over past observations, score the current view against stored memory by hand-designed rules or vision--language queries huang2023vlmaps, gu2024conceptgraphs , and do not predict the future states their actions produce. World-model agents can imagine ha2018worldmodels , but their spatial knowledge is implicit: the questions that determine search efficiency, namely where the agent has been, where it cannot fly, and what remains unexplored, are entangled inside a flat latent vector, and the actor--critic machinery further compresses long-run prospects into a single scalar that says how much value exists but not where it lies, even though every action moves the agent somewhere on the map. The reason the two lines are each insufficient is the same: spatial memory and prospective reasoning are not linked, and connecting them has remained challenging. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model grounded in explicit spatial cognition memory. Specifically, we organize this memory as a three-layer bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation: an exploration layer records where the UAV has been, an obstacle layer marks where it cannot fly, and a spatial value layer decoded from the latent state estimates where searching is worthwhile. We further introduce a cognition–action network, in which the decoded spatial value guides imagination-based planning to improve the agent’s action policy. A three-stage curriculum trains SearchWorld to learn state transitions and spatial representations, imitate expert search behavior, and refine spatial exploration through value-guided imagination planning. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld achieves 23.8 SR and 35.5 OSR overall, improves over the strongest published agent, and retains 19.9 success on unseen scenes. Our contributions are: To our knowledge, the first world model with explicit spatial cognition memory for aerial object search. SearchWorld combines a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) with allocentric exploration and obstacle channels and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer from the latent state. A cognition--action network and value-guided imagination. A decoded task-aware spatial value layer, supervised by exploration, obstacle, and training-time target signals but not given the target coordinate at inference, replaces the actor--critic's learned scalar critic as a structured value prior. Imagination-based value guidance then refines movement actions by pooling decoded value over imagined footprints, with the imitated stopping behavior kept intact. A staged training and evaluation study. The three stage curriculum learning separates world-model learning, expert task imitation, and value-guided movement refinement. Experiments and ablations on UAV-ON quantify its performance over baselines as well as the contributions of spatial memory, the value layer, and each training stage. Related Work sec:related World models for navigation. One line of world models plans navigation by generating future observations as pixels. PathDreamer koh2021pathdreamer synthesizes novel indoor viewpoints, DreamWalker wang2023dreamwalker imagines candidate plans with a learned scene synthesizer, DreamNav wang2025dreamnav and NWM bar2025nwm simulate candidate trajectories with large generative models, and ANWM zhang2025anwm extends such video prediction to aerial trajectories. Planning with these models requires autoregressively generating video at every decision, and the resulting latency is hard to reconcile with the hundreds-of-steps budget of large-region search. A second line keeps the world model in latent space, where an imagined rollout costs one latent transition rather than a video. MILE chen2022mile learns driving dynamics in latent space, X-Mobility liu2024xmobility and NavMorph yao2025navmorph carry RSSMs into outdoor and vision-and-language navigation, and WMNav nie2025wmnav instantiates the world model as a vision--language model (VLM) that predicts outcomes into an online curiosity value map. In all of these, memory of the environment stays implicit, and spatially grounded search planning with a latent world model has remained challenging. Aerial navigation and object search. Aerial navigation research has progressed from instruction-following flight (AerialVLN, ; CityNav, ) to object-goal search, formalized by UAV-ON xiao2025uavon . Recent aerial search agents couple explicit spatial memory with large language models (LLMs) and their multimodal variants (MLLMs). APEX zhang2026apex drives exploration with attraction, exploration, and obstacle maps constructed by a VLM; PRPSearcher ji2026cityavos has an MLLM reason over semantic-attraction and uncertainty maps; and OctMem-Agent zhou2026octmem aggregates the RGB-D history into an adaptive octree memory queried by instruction-modulated tokens. Across these systems the memory records where the agent has been, but the readout happens at execution time through hand-designed rules or model queries, and the agent does not model the consequences of its own actions, so exploration stays reactive. Applying world models to aerial object search has remained challenging, and advances one step in this direction. Method sec:method rests on three components. An explicit spatial-cognition memory makes the search state inspectable: exploration and obstacle layers are constructed from depth and pose, and a value layer is decoded from the world model's latent state (Section~ sec:bev_memory ). A task-oriented RSSM world model learns the search dynamics over this memory, predicts future states in imagination, and decodes the value layer along the way (Section~ sec:world_model ). A cognition--action network then turns the decoded spatial value into action selection: the task policy learned from experts is refined by value-guided updates that touch movement actions only (Section~ sec:value_imagination ). Section~ sec:formulation formalizes the problem, and Section~ sec:training presents the three-stage curriculum that trains the components. Figure~ fig:pipeline gives an overview. Problem Formulation sec:formulation We formalize aerial object-goal search as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) . The state comprises the full UAV pose and the environment occupancy, neither of which is directly observable. Each step yields an observation : the RGB and depth images, the 6-DoF pose , and an instance-level text instruction that describes the target. The benchmark's success criterion plays the role of a terminal reward but is used only for evaluation, not as a training signal (Section~ sec:training ). Because the Markov state is unavailable, the policy conditions on the full interaction history . The action space is fixed by the benchmark interface rather than designed by us: eight discrete atomic actions with fixed motion magnitudes, the last of which (stop) terminates the episode and triggers success evaluation (Appendix~ app:discretization ). Explicit Spatial-Cognition Memory sec:bev_memory A recurrent latent state is a sufficient statistic in principle but a poor interface for spatial reasoning. The questions that matter in object search, namely where the agent has been, where it cannot fly, and where it is worth searching next, have no explicit reading in an unstructured vector. therefore maintains an explicit spatial-cognition memory: a persistent, physically indexed record of the search. The carrier is a BEV grid covering the benchmark's search region, centered at its center. World points map to cells by a fixed affine rule, so the memory is allocentric and stable across episodes. Grid specifications and geometric parameters are given in Table~ tab:specs in Appendix~ app:implementation . The memory has three layers with distinct origins. The exploration layer and the obstacle layer are deterministic functions of the UAV pose and the depth image: fixed geometric rules update them from raw sensors, they involve no learned components, and they are exact given accurate sensing. The value layer is different in kind. It is an output of the world model, decoded from the latent state and conditioned on the search instruction, and it scores every cell by the utility of visiting it under the current task; its supervision is task-aware but available only at training time (Section~ sec:value_imagination ). The first two layers record what has already been observed, while the third predicts where the search should go next. Exploration layer: where have I been? Each executed step observes a field of view (FOV) of angular width and sensing range . For a cell , let and denote its range and bearing offset relative to the pose at step . The layer accumulates the maximum discounted visibility up to the current step , where the maximum over time implements persistent coverage and the linear/cosine attenuation weights a distant or oblique glimpse by its reliability. Obstacle layer: where can I not fly? The front-view depth stream is back-projected to a 3-D point cloud with the known camera intrinsics, transformed to world coordinates by the pose , and orthographically projected onto the grid. A cell is marked obstacle if the projected points within it exceed a height threshold above the ground. title: trACT: temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap
summary: Effective remote monitoring and surveillance using drones are frequently impeded by severe environmental and thermal clutter, dynamic vegetation, target camouflage, and system latency. Drawing inspiration from the hunting strategies of birds of prey that hover and stabilize their vision to isolate subtle ground motion, we introduce trACT (temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap), a lightweight, real-time aerial robotics framework designed for autonomous consumer drones. The system integrates Temporal Max Pooling (TMP), a low-level signal processing method that transforms imperceptible movement across a rolling integration window into robust value and time encodings, with self-supervised motion anomaly detection to isolate target motion from background environmental motion caused by wind gusts and drone drift. To overcome mechanical and processing delays, trACT combines motion prediction with automated gimbal-stabilized optical zoom verification and equitable multi-target verification balancing. Extensive real-world field experiments in densely forested wildlife habitats and surveillance scenarios demonstrate that trACT successfully bridges the gap between wide-area aerial monitoring and precise, autonomous target verification under challenging operational conditions.

title: Event-Aligned Visual Action Reasoning for World Action Models
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) utilize future visual prediction as an intermediate reasoning process to guide action generation. However, existing WAMs typically structure visual imagination according to predefined temporal intervals, without explicitly accounting for the different roles of task-critical interactions and connecting transitions. We argue that effective visual foresight should align directly with task-relevant interactions and their corresponding reasoning demands. To this end, we introduce an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework that organizes visual-action prediction around interaction events. Through event-aligned visual-action supervision, WAM learns to generate event-aligned visual context in each imagined rollout, placing greater emphasis on critical state changes that inform action generation. This shapes the visual reasoning granularity according to the underlying interaction dynamics, with detailed reasoning around task-critical events and coarser progression through connecting transitions. Furthermore, we introduce an execution validity head that identifies the valid portion of each predicted action sequence, avoiding redundant actions during chunked inference. Experiments demonstrate a 10.26 percentage point improvement in DOMINO success rate over baseline and competitive performance on RoboTwin 2.0. It also transfers from DOMINO Level 1 to Levels 2 and 3 without target-level adaptation.
