It also transfers from DOMINO Level 1 to Levels 2 and 3 without target-level adaptation. Introduction Recent World Action Models~(WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation by coupling action generation with future visual prediction li2026causalworldmodelingrobot,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2606-02800,ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot . Unlike conventional vision-language-action (VLA) policies that map current observations and instructions directly to actions pmlr-v270-kim25c,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-14734,pmlr-v305-black25a,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-20020,zheng2025xvlasoftpromptedtransformerscalable , WAMs additionally model how the scene may evolve and leverage the predicted future for action generation. Such visual prediction can be viewed as an intermediate reasoning process that simulates future scene evolution and grounds action generation in predicted visual states. From this perspective, a fundamental question is how a WAM should structure its visual imagination to best inform action generation. A key observation is that visual states along a manipulation trajectory contribute differently to action generation. Consider grasping an object: physical contact between the gripper and the object provides direct evidence of the interaction, while the preceding gripper closure and the subsequent lift provide the local context for how the grasp begins and proceeds. Meanwhile, the initial reach serves as a connective phase linking earlier task stages to the grasp itself. These phases serve distinct functions: The core interaction (grasp) evidence confirms whether the intended robot–object state transition has occurred; the surrounding motion (closing and lifting) provides the context of this change; and the connecting motion (approaching) determines how the robot transitions to it. However, the manipulation trajectory rarely reflects these functional task stages. Informative interaction events often span only a few frames, while connecting motions can take up the majority of the trajectory. Therefore, visual imagination based on fixed temporal intervals may risk fragmenting critical, fine-grained interactions across distinct prediction horizons. Despite rapid progress in WAMs, current paradigms largely overlook this functional gap. Existing works predominantly focus on how visual predictions should be integrated with actions. li2026causalworldmodelingrobot explicitly interleaves future visual prediction and action generation, yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels retains video modeling only during training, and zhang2026imagewamworldactionmodels replaces dense future videos with task-relevant visual transformations. However, as shown in ~ , these methods universally structure visual-action horizons uniformly across the demonstration timeline (denoted as Episode Uniform). They largely inherit the sampled trajectory structure from training data, without adapting visual imagination to different interaction events. To address the above limitations, we propose an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework that organizes visual imagination around task-critical interactions, rather than directly following the sampled trajectory structure. The key idea is to shape the temporal progression of imagined states according to the underlying interaction dynamics. We construct event-aligned visual-action supervision by first segmenting training trajectories according to interaction events and then building visual-action prediction chunks from the resulting event boundaries. Within this event-aligned organization, we reorganize training trajectories such that task-critical events preserve fine-grained visual-action evolution, while transitions toward the relevant states are represented with fewer intermediate states, as shown in~ . Through this supervision, the model learns to advance its visual imagination in alignment with interaction progress, generating visual context that captures how critical interactions unfold under actions and supports action generation. However, event-aligned visual action reasoning also introduces a practical challenge for action execution. Since interaction segments may span different durations, their corresponding action sequences can have different valid lengths. When mapped to fixed-size action chunks following li2026causalworldmodelingrobot , short segments use repeated or padded actions to fill the remaining prediction slots during training. Executing these padding-induced actions can unnecessarily prolong the segment before the next prediction. To address this issue, we further introduce an execution validity head that identifies the valid portion of each predicted action sequence. At inference time, the validity head determines which portion to execute, avoiding redundant actions while retaining actual actions associated with interactions. Experiments on DOMINO~ fang2026domino and RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin demonstrate improved manipulation performance, including a 10.26 gain in DOMINO success rate over LingBot-VA~ li2026causalworldmodelingrobot and competitive performance on RoboTwin 2.0. The framework also demonstrates successful transfer from DOMINO Level 1 to Level 2/3 without target-level adaptation. Our contributions are summarized as below, [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=1pt, parsep=1pt, partopsep=1pt] We proposed an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework that organizes future prediction with task-critical interactions as focus to reason more carefully over crucial state changes. Instead of inheriting a predefined temporal structure from sampled trajectories, our formulation enables the reasoning process to adapt its granularity to the interaction dynamics. We further introduce an execution validity head to identify the valid portion of each predicted action sequence under event-aligned reasoning. By avoiding the execution of redundant actions, it improves action continuity and leads to smoother action execution. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance, especially on the more challenging dynamic manipulation dataset DOMINO, with significantly better success rate and outstanding transfer performance. Related Works Vision-Language-Action Models VLA models transfer knowledge from pretrained VLMs to robot control by generating actions conditioned on vision observations and language instructions. OpenVLA~ pmlr-v270-kim25c formulates control as action-token prediction, while ~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel and GR00T N1~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-14734 combine pretrained VLM representations with generative action models. Recent works further improve generalization across tasks and embodiments through heterogeneous data and scalable adaptation, as in ~ pmlr-v305-black25a , Gemini Robotics~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-20020 , and X-VLA~ zheng2025xvlasoftpromptedtransformerscalable . Other works investigate how pretrained representations should be adapted for action generation, including explicit spatial modeling qu2025spatialvlaexploringspatialrepresentations , lightweight feature adaptation~ 10.1609/aaai.v40i22.38931 , representation insulation~ NEURIPS2025_94e93603 , and persistent object-centric representations~ ren2026closingloophumanoidvla . Despite their strong generalization, these approaches primarily map current observations and instructions directly to actions. Recent methods such as MEM~ torne2026memmultiscaleembodiedmemory and LingBot-VLA 2.0~ wu2026foundationapplicationimprovingvla begin to move beyond this formulation by incorporating temporal memory and future prediction, respectively. World-Action Models Beyond directly mapping observations to actions, recent WAMs leverage video generative models to jointly model future visual dynamics and robot actions. ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,li2026causalworldmodelingrobot,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2606-02800,xu2026forcingcausalworldmodeling couple visual prediction with action generation, using predicted future observations as an intermediate representation for reasoning. These approaches demonstrate that modeling the evolution of the visual world can provide richer structure than direct action prediction. Recent works further explore whether dense video prediction is necessary. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels reduces explicit visual generation at inference, while ImageWAM~ zhang2026imagewamworldactionmodels focuses on single target-image prediction instead of video rollout, suggesting that uniformly predicting every intermediate frame introduces substantial redundancy. In parallel, approaches explore temporal representation in world modeling. li2026wallwmcarvingworldaction models trajectories around action-relevant events, while he2026skipsparsekeyframeinterpolation,11246352 use sparse keyframes or subgoals to represent long-horizon dynamics. These methods highlight the importance of selecting task-relevant temporal information rather than modeling all future states uniformly. Interaction-Structured Visual Reasoning for WAM We propose an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework that organizes visual prediction according to the reasoning demands of robot manipulation. Rather than treating visual prediction as a uniform continuation of the sampled trajectory, we structure visual reasoning around task-relevant interactions and the visual context needed to support their corresponding actions. Our framework consists of event-aligned visual-action reasoning and execution validity prediction. World-Action Models sec:preliminary Problem Formulation We build on autoregressive latent-diffusion World-Action Models (WAMs)~ li2026causalworldmodelingrobot , which represents the episode as a sequence of visual-action chunks . Visual observations are encoded by a causal video VAE~ wan2025wan , where each latent visual frame is temporally aligned with a group of actions, following ~ li2026causalworldmodelingrobot sampling scheme. Given the initial visual context encoded from and the instruction , the model is trained to autoregressively generate the interleaved sequence , producing each visual or action chunk through iterative denoising conditioned on its preceding context in the sequence. title: SkillCycle: Co-Evolving Agent Policies and Skill Banks
summary: Internalizing external skills changes a language agent's capabilities and, with them, the value of its remaining guidance: rules can become redundant, misleading, or insufficient for newly encountered decisions. This creates a coupled problem of learning from skills and adapting the skills that supervise further learning. We introduce SkillCycle, a framework for co-evolving agent policies and skill banks through a feedback loop between skill internalization and rule revision. Our central contribution is to give distillation feedback a second role: token-level contextual differences help locate rules for inspection, while interaction outcomes guide edits to their content and applicability. SkillCycle alternates between two phases: policy learning with a fixed skill bank and router, and rule revision with a frozen policy. Candidate edits undergo rule-level and whole-bank environment comparisons before they guide the next learning cycle. On WebShop, SkillCycle with a 3B model achieves a success rate of 74.74% and a score of 88.37 without inference-time skill inputs, representing relative improvements of 0.73% and 3.96% over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model, respectively. In Cycle 3 ablations on ALFWorld and WebShop, SkillCycle's no-skill success rates improve by 10.18% and 18.11% relative to a static skill bank, and by 2.41% and 2.50% relative to a single bank update, respectively. These results show that continually revising skill guidance as the agent's capabilities change helps transform external skills into policy capabilities that require no skill inputs at inference. We will release code, configurations, skill banks, and evaluation protocols.

Introduction sec:introduction External skills help language agents act on observations yao2022react through executable libraries wang2023voyager , induced workflows wang2024awm , and accumulated reflections shinn2023reflexion,zhao2023expel . Skill augmentation supplies this guidance in context and can evolve alongside the policy xia2026skillrl,shi2026skill1 ; skill internalization transfers its benefits into parameters to reduce retrieval dependence. Skill0 withdraws context using on-policy helpfulness lu2026skill0 , while Skill0.5 combines internalization with difficulty-aware skill utilization at inference time zhu2026skill05 . Learning also changes what guidance the policy needs. A previously useful rule may become redundant, mislead the updated policy, or fail to cover newly encountered states. Withdrawing guidance addresses continued reliance on it, but does not determine how its content or applicability should evolve. We therefore ask: can feedback from internalization guide rule revisions that improve subsequent learning without inference-time skills? Figure~ fig:concept compares these approaches. The key difficulty is distinguishing mastery from ineffective guidance. A shrinking Teacher--Student gap can reflect successful learning or a skill that helps neither policy. Contextual self-distillation zhao2026opsd,yang2026opid supplies token-level log-probability differences that locate where guidance changes a sampled response. These differences identify decisions to inspect; task outcomes establish whether behavior succeeds. Together, they enable finer diagnosis than an aggregate helpfulness score; rule-removal rescoring then identifies influential instructions. We introduce , a framework that co-evolves agent policies and skill banks through a feedback loop between skill internalization and rule revision. SkillCycle treats the bank as training memory that is continually revised as the agent's capabilities change, alternating between two phases. During internalization, the bank and critical-first router remain fixed, while skill-conditioned supervision and environment rewards train a no-skill Student. During revision, the Student is frozen; token-level feedback, routing records, and interaction trajectories identify rules for inspection and guide candidate edits to their content and applicability. Verified edits are committed to the bank to supply updated guidance for the next learning cycle. The central innovation is to give distillation feedback a second role: beyond supervising policy learning, it provides diagnostic evidence for improving the skill guidance itself. Token-level contextual differences locate decisions to inspect, rule-removal rescoring identifies the relevant rules, and interaction outcomes inform whether those rules are effective and how they should be revised. To assess candidate edits, SkillCycle holds the policy fixed and conducts paired environment comparisons first at the rule level and then at the whole-bank level, testing both local benefits and effects on the assembled guidance. Only edits that pass both levels of verification are accepted. This process turns feedback from policy learning into improved guidance for subsequent learning, allowing the bank to adapt to the agent's changing capabilities and needs while supporting the transfer of external skills into policy capabilities that require no skill inputs at inference. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) Policy--skill co-evolution. SkillCycle alternates skill internalization and rule revision, adapting supervision to the evolving policy for inference without skill inputs. (2) State-aware, critical-first routing. Our router matches applicable skills to observable states, prioritizes critical rules, and records routing decisions to support subsequent revision. (3) Feedback-driven, verified revision. Token-level distillation feedback and interaction outcomes guide rule diagnosis and editing; paired rule-level and whole-bank environment tests verify candidate changes. (4) Extensive experiments and superior performance. Comparisons, ablations, multi-cycle evaluations, and API-model studies on ALFWorld and WebShop validate SkillCycle, which surpasses WebShop SOTA in success rate and score without inference-time skills and outperforms static and single-refresh banks. Related work is discussed in Appendix~ app:related-work . title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
summary: Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Robot manipulation is increasingly benefiting from demonstrations collected across embodiments. Teleoperated demonstrations on low-cost bimanual platforms zhao2023aloha have been complemented by handheld interfaces that allow people to record demonstrations without a robot in the loop chi2024umi, ohkawa2026yubi , making data collection more scalable. These interfaces record end-effector trajectories, from which policies can learn to predict sequences of actions (action chunks) intelligence2025pi05 that are realized on a target robot. This flexibility introduces an embodiment gap spanning morphology, kinematics, and dynamics ohkawa2026yubi . Successful deployment depends not only on whether the robot can reproduce a demonstrated motion, but also on how quickly and reliably it can execute it. The timing encoded in a demonstration is inherited from the demonstrator but does not necessarily transfer to the target robot. Near contact, the same motion may be too fast for a robot with different compliance, actuator limits, and tracking dynamics, leading to overshoot or unintended impact. In free space, the mismatch runs the other way: the demonstrator's pace is no bound on the robot, which could move faster. A single global speed factor cannot resolve this trade-off. Slowing the whole trajectory makes contact more reliable but gives up the speed available elsewhere, while speeding it up increases the risk of failure near contact. Resolving this trade-off requires execution speed to vary along the predicted motion according to predicted contact, while respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. Prior work adapts execution timing at training time or inference time. Training-time methods modify demonstration timing through acceleration or downsampling based on entropy or semantic criteria guo2025demospeedup, kim2026espada , or explicitly represent execution tempo in the policy ijspeert2013dmp, nam2026speedaug . Such approaches can improve execution efficiency, but adapting to a target robot with different dynamic limits may require modifying the training data or retraining the policy. Inference-time methods instead adapt execution while leaving the policy unchanged. Time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP) pham2018toppra has been applied to chunked policies kim2026race to retime predicted paths under the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints, but has no notion of contact. Criticality-based speed adaptation ranawaka2025sail instead switches between preset global rates based on motion complexity or gripper events. Neither line of work jointly derives a contact-dependent speed constraint along the predicted motion and incorporates it into retiming under the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. We address this gap with RoboPace, an inference-time retiming method that imposes a position-dependent velocity ceiling that limits speed near predicted contact and incorporates it with the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints in a single time-optimal path parameterization. RoboPace predicts contact using two complementary cues: geometric proximity and wrist-camera prediction. Forward kinematics places the robot's hand meshes along the predicted path and measures proximity to the other hand and the table, limiting speed when either is approached. The wrist-camera model predicts the remaining steps until hand-to-object contact. Either cue can tighten the velocity ceiling, with smooth transitions back to full speed away from contact. RoboPace retimes newly predicted action chunks online during execution, requires no policy retraining, and sits between trajectory generation and low-level tracking without modifying either the policy or the tracking controller. We evaluate RoboPace in real-world experiments on a dual-arm robot across five commands spanning three contact-rich tasks, , , and . We compare against the \,Hz rollout rate used in training (the demo speed hereafter), uniform speed scaling, and physical-limit-only retiming kim2026race . RoboPace achieves a overall success rate, compared with for slow uniform execution, while completing four of five commands in about half its time. Related Work Imitation-learned policies inherit the temporal sampling of demonstrations rather than selecting an execution rate for the target robot. This arises in vision-language-action (VLA) models black2024pi0,kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi05 as well as in earlier, smaller policies zhao2023aloha . Existing work addresses this mismatch during training or at inference time. Training-time speed adaptation One line of work changes the temporal structure of demonstrations before training. DemoSpeedup down-samples segments according to an entropy-based proxy for required precision guo2025demospeedup , whereas ESPADA uses semantic judgments to choose the down-sampling schedule kim2026espada . A complementary line makes timing part of the learned policy: dynamical movement primitives include an explicit temporal constant ijspeert2013dmp ; SpeedAug and TempoVLA condition policy execution on tempo through reinforcement fine-tuning and retimed data, respectively nam2026speedaug,jing2026tempovla ; and AutoSpeed learns stage-adaptive motion speeds hu2026autospeed . B-spline Policy instead changes the action representation to a continuous curve that can be temporally scaled at execution han2026bspline . These methods alter data, training objectives, or policy representations; adapting learned timing to a new embodiment generally modifies one of them. Inference-time speed adaptation Time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP) computes the fastest timing of a fixed geometric path subject to robot constraints. These solvers handle joint velocity, acceleration, and torque limits via convex optimization verscheure2009timeoptimal , numerical integration pham2014topp , or reachability analysis (TOPP-RA) pham2018toppra . Cartesian constraints, including end-effector velocity bounds, can likewise be imposed along the path. TOPP-RA, Cartesian velocity constraints, and proximity-based speed reduction are established components marvel2017ssm,haddadin2009safe . RACE kim2026race converts predicted action chunks into geometric paths and applies TOPP-RA under the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints; it also uses a test-time search over candidate chunks to address asynchronous-inference misalignment. While its retiming formulation uses the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints, it does not introduce a path-dependent velocity constraint from predicted contact. SAIL ranawaka2025sail adapts speed using criticality cues by switching among preset rates. SAIL exemplifies adaptive speed modulation, but its rate-selection rule does not formulate it as a path-parameterization problem subject to the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. Other inference-time methods address different aspects of action-chunk execution. Real-time chunking black2025rtc and masked action chunking wang2026mac maintain consistency across asynchronous chunk transitions; PACE nie2026pace selects an execution horizon; and TRACT liu2026tract routes chunks across procedural phases. Prior work has separately addressed two complementary aspects of execution-speed adaptation: robot-limit-aware time-optimal retiming and criticality-based speed modulation. To our knowledge, these elements have not been integrated for online retiming of policy-predicted action chunks by using predicted contact to define a path-varying velocity constraint that is jointly enforced with the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. RoboPace provides this inference-time integration while leaving the policy and its predicted geometry unchanged, without policy retraining. Problem Formulation sec:problem We consider online retiming of policy-predicted action chunks. The goal is to execute each chunk as fast as permitted by the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints while slowing near predicted contact. At inference time, the policy outputs end-effector pose deltas for each arm on the fixed demo-speed source grid with period . We separate the chunk's geometry from this source timing. Let , , denote the joint-space spline supplied to the retimer, through the retained waypoints of both arms, with uniform over the waypoints. Let denote the contact-critical portion of the path, comprising waypoints within a threshold of predicted or ongoing contact. We seek a monotone time parameterization by solving eq:problem Here, is the chunk duration, and are the velocity and acceleration limits of joint , representing the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints, is the Cartesian speed of hand body , is the contact speed limit, and is the path speed corresponding to the joint velocity commanded at the transition, allowing consecutive chunks to join without stopping. We solve with TOPP-RA pham2018toppra chunk by chunk, with the entry speed fixed by and the exit speed set as in Sec.~ sec:topp . The resulting timing is time-optimal per chunk. The contact speed limit is smoothly ramped over source steps on either side of each contact-critical waypoint (Sec.~ sec:topp ). The set is obtained from geometric proximity and a learned contact predictor (Sec.~ sec:cues ). RoboPace Overview For each predicted action chunk, RoboPace solves the time-optimal retiming problem in online (Fig.~ fig:overview ): each chunk from the deployed policy becomes the joint path , cues mark its contact-critical waypoints, contact-aware TOPP-RA solves , and the play-out commands and requeries the policy after a fixed interval of commanded source steps (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). The only learned component of RoboPace is the contact predictor; the rest is deterministic given fixed parameters and the robot's constraints. Action Chunks to Joint Paths sec:ik The chunk is converted to joint waypoints through sequential damped-least-squares inverse kinematics, which preserves the policy's geometry and drops only unreachable waypoints. Each row, a body-frame pose delta about the hand root, is composed into an target at the tool center point and integrated forward from the last commanded configuration. Targets are solved within the joint limits, each seeded from the previous solution, and the path is truncated at the first waypoint whose Cartesian residual exceeds an IK residual threshold. The joint paths of the two arms are combined into a single path, with each waypoint pairing their joint configurations at the same source step. If their valid IK solutions have different lengths, both are truncated to the shorter length before being combined. Consecutive waypoints on the combined path that advance by less than a dwell threshold are then compressed to their first row while retaining their source indices; this shortens geometric dwells and the gripper profile sampled over them (Sec.~ sec:playout ). Forward kinematics provides the world poses of the hand collision bodies at each retained waypoint for use by the contact cues. Contact Prediction and Gating sec:gates A waypoint is contact-critical when contact is imminent or ongoing: the retiming holds the hand at or below the contact speed limit of on contact-critical waypoints and elsewhere leaves the pace to the robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. We use two complementary cues: geometric proximity and camera-based contact prediction. The geometric cue applies two proximity conditions, hand--hand and hand--environment, and flags a waypoint when either distance falls below its threshold; it requires no sensing but accounts only for modeled geometry. title: YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.
full_text: Introduction A robot demonstration shows how the task was executed, but its label records only what the task was. A session of sorting industrial parts into bins shows which gripper acts, which part it contacts, and how that part is grasped, handed between grippers, and released. However, all of it is annotated as ``pick a part and place it in a box'', which omits interaction details. This matters because vision-language-action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capability from large-scale pretraining~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024,black2024pi0,black2025pi05 , and language is the only channel through which that capability is elicited. A language label therefore does more than document an episode, while current datasets include one task-level label per episode and repeat it across every demonstration of the same task class. For instance, recent robot-free handheld interfaces such as UMI~ chi2024universal and YUBI~ ohkawa2026yubi offer large-scale data ( ~hours of bimanual interaction by YUBI) at higher throughput than teleoperation systems~ zhao2023learning,fu2024mobilealoha . Yet fine granularity and diversity of that language remain the bottleneck. Existing VLA post-training pipelines rely on coarse episode-level language instructions and unsegmented action sequences~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid . This coarse supervision fails to convey spatio-temporal dynamics, such as gripper-object contact transitions, grip affordances, and bimanual coordination, required for contact-rich, high-precision manipulation. Inspired by the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis in LLMs~ zhou2023lima , which posits that pre-trained models already possess extensive world knowledge and post-training primarily elicits proper output formats, we argue that a similar paradigm holds for VLAs. Pre-trained VLAs already encode rich geometric and physical representations; their limitation is not innate capability but the lack of precise alignment signals during post-training~ chen2024sharegpt4v,yu2024rlaifv . We present YUBI-STAG, a framework that resolves this mismatch by annotating demonstrations with the interaction structure they already contain, and then post-training a VLA on those annotations. Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding (STAG) pairs a trained contact-object segmentation module with a staged annotator built on an off-the-shelf multimodal LLM~ qwen36_27b . The segmentation module localizes contact intervals and contacted-object masks from both wrist views. The resulting contact tracks identify when each gripper interacts with which object, allowing YUBI-STAG to chain localized visual evidence across interactions to recover object identities, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and state changes. Finally, we evaluate contact- and semantic-rich alignment of VLAs using the STAG annotations. We pre-train a -based policy~ black2025pi05 on ~hours of YUBI data Experiments on a bimanual Franka robot show that alignment with these rich annotations improves fine-grained language following, contact-robust manipulation, and compositional generalization to complex tasks. The contributions of this paper are: YUBI-STAG and YUBI-VLM ( ). A contact-anchored annotation pipeline that turns coarsely labeled bimanual demonstrations into grounded spatio-temporal annotations, and a distilled model that produces them directly from raw, unsegmented, wrist-view-only video without action-boundary supervision. YUBI-STAG-Bench ( ). Contact- and semantic-rich VLA post-training ( ). A contact and semantic-rich post-training recipe supplying handedness, contact phases, and contact-aware sampling to a -based policy, extending data-centric alignment from instruction text to physical interaction. Related Work Scalable Collection of Unconstrained Manipulation Data Recent advances in low-cost bimanual systems~ zhao2023learning,fu2024mobilealoha , teleoperation~ qin2023anyteleop , and portable handheld grippers~ chi2024universal,ohkawa2026yubi have enabled large-scale collection of diverse robot demonstrations~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid,walke2023bridgedatav2 . As collection scales toward in-the-wild settings, however, demonstrations increasingly contain background clutter, camera motion, operator variation, and lack explicit action boundaries~ mandlekar2022what,bharadhwaj2024roboagent,cui2023play . Converting such noisy, unsegmented data into fine-grained supervision therefore requires substantial curation and annotation, creating a new bottleneck for scalable robot learning. Video-Language Grounding and Automated Data Annotation Data-Centric Post-Training Alignment in VLA Policies In NLP, the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis~ zhou2023lima posits that vast knowledge and reasoning capability are acquired during pre-training, whereas post-training alignment primarily elicits output formats and behavioral styles using high-quality supervision signals. Its strong form is contested: stylistic alignment is recoverable from the base model~ lin2024unlocking , while task competence continues to scale with post-training data~ raghavendra2024revisiting . While this data-centric alignment paradigm is well-known in LLM/VLMs, its extension to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024,black2025pi05 has only recently begun to be explored. Existing VLA alignment efforts optimize preferences~ zhang2024grape , curate which demonstrations to train on~ chen2025curating , or pair fixed trajectories with fine-grained instructions~ hu2026finevla . However, these efforts, like standard behavior cloning, provide no explicit supervision at contact transitions (approach, grasp onset, hold, release) or bimanual coordination moments. Spatio-Temporal Interaction Annotation sec:stag To promote alignment between VLA policies and fine-grained manipulation language, we introduce two complementary annotation approaches. We propose YUBI-STAG ( ), a Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding (STAG) pipeline that enriches YUBI demonstrations with contact-aware, rich annotations grounded in space and time. We distill this multi-stage pipeline into YUBI-VLM ( ), which directly annotates raw videos at lower cost and supports wrist-only inference for portable data collection. YUBI-STAG subsec:stag YUBI demonstrations provide temporally localized primitive-action (PA) labels such as ``Open the lid of the jar.'' Following YUBI terminology, a PA denotes a composite manipulation unit, and we call its constituent actions (e.g., reach, grasp, rotate, and release) PA stages. The original annotations label only the coarse intent of the entire PA; they provide neither its stage boundaries and actions nor object attributes, bimanual coordination, or resulting object changes. YUBI-STAG takes the PA labels and synchronized videos from one overhead and two wrist cameras, and recovers the missing elements as spatio-temporally grounded, structured annotations that can be readily added as language supervision for VLA training. YUBI-STAG combines (i) a contact-object segmentation module and (ii) a staged VLM-based annotator; provides an overview, and the four annotation groups are detailed below. The given PA intervals serve as temporal scaffolds, while retaining PAs in the output schema allows YUBI-VLM to later learn the complete schema from raw wrist-camera videos without predefined PAs. (i) Contact-object segmentation module Fine-grained annotation requires knowing when each gripper contacts which object. A common proxy detects grasps from changes in gripper aperture, but it is unstable and misses non-grasping contacts used to stabilize or support objects. Because low-cost systems such as UMI and YUBI lack tactile sensors, we instead infer contact and the contacted object visually. Our module encodes both wrist-camera streams with a frozen DINOv2-L~ oquab2023dinov2 and jointly models their frame features using a lightweight temporal transformer. For each gripper, an MLP head predicts the contact state and a DPT-style decoder predicts the pixel-level mask of the contacted object. To train at scale, we derive pseudo-labels from gripper-aperture cues. When the aperture stabilizes, a point between the fingertips prompts SAM2~ ravi2025sam to segment and bidirectionally track a candidate object. We filter background candidates using point-tracking co-motion~ karaev2025cotracker3 and monocular-depth agreement, then manually filter the results for initial training. Finally, we self-train on more diverse data and fine-tune on a small set of precise human annotations. (ii) VLM-based annotation pipeline Rather than infer the full annotation in one MLLM call, YUBI-STAG organizes MLLM queries into four stages, each building on previously resolved annotations and relevant visual evidence. The preceding contact-object segmentation module provides contact tracks, each consisting of a contact interval and per-frame object masks. These tracks anchor when and where interactions occur. 1) Scene configuration. The first stage builds a scene-level inventory of object names and counts. The MLLM jointly examines the overall scene and object-centric observations localized by contact masks, providing both global scene context and clear views of objects during interaction. For each instance, it records color, material, shape, size, and role (part, container, surface, or fixture) under a persistent ID shared by all later annotations. Establishing this inventory first avoids assigning new identities to the same physical object at different interactions. 2) PA stages, per-gripper actions, and coordination. Before annotating gripper actions, we bind each contact track to an object ID from the inventory. Appearance alone is ambiguous when instances look alike, so we also exploit temporal continuity: tracks separated by a release and immediate re-grasp, or connected by a handover, should refer to the same object. Combining these constraints with appearance within the track masks provides stable object identities across interactions. The given PA intervals provide coarse temporal structure, which we refine into constituent stages using the contact tracks. For each stage, we record the participating object IDs, each gripper's action, and one of seven coordination types: left- or right-only, either gripper as primary with the other supporting, either handover direction, or bimanual. 3) Object changes. We determine how each interaction changes the manipulated objects and their relations, using wrist views for close-up evidence and the overhead view for broader spatial context. Comparing each contacted object before contact and after release, we record its source and destination relative to other objects, together with changes in state, assembly, or containment. 4) Unified grounded PA annotation. Finally, the MLLM combines the resolved PA stages, per-gripper actions, coordination, and object changes into a grounded PA description, with each object mention linked to its persistent ID. title: ΔWAM: Distilling Action Tangent Fields into World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAM) improve robot policies by augmenting sparse action supervision with dense future prediction. However, much of the predictable future is dominated by appearance and scene persistence rather than action-dependent dynamics. We observe that several recent WAM designs, including optical flow, motion-centric representations, and latent actions, can be understood from a common perspective in which world supervision becomes more efficient as it contains a higher proportion of action-relevant variation. Based on this insight, we introduce Action Tangent Fields, which reformulate world supervision through a local Taylor expansion of how actions induce changes in future dynamics. We represent future dynamics in Residual-VAE space, where the future latent remains recoverable from the current latent and its residual, and use a strong action-conditioned world model (ACWM) to probe the local correspondence between action variations and residual-world variations. This local first-order structure is distilled into the WAM to guide its denoising supervision toward dynamics that are more tightly coupled to action, rather than merely predictable from appearance. Across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and RoboTwin2.0-Plus, our method consistently improves robustness to lighting, background, camera, layout, and other environmental perturbations. Despite using no large-scale embodied pretraining, it achieves stronger robustness under several distribution shifts than pretrained policies. We further distill multi-step VideoDiT denoising into a single step for efficient inference. Our results suggest that effective WAM supervision should remain information-rich while concentrating its predictive capacity on the directions along which actions change the future.

Introduction Behavior cloning labels each demonstrated observation with an action. World Action Models (WAMs) also predict the future video, giving dense supervision for object motion, contact, and state changes that a single action label cannot describe. A video target, however, rewards predictability rather than control relevance. Backgrounds, camera views, and untouched objects are already determined by the current frame and persist as the robot acts, so a model that reproduces them reduces its loss substantially while learning little about the consequences of its own actions. The value of world supervision therefore depends less on how much of the future it covers than on how much of that future is action-dependent. Recent WAM designs change the target itself. Optical-flow and motion-centric targets keep only what moves, and latent-action targets compress the future into a compact code. Both reduce the supervision spent on static appearance, which is why they help, but both rely on motion as a proxy for action-dependence: a lighting change or a moving distractor alters the future with no contribution from the robot, and dropping appearance removes cues that contact-rich manipulation needs. A change of target also cannot reveal which directions of the future respond to the action, because each demonstration records one action and the single future that followed it. It is an isolated point of the action--dynamics relation, and its local neighborhood is never observed. Our first step therefore keeps the target information-rich and changes its coordinate instead. Given the current frame, we subtract a broadcast reference derived from it, so the residual describes how the scene departs from the observed frame rather than restating it. Reference and residual recover the future VAE latent exactly, so no information is lost, and because the reference depends only on the current frame, subtracting it leaves the response to an action perturbation unchanged. The second step supplies the missing neighborhood through a probe. For a fixed scene, an embodiment-specific action-conditioned world model (ACWM) is queried at small, temporally smooth perturbations of the expert action. The resulting residual futures differ mainly along directions the ACWM treats as action-sensitive, and their normalized differences span an Action Tangent Field (ATF), a low-dimensional estimate of those directions. Post-training keeps every element of the demonstrated residual in the loss and adds weight along the ATF, which makes the world loss anisotropic, ordinary world post-training is the isotropic special case. The probe sets the weighting, never the targets. We first mid-train the Wan VideoDiT on a modest amount of robot manipulation video to adapt its prediction space to the residual latent space, then post-train a Fast-WAM-style policy with cached ATFs. Caching keeps the ACWM out of policy training and inference. Extensive experiments show that supervising dynamics-relevant world representations enables our method to generalize to visual perturbations substantially better than competing methods. Our contributions are as follows. We introduce an information-preserving Residual-VAE target that shifts world prediction toward scene dynamics while retaining exact recovery of the future video. Motivated by a first-order Taylor expansion of the action-to-future dynamics map, we introduce Action Tangent Fields to estimate locally action-responsive directions and emphasize them during denoising supervision of the real demonstrated future. We obtain efficient world features with one VideoDiT evaluation at inference. Aggregate success improves from 51.5 to 87.8 over Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and from 72.7 to 79.3 on RoboTwin 2.0-Plus. Related Work World Action Models World Action Models (WAMs) complement sparse action labels with future prediction, encouraging policies to retain object states, interactions, and temporal dynamics. Predict-then-act methods such as GE-Act generate compact visual futures and recover controls through inverse dynamics, while GE-Act~2.0 scales this design with heterogeneous interaction data~ geact . Joint models instead couple world and action generation: LingBot-VA autoregressively interleaves both outputs, whereas Cosmos Policy represents future observations, actions, and values as latent frames of a video diffusion model~ lingbotva,cosmospolicy . A complementary line treats prediction primarily as representation supervision. Fast-WAM and Light-WAM retain video co-training but omit explicit generation at deployment~ fastwam,lightwam , whereas Efficient-WAM and Faster-WAM preserve future latents while reducing generation or video--action interaction costs~ efficientwam,fasterwam . The prediction target nevertheless determines how model capacity is allocated: full video latents preserve rich details but are dominated by static appearance and other variations weakly related to control, whereas flow, residual, and motion-centric targets emphasize change but may discard useful cues. In contrast, Action Tangent Fields retain an information-rich residual future space and selectively emphasize locally action-responsive directions. Action-Conditioned World Models Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) predict visual consequences under specified controls. Recent systems broaden the control interface: Cosmos~3 jointly models language, images, video, audio, and actions~ cosmos3 , Hydra-0 represents actions as pixel-space flow for cross-embodiment transfer~ hydra0 , and Pelican-Sim combines a unified numerical action space with rendered action videos~ pelicansim . These methods condition generation through native action tokens, visual motion, and action-rendered observations, respectively. Another line improves simulation reliability. ABot-PhysWorld uses physics-aware data and preference optimization to suppress implausible interactions~ abotphysworld . Ctrl-World combines multi-view prediction, frame-level action conditioning, and pose-aware memory for policy-in-the-loop rollouts~ ctrlworld , while WALL-SS uses coarse-to-fine autoregression and compressed memory for long streaming generation~ wallss . WorldSync addresses failures on off-expert commands through broader action coverage, dynamics grounding, and intervention-effect alignment~ worldsync . Unlike these approaches, we neither plan with generated rollouts nor use synthetic futures as supervision targets. Instead, we perturb demonstrated actions and use the ACWM as a local differential probe in Residual-VAE space, transferring the resulting first-order action--world geometry while retaining real demonstrations as prediction targets. Method sec:method We introduce WAM to train a world-action policy on real future video while transferring local action sensitivity from an action-conditioned world model (ACWM). Figure~ fig:delta-wam-pipeline outlines the method. We first adapt Wan to predict future video latents relative to the current frame~ wan2025wan . We then perturb demonstrated actions and query an embodiment-specific ACWM~ cosmos3 to extract action tangent fields (ATFs), which identify locally action-responsive directions. Finally, we post-train a Fast-WAM-style VideoDiT--ActionDiT policy~ fastwam on real action--future pairs, giving additional weight to prediction errors along those directions. At inference, one VideoDiT pass provides the world features used to generate an action chunk. title: AeroEval: Staged Program and Execution Validation for AI-Generated Drone Missions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate drone programs from natural-language mission descriptions, but syntactically valid programs may still violate user intent, environmental constraints, and mission-level behavior. This problem is pronounced in cyber-physical applications, where correctness depends on the interaction among generated code, mobile sensing, environmental geometry, event-driven analytics, and physical execution. Existing drone code-generation systems primarily use prompt guardrails or simulator outcomes and provide limited failure localization. We present AeroEval, an agent-assisted middleware for staged validation of AI-generated drone missions. AeroEval combines deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents. It first validates program syntax, platform API usage, and mission intent, and then evaluates the realized behavior using execution trajectories, mission requirements, and environmental context. Each stage returns structured failure information for iterative regeneration. In our evaluation using 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types over AirSim and Gazebo simulators, AeroEval improves navigation success from 55% to 95%. In a stagewise ablation study, our Code and Trajectory Validators by themselves achieve mean run-level success rates of 44% and 56%, respectively, while the full AeroEval pipeline achieves 88%; the stages detect complementary failures in program structure, API usage, mission intent, obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, and event-driven transitions and the guided regeneration corrects for them. Across the main analytics missions, AeroEval increases aggregate run-level success from 34% for one-shot AeroGen to 88% within the regeneration budget. These results demonstrate the benefit of combining program-level and execution-grounded agentic validation for AI-generated drone applications in the evaluated environment.

Introduction sec:intro Large Language Models (LLMs) allow users to construct drone applications by specifying missions such as delivery, survey, inspection, and target tracking in natural language~ liang-icra-2023,gsce,wang-icra-2026,aerogen . The generated programs coordinate navigation, mobile sensing, analytics, and control across drone, edge, and cloud resources. Their correctness therefore depends on more than syntactic validity. A program must use the available platform interfaces, preserve user intent, respond to sensed events, and satisfy spatio-temporal constraints imposed by the physical environment. AI-generated drone missions are consequently pervasive cyber-physical applications whose software behavior must be interpreted relative to their execution context~ 10.1145/3486607.3486750,9612021,uav-crowd-percom24, dronevlc-percom23 . However, existing code generation workflows provide limited evidence that a plausible program actually realizes its requested mission. A syntactically valid program may fly directly through an obstacle, survey a region along the wrong orientation, leave part of a search region uncovered, or fail to transition from search to tracking after detecting a target. These errors depend on environmental geometry, sensing events, and realized trajectories, and may remain undetected by code-level checks. Conversely, a simulator failure alone does not identify whether the cause is an invalid API call, an intent mismatch, or incorrect physical behavior. Hence, validating generated drone applications requires both program-level and execution-grounded evidence. Existing cyber-physical code-generation systems provide only part of this lifecycle. Structured prompting improves generated drone code but discovers failures primarily through subsequent execution~ gsce . Simulation-guided generation has also been applied to autonomous-driving software, where rule-based assessments of critical traffic scenarios are returned to an LLM for code repair~ nouri-simulation-guided-2025 . similarly uses simulator feedback to iteratively refine drone navigation programs~ wang-icra-2026 , while combines planning, code generation, sensing, and analytics for more complex missions~ aerogen . However, these systems do not systematically separate failures caused by program structure, platform API usage, mission interpretation, and realized physical behavior. Validation frameworks for autonomous systems combine formal specifications, simulation, digital twins, and domain-specific tests~ araujo-ras-vnv-2023,polyverif-2023 , but typically assume that the application logic and testable properties have already been authored. In contrast, an AI-generated mission is an untrusted program synthesized from an informal user specification~ safety-llm-driven-robotics,robotics-sw-engg . We present , an agent-assisted middleware that performs staged validation between AI-based mission generation and drone execution. Its Code Validator combines deterministic syntax and API checks with context-grounded validation of mission intent. Programs that pass this stage execute in a physics-based simulator. The Trajectory Validator then evaluates the realized behavior using the mission specification, robot and world descriptions, execution trajectory, and observed events. For navigation tasks with a reference path, uses numerical trajectory comparison. For analytical missions without a unique reference path, a bounded validation agent evaluates properties such as obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, orientation, and event-driven transitions. A failed stage returns a structured diagnosis to the generator for refinement. The key novelty of our work is the composition of program-level and execution-grounded validation within a common mission lifecycle. Figure~ fig:motivation summarizes both its impact and the reason for staged validation. Under a common budget of at most three regeneration cycles, the Code and Trajectory Validators alone achieve mean run-level success rates of and , respectively, while their composition in the complete workflow achieves . Relative to the underlying generators, improves navigation success over the closed-loop baseline from to tasks, and analytical run-level success over one-shot from to runs. This is because program validation detects structural, API, and intent errors, while execution-grounded validation detects violations that arise from the interaction between the generated program and its physical environment. In this paper, we make the following key contributions: [leftmargin=*] We propose a staged validation lifecycle that separates program validity, mission-intent alignment, and realized physical behavior, and returns stage-specific feedback for iterative regeneration (Sec.~ sec:design ). We develop context-grounded behavioral validation for analytical missions without a unique reference trajectory. The validation agents combine mission requirements, program artifacts, robot and world descriptions, and execution observations to evaluate spatio-temporal and event-driven properties (Sec.~ subsec:trajectory-validation ). We evaluate across 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types using two generators, two simulators and two reasoning models. The evaluation includes stagewise ablations, failure localization, limited physical-drone execution, and validation overheads (Sec.~ sec:eval ). Related Work sec:related-work lies at the intersection of AI-based drone program synthesis, validation of autonomous systems, and middleware for pervasive cyber-physical applications. Prior work has studied these concerns largely independently. We instead examine how program analysis, mission context, and execution observations can be combined to validate and repair AI-generated drone applications. AI-based drone program synthesis LLMs can translate natural-language specifications into executable programs for embodied control~ liang-icra-2023 . In the drone domain, GSCE uses structured prompts, API constraints, and examples, but detects failures primarily through subsequent execution~ gsce . incorporates simulator observations into a refinement loop for navigation tasks, regenerating programs that violate waypoint, altitude, yaw, or geometric requirements~ clgsce,wang-icra-2026 . extends single-shot generation to analytical missions that compose navigation, sensing, analytics, and deployment over heterogeneous resources~ aerogen . Simulation-guided generation has also been applied to autonomous-driving software, where generated control code is evaluated over predefined critical scenarios and rule-based assessments are returned for repair~ nouri-simulation-guided-2025 . Corrective robot-code generation similarly uses physics-based execution or static text-based simulation to predict navigation failures and refine generated operations~ wang-icra-2026 . These approaches demonstrate the value of execution feedback, but organize validation around scenario outcomes or deviations from specified navigation behavior. instead proposes a validation lifecycle that separates deterministic syntax and API checks, context-grounded intent validation, and post-execution behavioral validation. This distinction is necessary because invalid API usage may not be observable from a trajectory, while collision, coverage, orientation, and event-transition violations may not be inferred reliably from program text. Further, supports analytical missions with multiple valid trajectories by evaluating mission-specific spatio-temporal and event-driven properties using the mission specification, generated program, environment descriptions, and execution trace. Validation of autonomous systems Validation and Verification of autonomous systems commonly use formal specifications, simulation, digital twins, scenario-based testing, and runtime monitoring~ araujo-ras-vnv-2023, polyverif-2023,torens2013automated,matalonga2024verification, aslandere2025survey . PolyVerif treats validation of AI-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) as an infrastructure problem requiring reusable simulators, test environments, and analysis tools~ polyverif-2023 . Co-zyBench similarly uses co-simulation middleware and Digital Twins to evaluate context-dependent behavior before physical deployment~ cozybench-percom24 . These techniques typically assume that application logic has been authored and that the evaluated properties can be formally or procedurally specified. In contrast, an AI-generated mission is an untrusted program synthesized from an informal user specification and may misinterpret the task before controller-level properties can be examined. instead validates program structure, platform interfaces, mission intent, and realized spatio-temporal behavior before physical execution; formal verification and runtime assurance remain complementary. LLM-guided validation has also been used to translate natural-language driving policies into checkable specifications, analyze their consistency with autonomous-driving software, and generate simulation tests~ zhang-semantic-validation-2026 . This approach validates software against explicit safety policies, whereas localizes failures across generated program structure, mission intent, and realized behavior for navigation and analytical drone missions. title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

Introduction sec:introduction nmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have evolved from small remote-controlled platforms into core infrastructure for the low-altitude economy (LAE) Pongsakornsathien_2025 . They are now used in last-mile package delivery~ 11426817 , environmental monitoring and surveillance tagle2025effective , disaster-zone emergency response manzini2026deploying , infrastructure inspection ren2025 , and aerial communication services. In these applications, the critical challenge has shifted from single-UAV navigation to fleet-level dispatch and coordination. The dispatch system must decide which UAV should serve which task, when it should depart, which route it should follow, how energy and communication resources should be allocated, and how conflicts in dense low-altitude airspace should be avoided. We refer to this system-level problem as UAV dispatch: the scheduling, routing, resource allocation, association, and coordination of UAV fleets under physical, communication, safety, privacy, and regulatory constraints. Fig.~ fig:intro_overview organizes it as a tree: its roots ground UAV dispatch in mission and application demands, core dispatch problems, and physical and operational constraints. Its trunk traces the evolution from single-UAV systems to LLM-enabled applications, and its four branches show the paradigms we summarized in this survey. UAV dispatch is attracting rapidly growing attention in both research and real-world deployment. Commercial UAV markets are expanding in logistics, inspection, and public services, regulators such as the FAA and EASA are developing frameworks for high-density BVLOS and U-space operations, and China has positioned the LAE as a national growth engine. This deployment momentum motivates the central premise of this survey: large-scale UAV operations cannot be supported by isolated path planning or single-agent control alone. As the number of UAVs grows, collision-free trajectories and communication resources become harder to allocate jointly Gong_2026 . Early multi-quadrotor swarm systems 6577992 further show that scalable UAV coordination requires tight integration among planning, communication, localization, and collision avoidance. Dispatch decisions become tightly coupled across task assignment, trajectory planning, communication, energy, timing, and privacy. Human operators increasingly issue open-ended mission requests rather than fully structured optimization inputs. UAV dispatch therefore requires a framework that connects classical optimization and learning with semantic mission understanding, cross-layer coordination, and trustworthy human oversight. The emergence of LLMs makes this framework more tractable by providing new interfaces for semantic interpretation, tool use, and human-facing explanation. Recent vision-language and multimodal LLM studies provide the perception and grounding foundations needed for UAV missions involving aerial images, maps, and natural-language instructions han2023vitSurveyTPAMI,zhang2024vlmSurveyTPAMI,xu2025lvlmEhubTPAMI,yang2026defyingDistractionsTPAMI,huang2025causalityMLLMTPAMI,zhang2026beyondLlavaHdTPAMI,wang2026vlBiasBenchTPAMI,radford2021clip,li2023blip2,liu2023llava . Together with tool-use, agent, and embodied-model frameworks, these models can interpret natural-language missions, retrieve regulations or maps, reason over heterogeneous context, call external solvers, critique candidate plans, and explain dispatch decisions to human operators Chang_2024,shen2023hugginggpt,schick2023toolformer,yao2023react,besta2024graphOfThoughts,driess2023palmE . Recent UAV-oriented studies have already demonstrated a range of LLM-assisted capabilities, including path planning, vision-language navigation grounding, compliance-aware trajectory generation, multi-objective UAV network optimization, and edge-based multi-LLM orchestration Gong_2026,lin2024correctableLandmarkTPAMI,wang2026imagineNavTPAMI,lin2026evolveNavTPAMI,chen2025constraintAwareVLNTPAMI,li2025llmIsacUav,luo2025multiLlmEdge,liu2025llmInspection . However, these efforts remain fragmented across planning, communication, swarm coordination, inspection, and safety, lacking a unified abstraction to connect them. Existing surveys summarized in Table~ tab:intro_survey_comparison predominantly focus on UAV trajectory prediction and path planning shukla2025,ghambari2024 , swarm networking and collaborative control cao2024,tang2023 , security and privacy sciancalepore2024 , or broader LLM-related topics such as model evaluation, vision-language models, and LLM-agent systems Chang_2024,zhang2024vlmSurveyTPAMI,guo2024llmMultiAgentsSurvey . However, these surveys still lack a dispatch-centered taxonomy that systematically explains how LLMs reshape the end-to-end UAV operation pipeline—from mission intent and task assignment to trajectory planning, scheduling, resource allocation, and execution monitoring. In contrast, this work takes UAV dispatch as the central organizing abstraction, rather than using path planning, swarm control, or LLM agents as isolated lenses. We study how LLMs reshape dispatch interfaces, dispatch logic, and dispatch verification across four emerging paradigms, thereby filling this gap and motivating the central question of this paper: How should UAV dispatch be organized in the LLM era? To answer this question, we propose a dispatch-logic taxonomy based on the transformation from mission descriptions to executable dispatch decisions. At the top level, we organize dispatch logic into four paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. After this top-level classification, we organize papers within each paradigm along several secondary axes. These axes include the dispatch decisions they cover, namely task assignment, trajectory or route planning, scheduling, resource allocation, and cooperation or association among UAVs. We also record the solver family used by each study, including optimization, learning, auctions, heuristics, or LLM-tool orchestration, and the application context it targets. Among these categories, (1) pipeline dispatch covers methods that convert a mission into ordered stages, such as semantic parsing, task decomposition, assignment, trajectory generation, scheduling, and monitoring. Its dispatch process is organized as a stage-wise workflow in which LLMs can serve as parsers, tool selectors, and critics, rather than as a single global optimization problem. (2) Global assignment dispatch covers centralized or globally coordinated methods that jointly determine task matching, routes, schedules, resources, and associations when sufficient global state is available. It relies on a central dispatcher or equivalent global view, while the LLM layer interprets intent, retrieves rules, explains tradeoffs, or guides solver choice. (3) Decentralized agentic dispatch covers agent-led methods in which UAVs locally select tasks, bid, negotiate, replan, or learn policies from partial observations. Building on this decentralized decision-making paradigm, task ownership emerges from local autonomy, while LLM agents serve as complementary components that enhance the system with memory, semantic negotiation, and reflection, without replacing verified control mechanisms. (4) Divide-and-conquer dispatch covers methods that partition a large mission by dispatch decisions, objectives, regions, time windows, fleet groups, roles, communication links, knowledge sources, or model placement. The main design question is how to split and then reconnect subproblems through solvers, retrieval sources, edge models, and multi-agent orchestration. Together, these four paradigms cover the dispatch layer of UAV systems. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: We define UAV dispatch in the LLM era as a semantic--symbolic--physical decision process that maps human intent and environmental context to task assignment, trajectory, schedule, resource allocation, and cooperation decisions. We propose a dispatch-logic taxonomy with four LLM-era paradigms. This taxonomy connects classical UAV dispatch methods with emerging LLM-enabled dispatch architectures. We analyze how LLMs can serve as semantic parsers, retrieval-grounded planners, solver orchestrators, local agents, multi-agent coordinators, safety critics, and human-facing explanation interfaces, while emphasizing that physical feasibility must still be guaranteed by specialized modules. We identify open challenges and future directions for trustworthy LLM-enabled UAV dispatch, including grounding, hallucination control, edge deployment, multi-agent trust, privacy, accountability, benchmarking, and human governance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:preliminaries introduces the preliminaries and unified notation for UAV dispatch. Sections~ sec:pipeline_dispatch to~ sec:divide_conquer_dispatch review the four dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch for UAV missions, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. Section~ sec:opportunities_challenges synthesizes the four paradigms in the LLM era and discusses future challenges and research directions. Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the survey. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Before reviewing the four paradigms in detail, we first introduce the definitions and notation used throughout this survey. We begin with the traditional dispatch framework, which provides the classical notions of task assignment, scheduling, routing, and resource allocation. We then extend this view to unmanned dispatch systems, emphasizing how autonomous perception, communication, and online adaptation inherit from, yet differ from, traditional dispatch. Finally, we specialize this view to UAV dispatch systems, where UAV operations introduce three-dimensional mobility, airspace safety, endurance, communication, and regulatory constraints. title: Towards Accurate End-Effector Localization for UMI-Style Robotic Manipulation Teaching
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://mild-web.github.io
summary: Robot demonstration learning requires accurate and temporally complete end-effector localization during close-range manipulation and camera occlusion. Existing SLAM benchmarks emphasize navigation motions, whereas manipulation datasets prioritize policy learning over localization evaluation. We introduce MILD, a Manipulation-Interface Localization Dataset with real-world and simulation sequences. The real-world subset provides 86 sensor sequences from Insta360 X5 and Insight9 across 15 repeated tabletop tasks, calibration assets, and a per-execution robot end-effector reference trajectory. The simulation subset, MILD-Sim, extends task coverage in Isaac Sim for controlled manipulation-replay studies. Benchmarking visual-inertial and fiducial-aided systems on instrumented real-world recordings reveals large differences in both TCP-relative trajectory error and temporal coverage, even under the same nominal task. To support marker-augmented teaching workspaces without a pre-surveyed fiducial map, we present AprilVINS, which combines fisheye visual-inertial estimation with sequence-local AprilTag geometry and separates prior admission from guarded export of the jointly optimized state. On Insta360 AprilTag4 recordings, AprilVINS(full) under a unified protocol with sequence-specific profiles reaches millimeter-level SE(3)-aligned TCP-relative APE RMSE with high time completion and lower reported error than the tested routes under their respective protocols, whereas fisheye VIO without tag factors remains at centimeter scale. Ablations separate accuracy from exportability, and a MILD-Sim replay study provides task-specific tolerance references for interpreting those error magnitudes. Together, MILD and AprilVINS provide a diagnostic benchmarking framework for UMI-style demonstration collection. Code, datasets, and evaluation manifests will be released upon acceptance.

Existing SLAM benchmarks emphasize navigation motions, whereas manipulation datasets prioritize policy learning over localization evaluation. We introduce , a Manipulation-Interface Localization Dataset with real-world and simulation sequences.
