Code, datasets, and evaluation manifests will be released upon acceptance. --- Manipulation-interface localization, visual--inertial odometry, AprilTag, robot teaching, benchmark dataset. Introduction sec:introduction Demonstration collection for robot manipulation requires recovering the demonstrated end-effector trajectory from a portable manipulation interface. UMI systems have made in-the-wild data acquisition practical through a map-then-localize pipeline~ chi2024umi , but close-range manipulation stresses localization: hands and objects occlude the camera, useful features leave the field of view near contact, and slow motions can break visual--inertial initialization. These conditions resemble the degradation cases studied in ground-robot SLAM~ yin2023ground,yin2024ground , but at tabletop scale with tighter coverage requirements. A low-error fragment is not enough when the rest of a demonstration is untracked, so manipulation-interface localization should report both trajectory accuracy and temporal coverage. Existing localization benchmarks target aerial, hand-held, and mobile-robot motion~ burri2016euroc,schubert2018tum,yin2021m2dgr,zhang2025towards , whereas manipulation datasets focus on policy learning~ khazatsky2024droid_dataset,fang2023rh20t,zhaxizhuoma2025fastumi,jin2026umibench . complements the latter by benchmarking the sensing layer that determines whether a collected demonstration is replayable, rather than evaluating downstream policy quality directly. This gap matters because localization error enters a demonstration twice: it changes the recovered path used for learning and, during replay, changes the spatial relation between the gripper and the object. The relevant tolerance is task dependent. Free-space transport may absorb centimeter-scale offsets, whereas insertion, stacking, and sustained contact can fail after only a few millimeters. A useful benchmark should therefore connect estimator-level metrics to task-level consequences instead of treating aggregate trajectory error as the final criterion. We introduce with real-world and simulation subsets. An AGIbot G2 humanoid executes 15 tasks under uninstrumented, textured, and fiducial-marker workspace variants while Insta360 X5 fisheye and Insight9 stereo/RGB-D sensors record the motion. Each execution has its own TCP reference, so error is measured against the motion actually executed. adds Isaac Sim tasks for controlled replay studies (Sec.~ sec:exp_replay ). Benchmarking on motivates (Sec.~ sec:aprilvins ), which estimates sequence-local AprilTag geometry without a pre-surveyed map, inserts admitted tag priors into a fisheye VIO window, and guards export of the optimized trajectory. We summarize the core contributions of this work as follows: We introduce a manipulation-interface localization benchmark named for demonstration collection, featuring repeated tabletop tasks, multi-sensor recordings, scene variants, calibration assets, per-execution end-effector reference trajectories, and a paired simulation subset . We develop , an AprilTag-assisted fisheye VIO system that estimates sequence-local tag geometry without an externally surveyed map, inserts admitted tag priors into a sliding window, and guards export of the joint state; ablations show that tag factors drive most accuracy gains while the output gate restores export continuity. We establish a multi-metric evaluation protocol---APE RMSE, time completion, and continuity---for vision-only, fiducial-aided, visual--inertial, and commercial demonstration-tracking routes, and use replay curves as task-specific tolerance references for the reported error magnitudes. Related Work Visual--Inertial Localization Modern VIO and visual SLAM systems combine feature tracking, inertial preintegration, and sliding-window optimization~ forster2016manifold,qin2018vins,geneva2020openvins,campos2021orb,von2022dm . Handheld interfaces already carry cameras and IMUs, and fisheye models are common on manipulation-mounted cameras~ kannala2006generic . Close-range demonstrations nonetheless break navigation assumptions: short trajectories, fast rotation near the workspace, repeated occlusion, and the need to convert camera poses into replayable end-effector trajectories. Localization Benchmarks and Multi-Sensor SLAM EuRoC and TUM-VI standardize visual--inertial evaluation~ burri2016euroc,schubert2018tum , while ground-robot datasets such as M2DGR, Ground-Challenge, MARS-LVIG, and FusionPortable broaden sensor coverage and degradation cases~ yin2021m2dgr,yin2023ground,li2024mars,jiao2022fusionportable . Recent fusion systems target visual degradation, LiDAR degeneracy, and GNSS denial~ yin2024ground,zhang2025towards,tian2026ultrafusion,he2025ligo . complements these lines by benchmarking close-range manipulation-interface localization with repeated workspace variants and end-effector references. Manipulation introduces a different failure regime: the workspace is compact, but occlusion is frequent and trajectory completeness directly determines whether a demonstration can be replayed. Manipulation and UMI-Style Datasets Large-scale manipulation datasets such as DROID, BridgeData V2, RH20T, and Open X-Embodiment target policy learning~ khazatsky2024droid_dataset,walke2023bridgedata,fang2023rh20t,openx2023rtx . UMI-style interfaces reduce collection overhead~ chi2024umi,zhaxizhuoma2025fastumi,jin2026umibench,wang2026umi3d but rarely evaluate localization directly. is intended as a complementary diagnostic benchmark for that collection stack. Fiducial-Aided Localization Fiducial markers provide six-degree-of-freedom pose observations from images~ olson2011apriltag . TagSLAM and UcoSLAM combine fiducials with factor-graph or feature-based pipelines~ pfrommer2019tagslam,munoz2020ucoslam . Marker visibility alone does not guarantee a replayable trajectory, because fisheye projection, map consistency, synchronization, and temporal coverage all matter under close-range manipulation. This motivates estimating tag geometry online and guarding the exported trajectory rather than treating every detected tag pose as ground truth. The MILD Dataset sec:mild_dataset Dataset Scope targets end-effector trajectory recovery from a manipulation-mounted sensor stream. The evaluation unit is a task--scene--sensor recording with calibration and its own executed TCP reference. The reference comes from logged end-effector poses rather than external motion capture, so reported accuracy is relative to executed robot motion. The benchmark follows three design choices. First, repeating a nominal task across scene and sensor variants separates task geometry from sensing conditions. Second, retaining raw observations and calibration permits evaluation with vision-only, visual--inertial, and fiducial-aided estimators. Third, every execution has its own reference rather than reusing the command trajectory: record-and-replay preserves the intended motion but does not guarantee identical realized motion. Real-World Data An AGIbot G2 humanoid executes 15 tabletop tasks: Analemma, Circular, Zigzag, Bookshelf 01--02, Box 01--02, Pick-and-place 01--06, and Wiping 01--02. The release contains 86 sequences (67 Insta360 X5, 19 Insight9) under uninstrumented, textured, and fiducial-marker workspace variants. Fig.~ fig:Scene_overview shows representative views from all three sensor domains, and Fig.~ fig:mild_overview summarizes the acquisition platform, scene variants, and annotated task trajectories. A record-and-replay procedure keeps nominal motion consistent: a reference demonstration logs joint commands, TCP poses, gripper feedback, and timestamps, and each replay yields a new sensor recording, calibration metadata, and executed TCP trajectory. The variants serve distinct diagnostic roles. The uninstrumented tabletop tests natural-feature tracking under sparse close-range structure. The tablecloth changes texture without changing the nominal task, helping distinguish feature scarcity from motion-induced failure. ArUco and AprilTag layouts provide controlled observations with two or four markers. Their identities and sizes are known, but their global poses need not be surveyed. The marker recordings therefore also test sequence-local map construction. Table~ tab:mild_dataset_overview summarizes the task inventory by family from the 86 indexed real-world recordings and 9 listed entries. Released calibration assets express camera or visual--inertial estimates in the robot TCP frame for both Insta360 X5 fisheye and Insight9 stereo/RGB-D routes. Each task--scene--sensor recording is evaluated against its own executed TCP reference because replays share nominal commands but not identical measured motion. The reference is derived from logged robot kinematics and encoder feedback, so TCP-relative error reflects the trajectory available to the teaching pipeline together with residual calibration, synchronization, and robot-state uncertainty. We report SE(3)-aligned APE RMSE in this frame throughout the experiments. Simulation Data uses Isaac Sim for pick-and-place, wiping, throwing, stacking, and insertion tasks with observable robot, object, and trajectory states (Fig.~ fig:mildsim_overview ). Quantitative localization results in this paper come from the real-world subset, whereas provides controlled replay episodes for the downstream diagnostic in Sec.~ sec:exp_replay . AprilVINS sec:aprilvins Overview targets marker-augmented teaching workspaces without a pre-surveyed fiducial map by combining a fisheye visual--inertial backbone with a fiducial front end that estimates sequence-local tag geometry from known tag IDs and sizes. Admitted tag-pose priors enter a fixed-lag sliding window, and a separate guarded-continuation rule filters the joint state exported as the reported trajectory. A VIO run without tag factors is retained for ablation. Fig.~ fig:aprilvins_pipeline summarizes the data flow from fisheye/IMU inputs to the guarded TCP trajectory. title: Juno: Taming Predictive Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future observations in representation space, offering a natural source of predictive latents for vision-language-action (VLA) models. Yet making these latents useful across pretraining, policy learning, and deployment requires addressing three failures: mismatch with embodiment-specific control, interference with action learning, and teacher miscalibration under distribution shifts. We introduce Juno, a unified framework built around one action-conditioned JEPA that serves as a control-aligned representation backbone, a predictive teacher, and an adaptable dynamics model. During pretraining, we train it on embodiment-matched trajectories and use a dynamic CLS loss to transfer motion-weighted patch dynamics to a compact global state. During policy learning, we fuse current-frame JEPA patches into VLA perception and use a decoupled reasoning branch with separate transformation parameters to distill future latent states for action generation. During deployment, we adapt the world model on all observed transitions, including failed rollouts, freeze the adapted teacher, and re-align the policy on verified executions using LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or task rewards. On SimplerEnv, Juno raises average success from $60.9\%$ to $68.5\%$ over Qwen3GR00T, the strongest baseline, and test-time adaptation further reaches $72.7\%$; on a real robot, it retains $70\%$--$75\%$ success under background, height, and object shifts where the base policy collapses to $0\%$.

Introduction Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future observations in representation space rather than in pixels~ lecun2022path,baevski2022data2vec,assran2023self,bardes2024revisiting . This principle has progressed from image and video level self-supervision to action-conditioned prediction for embodied agents~ assran2025v,maes2026leworldmodel . A growing number of vision--language--action (VLA) systems further show that such predictive latents benefit policy learning, whether through latent world models~ sun2026vla,wang2026repwam , future-representation alignment~ zheng2025flare,zhao2026frappe, xu2026futurevla,xia2026vlaflow , foresight tokens~ ma2026internvla,qian2025physical , or latent subgoals~ chen2026lawam,huang2026h . The question is therefore no longer whether prediction helps, but how to make it useful across the VLA lifecycle. Making a predictive latent useful meets three obstacles, one per stage. At pretraining, representations learned from broad internet video are visually strong but poorly matched to embodiment-specific controllable motion~ assran2025v . At policy learning, predictive objectives are typically grafted onto the shared vision--language pathway~ zheng2025flare,sun2026vla,xu2026futurevla , where prediction gradients interfere with control and future-aligned states need not be action-decodable. At deployment, adaptation methods assume a reliable frozen teacher~ zhang2026ttt,park2026test,yuan2026adaworldpolicy , yet severe shifts miscalibrate the teacher itself, and the failed rollouts dominating deployment data cannot serve as policy targets. We show that a single action-conditioned JEPA addresses all three, serving as a control-aligned representation backbone, a predictive teacher, and an adaptable dynamics model. realizes these roles through Control-Aligned Pretraining, Decoupled Predictive Reasoning, and Dynamics-First Test-Time Adaptation. For representation learning, we choose a lightweight action-conditioned JEPA~ maes2026leworldmodel and train it from pixels on the same embodiment-matched trajectories used for policy learning. This choice is motivated by the qualitative evidence in Fig.~ fig:method-representation : its patch features respond locally to robot--object interaction, while features from a large internet-video teacher spread across the scene. Its compact global token, however, dilutes exactly these local changes, so we introduce a dynamic CLS loss that transfers motion-weighted patch dynamics onto the global token, applied in a second stage with a frozen patch supervisor. For policy learning, we fuse current-frame JEPA patch features into the VLA's visual tokens~ miao2026jepa,li2023blip and append learnable reasoning queries processed by a decoupled branch with separate transformation parameters under shared causal attention~ liang2025mot,luo2026being,qian2025liquid . The branch is distilled against the frozen teacher's future latent states, one reasoning query per future step, and its hidden states condition the flow-matching action decoder. Future observations provide targets only during training; at deployment the branch acts on the current observation and instruction. Since the branch receives both alignment and action gradients, the aligned state is trained to be decodable into actions rather than merely predictive. For deployment, even a control-aligned teacher miscalibrates under severe shifts, and updating a policy against a miscalibrated teacher confounds world-model error with policy error. Our key observation is an asymmetry: failed actions are poor policy targets, but their consequences remain valid dynamics supervision. Juno-TTT therefore adapts the world model on all observed transitions, freezes the adapted teacher, and re-aligns the policy on verified executions with LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or task rewards. Our contributions follow the three stages: [leftmargin=*, nosep] Control-Aligned Pretraining. We propose a dynamic CLS loss that aligns the global state token with motion-weighted patch dynamics, and show that matching the predictive teacher to the embodiment and control distribution can matter more than pretraining scale alone. Decoupled Predictive Reasoning. We integrate JEPA features into a VLA through patch-level fusion and a decoupled reasoning branch distilled from future latent states, so that predictive computation supports action generation without restructuring the VLA backbone. Dynamics-First Test-Time Adaptation. We propose a failure-aware adaptation procedure that exploits all deployment transitions, successful or not, for world-model adaptation, followed by conservative policy re-alignment on verified data with the adapted teacher held fixed. Related Work Latent Predictive World Models. Generative world models often expend capacity on task-irrelevant visual details hafner2025mastering,hansen2024td,zhang2020learning , whereas Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict future representations directly, without pixel reconstruction lecun2022path,baevski2022data2vec,assran2023self, bardes2024revisiting,balestriero2025lejepa . This principle now extends to action-conditioned prediction and embodied planning assran2025v,mur2026v,zhou2024dino,terver2025drives,zhang2026delta, maes2026leworldmodel,sun2026vla,xu2026futurevla , and to latent-action abstractions from unlabeled videos bruce2024genie,ye2025latent,bu2025univla,tharwat2025latent . Yet none of these works determines which predictive state best matches a particular robot controller. World Action Models. VLA policies increasingly incorporate world-model signals for temporal reasoning zheng2025flare,sun2026vla,chen2026lawam,wu2024unleashing,cen2025worldvla : representation-centric methods align policy states with future-observation embeddings from visual teachers miao2026jepa,zhao2026frappe,xu2026futurevla,xia2026vlaflow , while others expose predicted dynamics to action generation through foresight tokens, latent subgoals, or aligned visual--action tokens ma2026internvla,huang2026h,su2026world,hu2024video, wang2026repwam,luo2026being . Across these granularities, however, future alignment alone does not show that the aligned policy state can be decoded into the corresponding action. Test-Time Training in Robotics. Test-time training (TTT) adapts models to deployment inputs via self-supervised inner-loop optimization, without revisiting the training set sun2020test,wang2020tent,wang2022continual,hansen2020self,liu2021ttt++ . In robotics, test-time updates either adapt latent prompts, adapters, or policy components via state-grounding, future-consistency, prediction-error, or progress signals zhang2026ttt,park2026test,yuan2026adaworldpolicy,bai2025evolve,ji2026vane , or serve as adaptive memory over interaction histories and unlabeled videos sun2024learning,zhang2026test,jiang2026robottt,feng2026wamtttsteeringworldactionmodels, wang2026adajepa . These methods, however, all assume a reliable frozen teacher: under a severe shift, the world model that provides the adaptation target may itself be miscalibrated. The world model is trained from pixels on the same embodiment-matched trajectory data used for policy learning (Sec.~ sec:exp-setup ), so that its representation is aligned with the downstream control distribution. title: Many Ways to Succeed: Diversity-Driven RL Fine-Tuning for VLA Generalization
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through closed-loop experience, yet generalization beyond the fine-tuning distribution remains limited. Our analysis reveals a selective reshaping of exploration: RL contracts behavior globally, yet diversifies successful trajectories, elicits success with fewer rollouts, and covers more of the latent task-valid solution space than supervised fine-tuning. Broader successful-mode coverage may provide alternative strategies under distribution shifts. Inspired by this, we introduce DRIVE (Diversity-driven RL fIne-tuning for VLA gEneralization), which turns successful-behavior diversity into an explicit RL objective. DRIVE groups rollouts under matched task conditions, compares their trajectories with temporal alignment, and derives a success-conditioned intrinsic reward from relative behavioral diversity. This design encourages broader coverage of feasible solutions without rewarding diverse failures or superficial timing differences. Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin 2.0, DRIVE improves the average out-of-domain (OOD) performance over vanilla RL fine-tuning by 5.3 points on $π_0$ and 2.0 points on $π_{0.5}$. On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success from 64.1% to 73.3% (+9.2 points), demonstrating gains that persist under physical deployment.

Inspired by this, we introduce DRIVE (Diversity-driven RL fIne-tuning for VLA gEneralization), which turns successful-behavior diversity into an explicit RL objective. DRIVE groups rollouts under matched task conditions, compares their trajectories with temporal alignment, and derives a success-conditioned intrinsic reward from relative behavioral diversity. This design encourages broader coverage of feasible solutions without rewarding diverse failures or superficial timing differences. Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin~2.0, DRIVE improves the average out-of-domain (OOD) performance over vanilla RL fine-tuning by 5.3 points on \( _0\) and 2.0 points on \( _ 0.5 \). On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success from 64.1 to 73.3 (+9.2 points), demonstrating gains that persist under physical deployment. Introduction sec:introduction r 0.45 Beyond task success, diverse successful trajectories reveal broader solution modes. This diversity provides a new opportunity for improving VLA generalization. fig:teaser Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially expanded the range of manipulation tasks that robots can perform from visual observations and language instructions~ kim2024openvla . VLA models are trained primarily through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on robot demonstrations, acquiring broad manipulation skills by imitating a fixed behavior distribution~ intelligence2025pi05 . Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) complements this paradigm with self-generated experience, using outcome feedback to explore beyond demonstrations and optimize closed-loop task performance~ intelligence2025pi . Recent studies have shown that RL fine-tuning, particularly with PPO, can improve VLA generalization in semantic understanding and execution robustness~ liu2025rlvla . However, such gains do not transfer uniformly across distribution shifts, and VLA policies remain sensitive to changes in visual appearance, scene configuration, and execution conditions~ fei2025liberoplus . Robust VLA generalization is essential for real-world deployment, yet remains challenging beyond the fine-tuning distribution. To understand how RFT reshapes the range of behaviors available to VLA policies, we analyze both how rollout distributions evolve and how readily their successful modes can be elicited (see Sec.~ sec:exploration_dynamics ). As training progresses, similarity increases across all rollouts but decreases among successful ones, revealing global behavioral contraction alongside successful-mode diversification. Pass@k measures how readily any successful behavior can be elicited, showing that RFT requires far fewer rollouts than SFT to obtain a success. Coverage@k instead measures the breadth of these successes, showing that, under the same rollout budget, RFT covers a substantially broader portion of the latent task-valid solution space than SFT. Together, these results suggest that RFT makes task-valid solutions more accessible even as the overall behavior distribution contracts. Broader coverage of this space may provide alternative strategies under distribution shifts, revealing an underexplored opportunity to improve generalization through successful-behavior diversity. Turning this opportunity into a useful training objective is nontrivial. Standard binary task rewards distinguish success from failure but not among different successful solutions, providing no explicit incentive to maintain broad successful-mode coverage. Although diversity has been studied in unsupervised skill discovery~ eysenbach2019diayn , policy diversification~ masood2019dipg , and embodied exploration~ chen2026curiousvla , directly applying these approaches to VLA fine-tuning can reward superficial differences caused by execution speed, temporal misalignment, or irrelevant motion, as well as noisy and unsuccessful behaviors. A suitable diversity objective must therefore compare trajectories under matched task conditions, account for temporal variation, and reward behavioral differences only when the trajectories remain task-valid. Motivated by these observations, we propose DRIVE (Diversity-driven RL fIne-tuning for VLA gEneralization), a framework that turns successful-mode diversity into an explicit optimization target for promoting generalization. DRIVE groups rollouts collected under matched task conditions, quantifies their behavioral novelty using temporally aligned GAK (global alignment kernel) similarity, and assigns a relative novelty bonus only to successful trajectories. This design focuses the diversity incentive on distinct task-valid solutions rather than arbitrary variation across tasks, timing, or failures. Then, we formulate the intra-group diversity as an intrinsic reward and design a potential-based reward shaping scheme to preserve optimal policy invariance. By encouraging broader coverage of successful behaviors during fine-tuning, DRIVE provides alternative task-solving strategies that may transfer under distribution shifts. Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin~2.0, DRIVE improves 11 of 12 benchmark-split results on each backbone, raising the OOD macro-average from 48.1 to 53.4 for \( _0\) and from 71.1 to 73.1 for \( _ 0.5 \). On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success across two tasks and three distribution shifts from 64.1 to 73.3 (+9.2 points). Together, these results validate successful-mode diversity as a practical objective across simulated distribution shifts and physical deployment. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: [itemsep=0.25em, leftmargin=1.25em] We show that global behavioral contraction coexists with successful-mode diversification, revealing successful-behavior diversity as an underexplored route to VLA generalization. We introduce DRIVE, which converts temporally aligned comparisons of grouped trajectories into a success-conditioned intrinsic reward for diverse task-valid exploration. We demonstrate consistent generalization gains across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill, and RoboTwin, and confirm that DRIVE’s improvements persist under physical deployment. Related Work sec:related_work VLA Models and Generalization. VLA models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, typically combining pretrained vision-language representations with supervised learning from robot demonstrations~ kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,xie2026look . However, systematic evaluations reveal sensitivity to changes in visual appearance, scene configurations, robot initial states, and execution conditions~ fei2025liberoplus,liu2025rlvla . To improve generalization, prior work has explored data augmentation and domain randomization~ chen2025robotwin,xue2025resample , large-scale pretraining and heterogeneous co-training~ zitkovich2023rt2,intelligence2025pi05 , and model designs that strengthen spatial representations and embodied reasoning~ qu2025spatialvla,zawalski2024ecot . These efforts primarily focus on training data and model capabilities, with less attention to how behavior distributions shaped during RFT affect generalization. Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for VLA. RFT complements demonstration-based SFT with self-generated experience and task-level feedback from closed-loop interaction, with successful deployments in LLMs~ guo2025deepseek,yan2025learning,zhan2026exgrpo , VLMs~ liu2025visual,hu2026bridging , and VLAs~ intelligence2025pi,liu2025rlvla . Recent PPO-based~ lu2025vla,tan2025interactive and GRPO-based methods~ li2026simplevla use this feedback to optimize task-completion or progress rewards. Empirical studies report that such fine-tuning improves task success over SFT and can enhance OOD generalization, particularly in semantic understanding and execution robustness~ liu2025rlvla,chen2025pirl . However, this line of work primarily examines the performance benefits of task-reward optimization, with less attention to how successful-behavior distributions evolve during RFT or how broader coverage of the successful behavior space can be explicitly promoted. Behavioral Diversity and Exploration. Unsupervised skill discovery promotes diverse behaviors without task rewards~ eysenbach2019diayn,sharma2020dads , while intrinsic-motivation methods encourage exploration through prediction-based novelty rewards~ pathak2017curiosity,burda2019rnd . Task-aware methods instead combine return maximization with differences between policy-induced trajectory distributions~ masood2019dipg or encourage diversity among near-optimal behaviors~ kumar2020smerl,hu2026diversity,liu2026beyond . In VLA learning, diversity has been used to guide exploration through trajectory expansion and behavior conditioning~ chen2026curiousvla,kong2026extoken , and to enrich pretraining data with diverse successful trajectories~ yang2025dlr . In contrast, DRIVE applies a success-conditioned diversity reward across rollouts under matched task conditions, targeting broader task-valid solution coverage rather than global behavioral variation. Exploration Dynamics in VLA Reinforcement Fine-Tuning sec:exploration_dynamics We study how RFT reshapes the diversity and accessibility of successful behaviors in \( _0\) and \( _ 0.5 \) on ManiSkill3~ taomaniskill3 , evaluating the SFT and intermediate/final RFT checkpoints. Using SDE sampling under matched task conditions, we measure trajectory similarity separately across all and successful rollouts. For the sampling-budget analysis, we evaluate SFT and final-RFT \( _0\) on 32 task-initial-state configurations, sampling up to 256 rollouts per policy and configuration. Global Contraction Masks Successful-Mode Diversification. Fig.~ fig:rft_exploration_dynamics (a--b) reveals a contrasting trend: normalized Global Alignment Kernel (GAK) similarity increases across all rollouts but decreases among successful ones as RFT progresses. Meanwhile, success rates rise from 41 to 75 for \( _0\) and from 52 to 77 for \( _ 0.5 \). Thus, RFT concentrates the overall behavior distribution while improving task success and diversifying successful executions. Global contraction therefore masks successful-mode diversification rather than implying a collapse of task-valid exploration. RFT Makes Latent Successful Behaviors More Accessible. We measure the accessibility of successful behavior using Pass@\(K\), the probability that at least one of \(K\) rollouts succeeds for a task-initial-state configuration. Fig.~ fig:rft_exploration_dynamics (c) shows that RFT achieves substantially higher Pass@\(K\) at small \(K\), while the gap narrows as SFT saturates with larger budgets. This pattern suggests that successful behavior is often latent in SFT but difficult to elicit. RFT makes such behavior accessible with far fewer rollouts, converting sparse success into reliable execution under limited sampling. Elicitation Spans a Broad Task-Valid Solution Space. title: Borrowed Eyes: Markerless Nano-UAV Flight with an Active Quadruped Observer
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs) can navigate confined spaces that larger robots cannot, but their payload capacity severely limits the sensors and compute available for self-localization in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. We present a vision-based system that localizes a nano-UAV from a quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera. The quadruped tracks the drone, estimates its position in its own coordinate system using segmentation masks and depth, and transmits that position over a real-time radio link. To ensure continuous tracking, we developed a perception-aware nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that dynamically adjusts the quadruped's body and arm to maximize the drone's visibility, treating observation reliability as a primary control objective. Relying solely on this external estimate, the nano-UAV executed predefined trajectories from takeoff to landing with a median 3D localization error of 59 mm. The system demonstrates robustness against short visual occlusions by smoothly transitioning to onboard inertial flight when line-of-sight is temporarily lost. Ultimately, this framework allows a quadruped to offload the localization burden of a nano-UAV, enabling inspection of complex spaces that neither robot could navigate alone.
full_text: Borrowed Eyes: Markerless Nano-UAV Flight with an Active Quadruped Observer Alejandro Lorite Mora , Dimitrios Arapis and Andr\'es Fa\'i na IT University of Copenhagen, Denmark \ lori, anfv\ @itu.dk . A.~Lorite Mora is also with Helix Lab and Novo Nordisk A/S, Denmark. Novo Nordisk A/S, Hiller d, Denmark dim.arapis@outlook.com Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs) can navigate confined spaces that larger robots cannot, but their payload capacity severely limits the sensors and compute available for self-localization in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. We present a vision-based system that localizes a nano-UAV from a quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera. The quadruped tracks the drone, estimates its position in its own coordinate system using segmentation masks and depth, and transmits that position over a real-time radio link. To ensure continuous tracking, we developed a perception-aware nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that dynamically adjusts the quadruped's body and arm to maximize the drone's visibility, treating observation reliability as a primary control objective. Relying solely on this external estimate, the nano-UAV executed predefined trajectories from takeoff to landing with a median 3D localization error of 59\,mm. The system demonstrates robustness against short visual occlusions by smoothly transitioning to onboard inertial flight when line-of-sight is temporarily lost. Ultimately, this framework allows a quadruped to offload the localization burden of a nano-UAV, enabling inspection of complex spaces that neither robot could navigate alone. Introduction Industrial assets such as storage tanks, pressure vessels, pipes, and tunnels require regular inspection for corrosion, cracks, and other structural damage. Manual inspection is time-consuming, costly, and hazardous, especially in narrow or elevated spaces. Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs), weighing only tens of grams, are well suited to reaching and inspecting areas inaccessible to larger robots. However, autonomous nano-UAV deployment is severely constrained by onboard localization. Larger UAVs can carry stereo cameras or LiDAR to run visual-inertial odometry (VIO) or simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), but these sensors exceed the payload and power capacity of nano-scale platforms~ niculescu_nanoslam_2024 . Confined industrial settings also feature repetitive, textureless steel surfaces and uneven illumination, which degrade feature-based localization even when sufficient computation is available. In laboratory settings, nano-UAVs rely on external localization infrastructure like motion capture or ultra-wideband (UWB) beacons. However, installing fixed infrastructure across industrial facilities is costly, inflexible, and often impractical. Operating in real environments requires localization that preserves the nano-UAV's payload margin without permanent infrastructure. Rather than increasing the sensing burden on the drone or instrumenting the environment, we offload localization to a mobile ground robot with greater sensing and computational capacity (Fig.~ fig:system ). The quadruped localizes itself and estimates the 3D position of the nano-UAV using an arm-mounted camera, while the drone flies using this externally supplied estimate. Crucially, the estimate is expressed directly in the quadruped's global coordinate map rather than in an onboard frame. This provides a shared spatial representation for heterogeneous collaboration, allowing the nano-UAV to scout confined spaces and report points of interest in a frame the ground robot can directly use. Our prior work~ loritemora_clawar_2026 demonstrated this cooperative division of labor using fiducial markers on a nano-UAV~ olson_apriltag_2011 . However, physical markers add considerable payload mass, increase aerodynamic drag, and enlarge the vehicle's footprint. In addition, reactive camera tracking often loses visual contact during fast maneuvers or temporary occlusions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a markerless localization and active observation framework for nano-UAVs. Our main contributions are: (i)~Markerless external localization: A position-only perception pipeline that estimates the 3D position of a bare nano-UAV in the quadruped's map frame, using depth-integrity gates to discard corrupted measurements and convert sensor failures into safe dropouts. (ii)~Perception-aware active observation: A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that coordinates the quadruped's body and arm motion to preserve line-of-sight and optimize viewing geometry. (iii)~Closed-loop flight under intermittent perception: Closed-loop flight validation from takeoff to landing on the external vision feed alone, demonstrating autonomous recovery from visual occlusions through onboard inertial coasting. Related Work sec:rw-markerless Ground-Aerial Collaborative Localization. Leveraging ground robots to assist UAV localization is an established strategy for global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. Existing approaches utilize ultra-wideband radios on both platforms to achieve decimeter-level localization~ queralta_uwb_2020 , employ ground vehicles as external references to refine onboard state estimates~ depetrillo_ugv_uav_2024 , or use legged robots as mobile magnetic beacons, achieving tracking errors of 8 to 11\,cm~ brunacci_flytrackland_2026 . These methods either require dedicated onboard payload hardware~ depetrillo_ugv_uav_2024 or provide lower accuracy than close-range visual localization~ queralta_uwb_2020,brunacci_flytrackland_2026 . Markerless inter-robot observation has been explored in multi-robot SLAM, where mutually observing robots use visual detections to refine their state estimates~ rueggeberg_markerless_2026 . However, such observations have not been demonstrated as the primary external position source for closed-loop flight of a nano-UAV. Removing fiducial markers eliminates added mass and aerodynamic penalties, but requires localizing a small, dark, weakly textured, and symmetric airframe directly from appearance and depth. While render-and-compare 6D pose estimators~ wen_foundationpose_2024,leeAny6DModelfree6D2025 address similar challenges, we exploit the flight controller's internal attitude estimation and compute only 3D position, reducing the vision pipeline to the essential external state (Section~ sec:posestimator ). Vision-Based Localization of Small Aerial Targets. Prior work on aerial target detection predominantly targets larger platforms. Vrba et al.~ vrba_noncoop_2019 detected a 0.55\,m quadrotor using stereo vision up to 50\,m, with subsequent work reporting ranges up to 20\,m~ vrba_mav_2020 . Carrio et al.~ carrio_depthmaps_2020 localized drones using onboard depth maps at 16\,Hz up to 8\,m, but evaluated a 517\,mm platform and attributed range limits to sensor constraints rather than target dimensions. In LiDAR-based studies~ vrba_lidar_2025 , classification degrades when a target returns fewer than 40 points. A bare nano-UAV challenges these limits at much closer range, where its small surface area returns very few depth points. We explicitly quantify this relationship up to 3.1\,m in Section~ sec:exp-perception . Aerial Navigation Through Narrow Apertures. Navigating confined spaces has been addressed through collision-tolerant platforms operating through manhole-sized openings~ depetris_manhole_2020,tranzatto_cerberus_2022 , or commercial caged inspection drones with full onboard SLAM. Flyability Elios 3, Both strategies require structural protection and compute payloads well beyond the capacity of nano-UAVs. This leaves an important capability gap for nano-UAVs, which can access tighter spaces but cannot carry the heavy sensor packages assumed by existing platforms. Problem Formulation sec:problem From fiducial to markerless observation Our prior system~ loritemora_clawar_2026 composes the drone's map-frame pose as a chain of transforms where the last two links come from detecting an AprilTag and applying a fixed tag-to-body offset. We replace the fiducial link by a single markerless estimate where compares rendered views of a metrically scaled CAD model of the drone against the camera image , using the registered depth to fix the scale. Section~ sec:poc reports that this full 6-DOF estimate is unreliable to initialize on a thin, dark airframe, and unnecessary in any case, since flight consumes only the translation. We replace it with a position-only estimate where segments the drone in image into a mask and reads the registered depth at that mask. Orientation is calculated from the drone's IMU (Section~ sec:poc ). Everything upstream of the fiducial link is untouched, so the substitution is local and the position handed to the drone stays in the same map frame as before. Bounded coasting across the aperture sec:coast Localization must stay anchored to the infrastructure. The drone may carry an IMU but must never define the map on its own, which would reduce to the onboard self-localization the approach avoids. Between detections its extended Kalman filter (EKF) coasts on that IMU alone, dead-reckoning the map-frame position from the last fix by integrating its IMU-derived velocity estimate until the quadruped re-acquires it. With no reference to correct against, what matters operationally is how long that coast runs. This paper does not measure a coast-drift sizing curve, reporting coasting through the beyond-volume route's dropout statistics instead (Section~ sec:exp-usecases ). Method sec:method System overview sec:overview The proposed system is shown in Fig.~ fig:system and its processing pipeline in Fig.~ fig:pipeline . A Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped serves as the mobile base, equipped with its own arm-mounted gripper camera, which provides color and registered time-of-flight depth (Section~ sec:camera ), and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin onboard computer. This computer handles quadruped control, arm articulation, and drone pose estimation. From each RGB-D frame, the pipeline extracts at most one 3D position of the drone, referenced to the quadruped's map frame. Validated position estimates are transmitted via a low-latency radio link to the drone (a Bitcraze Crazyflie relying solely on an inertial measurement unit (IMU)) using the crazyswarm2 server. Crazyswarm2, The quadruped tracks its motion via onboard odometry, anchored to the world map frame by a static transform ( in Eq.~ ). In these experiments, an OptiTrack motion-capture system supplies that anchor and records ground truth for calibration and evaluation. Motion capture never provides state estimates to the flight controller: the drone completes its entire flight profile, from takeoff to landing, relying on the markerless pipeline. Anchoring instead to the quadruped's onboard SLAM map adds negligible error: Spot's internal map drifted \,cm (P95). We use the motion-capture anchor to keep reported tracking performance independent of ground-robot self-localization error. Mask-Based Position Estimation sec:posestimator The drone's map-frame position is constructed from rigid transforms anchored to the quadruped's self-localization, closed by a markerless camera-to-drone estimate: Here is the pose of frame expressed in frame , so each factor carries a point from into , acting on the homogeneous point. The first three encapsulate the quadruped's state: its localization in the map frame, its internal odometry, and the arm's forward kinematics. Only the final link is derived visually. Because the drone's IMU maintains its attitude and yaw, full 6D pose estimation is unnecessary. The visual problem reduces to estimating the drone's 3D position in the camera frame, extracted from a 2D segmentation mask and the registered depth map , where reads the finite, positive depth returns under a mask: enabling 3D unprojection via camera intrinsics . title: TERRA: Learning Transportable Latent Actions through Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment
comment: Preprint. Code and project page coming soon
summary: Latent actions supervise robot policies with action-like codes inferred from visual transitions, and their usefulness hinges on two questions: what a code keeps from a transition, and whether it still means the same thing when reused in a different initial state. The first is a tension in time: an endpoint difference discards how motion unfolds, while the full sequence admits nuisance variation. The second is left open by reconstruction, which only ever observes a latent together with the state it came from. We argue that both questions can be answered in the same place. TERRA (Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment) describes a transition by a compact temporal effect, its net feature change together with a low-order within-window dynamics component, and learns a continuous latent from this effect. The same effect space then serves as the reference for reuse: Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT) decodes a latent in other initial states and anchors the resulting effect to the one observed at its source, so that the latent is shaped by what it does across contexts rather than only by the transition it came from. With frozen linear readers, TERRA predicts actions more accurately than UniVLA and a LAPA-style baseline, degrades more slowly under visual distractors, and keeps transported transitions faithful to the donor action as the recipient context moves farther away; a same-budget control shows that these gains come largely from EAT. At matched pretraining scale, the complete system reaches 93.4% average success on LIBERO, compared with 91.8% for UniVLA.
full_text: Latent actions supervise robot policies with action-like codes inferred from visual transitions, and their usefulness hinges on two questions: what a code keeps from a transition, and whether it still means the same thing when reused in a different initial state. The first is a tension in time: an endpoint difference discards how motion unfolds, while the full sequence admits nuisance variation. The second is left open by reconstruction, which only ever observes a latent together with the state it came from. We argue that both questions can be answered in the same place. TERRA (Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment) describes a transition by a compact temporal effect, its net feature change together with a low-order within-window dynamics component, and learns a continuous latent from this effect. The same effect space then serves as the reference for reuse: Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT) decodes a latent in other initial states and anchors the resulting effect to the one observed at its source, so that the latent is shaped by what it does across contexts rather than only by the transition it came from. With frozen linear readers, TERRA predicts actions more accurately than UniVLA and a LAPA-style baseline, degrades more slowly under visual distractors, and keeps transported transitions faithful to the donor action as the recipient context moves farther away; a same-budget control shows that these gains come largely from EAT. At matched pretraining scale, the complete system reaches 93.4 average success on LIBERO, compared with 91.8 for UniVLA. Introduction sec:introduction Latent actions provide an intermediate supervision signal between visual transitions and robot control. A latent-action model assigns an action-like representation to an observed transition, which can then supervise a policy conditioned on the current observation and instruction. Recent work has explored discrete task-centric latents~ ye2025lapa,bu2025univla , continuous latent motion from frame-pair feature differences~ yang2026como , and structured continuous action spaces~ li2026rotvla . Despite this progress, a basic question remains unresolved: what should a latent action preserve from a visual transition, and how should it behave when reused? A first challenge is selective temporal information preservation. Strong compression can remove distinctions that matter for control, whereas increasing latent capacity can also admit action-irrelevant appearance and exogenous variation~ yang2026como,lee2026why . This tension is particularly important in time. Continuous latent-motion models operate on a frame pair, so their input reduces to the endpoint difference: it records how much the scene changed, not how the change unfolded within the window. Two executions that reach the same state at different speeds therefore receive the same latent (Fig.~ fig:teaser a), although they correspond to different actions. Conversely, retaining the entire temporal sequence exposes the representation to substantially more visual variation. A second challenge is cross-context effect consistency. Standard reconstruction objectives observe only matched state--transition pairs and can therefore encode context-specific variation into the latent~ lee2026why . Policy supervision is most useful when similar effects receive compatible latents across episodes, so it matters how a latent behaves when applied in a different initial state; we refer to this reuse as transport. A latent that fits its source transition can still decode to a different effect once the scene changes (Fig.~ fig:teaser b). We address both challenges with one principle: the compact effect space that decides what a latent should keep also provides the reference for how it should behave in a new context. We instantiate this principle with TERRA (Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment), which first summarizes a short transition by its temporal evidence, a net component that captures accumulated feature change and a dynamics component that captures its low-order within-window trend, and compresses this evidence into a continuous latent. It then applies Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT): the latent is decoded in recipient states from the same data source, and the direction of the resulting effect is anchored to the one observed at the donor. Relative-effect consistency, transition-distribution matching, and nuisance invariance regularize this refinement. Figure~ fig:terra summarizes the framework. Adding the dynamics component to the endpoint difference lowers action NMSE and makes the within-window action trend linearly recoverable. EAT lowers action NMSE further and keeps transported transitions faithful to the donor action as recipient distance grows, which the same amount of additional reconstruction does not achieve. The complete system reaches 93.4 average LIBERO success against 91.8 for UniVLA at matched pretraining scale. Our contributions are: A temporal-effect representation that extends frame-pair latent motion with a low-order within-window dynamics component, retaining how change unfolds without encoding the full sequence. Effect-Anchored Transport, which uses the same effect space to supervise how a latent behaves when decoded in other initial states, constraining what the latent does rather than what it is. Controlled evaluations showing that each component contributes to action alignment, nuisance robustness, and transport stability, and a matched-scale system comparison showing higher LIBERO success than UniVLA. Related Work sec:related_work Latent action representations. Latent action models infer action-like representations from visual transitions and use them as intermediate supervision for robot learning. Early work learned inverse-dynamics labels from unlabeled video~ baker2022vpt and discrete latent actions for controllable generation and policies~ bruce2024genie,schmidt2024lapo ; LAPA and UniVLA scale this recipe to vision-language-action pretraining with quantized codes~ ye2025lapa,bu2025univla , and Moto, IGOR, AdaWorld, and villa-X refine what such codes capture~ chen2025moto,chen2024igor,gao2025adaworld,chen2025villax . More recent work explores continuous representations to preserve richer motion structure: CoMo learns continuous latent motion from frame-pair feature differences~ yang2026como , and RotVLA introduces structured continuous latents with temporal composition for VLA learning~ li2026rotvla . Zhang et al.~ zhang2025lamlearn analyze what these models actually encode. These works establish both discrete and continuous latent actions as viable interfaces between visual transitions and downstream control. Cross-context grounding and latent consistency. A separate line of work studies how latent actions remain meaningful beyond the transition from which they are inferred. Olaf-World orients latent actions using temporal feature differences from a frozen video encoder for controllable video world models jiang2026olaf , while cycle-based approaches regularize latent identity through generated transitions chen2025vivla . LAOM shows that action-correlated distractors degrade latent actions learned by reconstruction and measures latent quality by linear probing~ nikulin2025laom ; recent analyses further examine nuisance sensitivity, action recoverability, and the relationship between latent-quality proxies and downstream control~ lee2026why,bu2026whatmatters . Continuous VLA prediction. Continuous action prediction is increasingly common in vision-language-action models. OpenVLA-OFT replaces autoregressive action-token decoding with continuous action heads kim2025oft , while uses a flow-matching action expert black2025pi0 . RotVLA jointly models continuous latent and physical actions li2026rotvla , and LAFP studies latent-policy learning with flow matching lyu2026lafp . These prior works have studied temporal latent construction, cross-context consistency, and continuous policy prediction largely as separate problems. TERRA uses one effect space for both: temporal evidence defines what the latent keeps, and Effect-Anchored Transport uses the same evidence to supervise how it behaves in other states. TERRA: Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment sec:method TERRA learns transportable continuous latent actions through two complementary components: Temporal Effect Representation (TER) and Relational Alignment (RA). TER constructs a compact latent from the temporal evidence of an observed transition, while RA refines how this latent behaves when applied in a different initial state, through Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT). We call a latent transportable within a data source if, when applied in a different initial state, the resulting transition preserves the direction of its source temporal effects. We refer to this cross-context reuse as transport. Both components use frozen visual features without robot action labels. After refinement, the latent tokenizer is frozen and used to provide latent-action targets for downstream policy training. Temporal Effect Representation (TER) sec:temporal_effect_representation Temporal evidence. For a transition , we extract frozen DINOv2 features~ oquab2023dinov2 and spatially pool them into , where denotes the number of spatial cells and the feature dimension. Let . We omit the transition index when unambiguous. Rather than retaining either only the endpoint difference or the full increment sequence, TERRA summarizes a transition by two low-order temporal components, which we call its temporal evidence. For any increment sequence , we define the net component and the dynamics component as The net component corresponds to the constant temporal mode and captures accumulated change; for observed transitions, by telescoping. The dynamics component uses the lowest-frequency nonconstant DCT-II mode and captures coarse within-window variation. Together they retain the two lowest-order temporal components of the increment sequence. The temporal evidence is the measured form of the temporal effect that TERRA represents; Section~ sec:eat reuses the same two components to supervise transport. title: RealtimeWAM: How Fast Can I Run My World Action Model?
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics modeling with action generation, but their high inference latency limits responsive robot control. Recent efforts accelerate inference by removing explicit future-video generation at test time, as in FastWAM, an approach that requires a specially tailored architectural design. More general caching strategies exploit feature redundancy, but redundancy alone does not capture the changing computational demands of closed-loop control. To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a general, training-free framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for low-latency inference across diverse WAM architectures. We exploit layerwise dependencies to overlap observation processing with prediction. However, concurrent branches still compete for GPU resources, limiting the benefit of parallel execution. We therefore adapt computation throughout the pipeline through selective reuse, caching observation features in visually stable regions and reusing Transformer residuals while reserving additional refinement for small predicted adjustments. We evaluate RealtimeWAM on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. On an RTX 4090, measured mean inference latencies are 24.09 and 63.09 ms, corresponding to average speedups of 8.90$\times$ and 10.67$\times$. Average success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, respectively, within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. Across five real-world tasks, RealtimeWAM improves average success rates over native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points on FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.

Introduction 1 World Action Models (WAMs) integrate visual dynamics modeling with action generation, providing predictive representations for robotic control cen2025worldvla,bi2025motus,kim2026cosmospolicy,yuan2026fastwam,wang2026openwam . However, their substantial inference cost limits how quickly a robot can respond to changes in its environment. This limitation is particularly problematic in dynamic manipulation, where the scene continues to evolve while the model generates an action~ black2025rtc . For example, a moving object on a conveyor may shift away from its observed position before the predicted action is executed. Reducing latency from observation to action is therefore essential for using WAMs to control robots in real time. Recent work has reduced inference cost through architectural simplification and computational reuse. For example, FastWAM removes future-video generation at inference while retaining joint training with video yuan2026fastwam , and diffusion caching methods such as TeaCache avoid repeated Transformer computation by reusing residual features liu2025teacache . These advances leave two further questions for WAM execution in real time. First, reducing computation alone does not resolve how observation processing and prediction should be scheduled under their data dependencies and shared hardware constraints. Second, caching decisions based on denoising similarity are not explicitly tied to the responsiveness and precision required by the current action. Fixed evaluation schedules likewise apply the same computational budget throughout a rollout, despite changing execution requirements. Further acceleration therefore calls for coordinating parallel execution with computation that adapts to the current observation and predicted motion. To address these challenges, we present , a framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for existing WAM architectures without additional training. We first exploit the layerwise dependencies between processing the current observation (Prefill) and prediction. As each layer produces the required observation features, the corresponding prediction computation can begin while Prefill continues (Figure~ fig:ffn-runtime ). This allows Prefill to overlap with action prediction and, when present, future-video generation. However, concurrent branches compete for shared GPU compute resources, limiting the speedup achievable through overlap alone. To ease this contention, we exploit temporal redundancy across observations to reduce the Prefill workload. Changes in the current observation guide which tokens receive fresh computation, while cached features supply the remaining positions. However, reducing the number of refreshed tokens does not always reduce latency, as different token counts can fall within the same latency plateau (Table~ tab:component-ablation , right). We use this available capacity to refresh additional tokens with larger feature changes in the first layer, limiting reuse error at little extra latency. This reuse policy accounts for hardware latency and reduces the workload competing with prediction while keeping observation features current. Token reuse reduces the cost of the first stage, but subsequent denoising still requires repeated network evaluations. To further accelerate inference, we adapt the refresh schedule of cached Transformer residuals according to predicted motion. A coarse action prediction provides a displacement signal for deciding whether further refinement is needed. Motion amplitude and the effect of additional computation vary within an episode (Figure~ fig:motivation ), motivating a budget adapted to motion. We allocate fewer evaluations to large predicted movements to favor rapid replanning, while retaining additional evaluations for small adjustments. We evaluate this allocation through closed-loop ablations in Section~ sec:motion-analysis and paired prediction comparisons in Appendix~ app:motion-motivation . Refinement continues from the same initial denoising trajectory, preserving the computation already performed. We evaluate FastWAM and OpenWAM on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. Combining execution optimizations with adaptive computation gives measured average speedups of 8.90 and 10.67 , respectively, relative to native inference. Average success rates decrease by 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points (Table~ tab:main-comparison ). Controlled experiments examine which scheduling and computation allocation choices account for these gains. title: Lifelong small-object navigation in changing object layouts: a benchmark and method
summary: Household robots need to continually navigate to different objects in the same environment, many of which are small and portable, such as tools and toys. Their small visual footprint and frequent occlusion make reliable observation difficult, and they may be moved by people without the robot observing the changes. We formulate this challenging task as Lifelong Small-object Navigation in Changing Object Layouts (LiSoNav-COL). Agents must seek suitable viewpoints for reliable observation, accumulate and reuse scene knowledge to efficiently locate subsequent targets, and update outdated memory after object relocation. To eliminate the need for prior scene scanning, we also require agents to start navigation with empty scene memory. Although practical, this task still lacks benchmarks designed around its defining assumptions. To bridge this gap, we introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark spanning 28 indoor scenes with 45 small-object categories. Its lifelong navigation sequences include both unchanged and relocated targets to evaluate memory reuse and adaptation to object relocation. To address this challenging task, we propose a navigation method based on multi-view Inspection with Viewpoint-Anchored Memory, dubbed IVAM-Nav. IVAM-Nav actively observes supporting surfaces from complementary viewpoints for reliable small-object perception and anchors the resulting memory to their observation viewpoints, supporting relational memory reuse and revalidation under similar viewing conditions. Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods. Benchmark analyses also show that smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances pose greater challenges. The dataset and code are available here.

Introduction Object-goal navigation requires embodied agents to search for and navigate to target objects specified by images or language~ krantz2023navigating,zhu2021soon . In household environments, robots may repeatedly perform such tasks in the same scene, motivating lifelong navigation that retains and reuses experience across successive tasks~ khanna2024goatbench . Scene memory supports this process by preserving previously acquired object information to reduce redundant exploration. In everyday household activities, many objects that robots need to locate and manipulate are small, portable items, such as tools and toys. People may move objects unnoticed by the robot, leaving its scene memory outdated and requiring verification and updates. These objects also occupy only a small portion of the visual field and are often occluded, making them difficult to observe clearly~ wang2023smallobject . These real-world challenges motivate us to study Lifelong Small-object Navigation in Changing Object Layouts (LiSoNav-COL). In this task, an agent starts with no prior scene memory and navigates to successive small-object goals within the same environment, incrementally acquiring scene knowledge throughout the navigation. Given that unobserved object relocations may render its memory outdated, the agent must learn to reuse accumulated scene knowledge while adapting to these changes for accurate and efficient navigation. Starting with an empty memory eliminates the need for a separate scene-scanning phase in real-world applications. Existing navigation benchmarks adopt task assumptions that differ from those of LiSoNav-COL. The mainstream lifelong navigation benchmarks~ wani2020multion,khanna2024goatbench,Wang2026ExploreWL mainly evaluate experience reuse in static scenes, where target locations remain unchanged across subtasks. OpenIN~ tang2025openin evaluates sequential navigation after object relocation, but starts with a preconstructed scene graph and relocates objects before the task sequence begins. This setting assesses the use of prior scene knowledge after relocation, rather than its online acquisition and maintenance through repeated changes. Meanwhile, the small-object navigation benchmark~ wang2023smallobject focuses on perception and target search in static scenes under a single-goal setting. These evaluation settings do not jointly capture the requirements of LiSoNav-COL: acquiring scene knowledge from an initially empty memory, reusing it across small-object navigation tasks, and adapting to repeated object relocation. To support systematic evaluation of LiSoNav-COL, we introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a new benchmark comprising navigation sequences and an evaluation protocol for this task. Figure~ fig:reslon_overview presents an illustrative example of our benchmark, where the agent completes a sequence of small-object navigation subtasks (each corresponding to a specific goal) in the same environment, starting with no prior scene memory and retaining the knowledge acquired during task execution. Specifically, each navigation sequence comprises multiple episodes, each containing several navigation subtasks. Object locations remain unchanged within each episode, while randomly selected objects are relocated between episodes without the agent observing the changes. By including both unchanged and relocated targets, LiSoNav-Eval preserves opportunities to benefit from previously acquired knowledge while testing adaptation when remembered locations become outdated. Together, these settings support the evaluation of small-object navigation as agents accumulate scene knowledge, reuse it across tasks, and respond to changes in object layouts. In LiSoNav-COL, incomplete or unreliable small-object observations can limit the effectiveness of existing scene-memory methods~ huang2025msgnav,yang2025threedmem,tang2025openin . Object relocation compounds these observation difficulties, making memory reuse and revalidation more challenging. In this paper, we propose IVAM-Nav, a lifelong small-object navigation method based on multi-view Inspection and Viewpoint-Anchored Memory, to address these challenges. Our key idea is to actively inspect the supporting surfaces where the target may be located from multiple viewpoints and anchor the memory to these viewpoints. Specifically, the agent acquires reliable and complementary observations around potential supporting surfaces and stores them with their camera poses and semantic associations. These records enable reobservation under similar viewing conditions to effectively verify and update the memory. Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm. Our contributions can be summarized as: [leftmargin=1.5em] We formulate LiSoNav-COL, a new task for lifelong small-object navigation from empty scene memory under changing object layouts. We also introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating agent performance on this task. We propose IVAM-Nav, which constructs a viewpoint-anchored graph memory through active multi-view inspection. This design supports relational memory reuse and memory revalidation under similar viewing conditions, enabling robust navigation. Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods, and benchmark analyses identify smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances as persistent challenges. Related Work navigation in changing environments. Existing navigation tasks and benchmarks span single-goal, sequential, and lifelong settings in largely static scenes~ chaplot2020objectnav,krantz2023navigating,zhu2021soon,wani2020multion,khanna2024goatbench,miao2026langmap,yu2025cnav,wang2026lenl , while dynamic settings consider moving objects and spatiotemporal retrieval~ kurenkov2023modeling,dorbala2026personalized,jiang2025dualmap,bogenberger2026glasses,chen2025star . Most closely related to our setting, OpenIN studies changing object layouts but requires a preconstructed scene representation before navigation, with its evaluation data and implementation currently unavailable~ tang2025openin . LiSoNav-Eval instead evaluates lifelong small-object navigation from empty memory under changing object layouts. construction, reuse, and revalidation. Existing navigation methods construct and query scene memory through object- or scene-centric graphs, visual observations, and spatial representations~ gu2024conceptgraphs,werby2024hovsg,yang2025threedmem,liu2025dynamem,jiang2025dualmap,zhu2025mtu3d,chang2024goat,wang2023smallobject,xu2026dream,ge2026evomemnav , while dynamic-memory methods further update or reassess stored information based on new observations~ tang2025openin,jiang2025dualmap,liu2025dynamem,yan2025dovsg,zhao2026supermap,ko2025care . APRR and MSGNav actively adjust viewpoints after target detection or localization for manipulation or final-view selection~ qin2025aprr,huang2025msgnav . In contrast, IVAM-Nav builds reliable small-object memory via complementary multi-view inspection and uses acquisition viewpoints as persistent anchors for relational retrieval and revalidation. It needs to retain the knowledge acquired during subtask execution to facilitate the subsequent subtasks. The lifelong navigation sequence in LiSoNav-Eval spans three or four consecutive episodes, with each episode containing two or three navigation subtasks. Figure~ fig:reslon_overview illustrates such a sample. The goal object of each subtask is specified by a natural language instruction. To clearly specify the target object, the instruction is designed to include coarse contextual cues, such as its supporting surface or nearby surroundings, while leaving its exact current location unspecified. This formulation also aligns with how people typically describe the location of a small object in a home environment. Herein, we show two instruction samples: Instruction 1: Find the tissue box on the speckled countertop near the sink. Instruction 2: Find the turquoise Lego Duplo brick on a small wooden table next to a bed. We also provide an optional reference image to aid small-object recognition, which reveals no information about the current location of the target. In real-world applications, such images could be obtained through online searches or other external sources. Within an episode, object locations remain unchanged, and subtasks are executed sequentially from the terminal pose of the preceding subtask. Objects are relocated only between episodes to render memory outdated, not during navigation, to avoid turning the task into online tracking of moving objects. A subtask is successful when the agent stops within 1.5\,m of the valid instance matching the target description. Each subtask has a path-length budget of 10 times the shortest geodesic distance from the start to the target, and terminates immediately once this budget is exceeded. This budget allows exploration and recovery from outdated location information after object relocation while limiting excessive search. We report standard navigation metrics (SR and SPL), together with Historical Revisit (HR) and Relocated-target SR. Detailed definitions are provided in~ sec:exp_setup . title: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Understand Instructions? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study on Language Grounding
summary: Vision-Language-Action models are designed to generalise across environments and task descriptions, raising the question of whether their action generation actually depends on the language instruction, or whether they largely rely on visual cues and superficial correlations. Robustness to variance in the visual and linguistic observation space is critical for real-world deployment, yet VLAs lack explicit grounding modules and instead rely on the intrinsic language grounding capabilities of their Vision-Language model backbones. For this reason, we conduct a controlled mechanistic interpretability study on the language grounding capabilities of two state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action models, $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7, by applying activation and attribution patching to the residual stream of the action generation modules. We systematically corrupt the task instruction of input samples of the LIBERO benchmark following five strategies: synonym replacement, semantic scaling, directional corruption, random object substitution, and empty string. Our experiments find that both models are comparatively insensitive to abstract rephrasing and to referencing non-existent objects, but react strongly to empty task descriptions and, especially, to directional language. During action generation, this sensitivity is concentrated in different loci for each model: mainly in the early, periodic cross-attention layers for GR00T N1.7, versus distributed across the earliest and selected later layers for $π_{0.5}$. For GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations drive some of the largest causal effects while leaving the internal representational geometry comparatively unchanged, a dissociation we do not observe clearly for $π_{0.5}$. Finally, the reliability of attribution patching is model-dependent: it closely tracks activation patching for GR00T N1.7 but not for $π_{0.5}$.
