Introduction Robotic systems deployed in real-world environments must be robust, as unpredictable behaviour may lead to severe and potentially catastrophic consequences. Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) achieve impressive generalisation across different environments and task formulations, and yet the internal mechanisms underlying this behaviour remain largely a black box. This creates a gap between empirical performance and scientific understanding. Mechanistic interpretability has yielded insights in Large Language~ wangInterpretabilityWildCircuit2022 and Vision models~ gohMultimodalNeuronsArtificial2021 , but only a handful of works exist that investigate Vision-Language-Action models from a model-internal perspective~ grantNotAllFeatures2026,miaoContrastiveConceptorActivation2026 , particularly with respect to their action decoding strategies. While findings in NLP and Computer Vision might transfer to the shared underlying Language and Vision-Language model backbones, VLA action generation strategies regularly introduce specific action expert modules with varying decoding strategies that particularly require the generation of language-conditioned outputs. To this end, we address the gap between generalisability and understanding of the model's internal computations by analysing the action expert modules of two state-of-the-art VLAs: ~ black VisionLanguageActionModel2025 and GR00T N1.7~ GR00TN1Open2025 . Like many VLAs, both models employ a modular architecture in which an action expert incorporates visuolinguistic information from a Vision-Language model (VLM) backbone into a conditional flow-matching process for action generation. However, they differ in how this conditioning is implemented: integrates language via shared attention between action expert and backbone layers, while GR00T uses dedicated masked cross-attention layers. This contrast lets us ask whether such differences in conditioning have measurable consequences for how language is causally used inside the action expert. We apply the mechanistic interpretability techniques attribution patching and activation patching to the residual stream of the transformer layers in each model's action expert, and complement these causal measures with Centred Kernel Alignment (CKA) between clean and perturbed activations. Pairing a causal measure with a representational-similarity measure lets us distinguish two failure modes that are otherwise easy to conflate: (i) where a model's representations are simply insensitive to a perturbation, and (ii) where representations shift but the action expert routes only a subset of that shift into behaviourally relevant computation. By following a systematic language perturbation scheme, we construct the required corrupted instructions from the clean instructions for the corresponding patching methods. Our perturbation scheme operates on five categories of increasing severity: synonym replacements, semantic scaling, directional perturbations, random object substitution, and empty string. While the first two address sensitivity toward less specific inputs and alternate formulations on a verb and noun level, the directional perturbations directly investigate the effect of processing directional attributes within the action expert. We test whether the model can fall back on purely visual information by rendering the task impossible due to referencing objects not visible in the current scene or dropping the instruction altogether. Since all perturbed predictions are evaluated against the original demonstration, our experiments establish whether and where language causally influences the action, not whether it is interpreted correctly. Specifically, our contributions can be summarised as follows: A combined causal/representational analysis framework for diffusion/flow-matching VLA action experts. We integrate attribution patching, activation-patching verification, and CKA into a single evaluation framework applicable to transformer-based diffusion action heads, and use activation patching to directly quantify where attribution patching's linear approximation deviates from the true causal effect of language conditioning, and for which model this approximation is reliable. Language-perturbation sensitivity is model-specific. GR00T N1.7 exhibits a periodic layer-wise pattern that coincides with the placement of its cross-attention conditioning blocks, whereas shows stronger effects concentrated in early and selected later layers. Because the two models differ in more than their conditioning mechanism, we regard the link to architecture as a hypothesis. is comparatively more sensitive to verb perturbations, while GR00T N1.7 is more sensitive to noun perturbations. GR00T N1.7 also exhibits larger CKA shifts across several perturbation conditions, whereas 's global representational geometry remains relatively stable. Causal attribution and representational geometry dissociate for directional language in GR00T N1.7. In GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations elicit some of the largest attribution-patching effects of any perturbation type, yet leave the residual stream's representational geometry, as measured by CKA, comparatively unchanged. We do not observe this dissociation clearly for . For synonym, hypernym, and empty-string perturbations, causal and representational effects track one another more closely and follow our proposed perturbation-severity ranking. We hypothesise that this dissociation arises because directional phrases occupy a narrow, tightly clustered region of the embedding space, so the model's action output is highly sensitive to the perturbation despite the underlying representation shifting comparatively little. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Inspired by the successes and generalisable capabilities of foundation models in domains such as NLP and image generation~ openaiGPT4TechnicalReport2023,dubeyLlama3Herd2024,betkerImprovingImageGeneration,rombachHighResolutionImageSynthesis2022 , Vision-Language-Action models aim to create robot policies that generalise across tasks, environments and embodiments~ liuRDT1BDiffusionFoundation2024,teamGeminiRoboticsBringing2025,SpatialVLA2025,belkhaleRTHActionHierarchies2024,GR00TN1Open2025,kimOpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageAction2024a . VLAs are usually built on top of pretrained VLM backbones to inherit their vision-language understanding. They either add a dedicated action decoder module~ black VisionLanguageActionModel2025,GR00TN1Open2025 to generate embodiment-specific trajectories or utilize the VLM vocabulary to assign discrete actions to tokens~ kimOpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageAction2024a . The action decoding strategies employed by VLAs range from simple linear mappings to sophisticated diffusion-based action decoders. The latter employ flow matching or traditional diffusion denoising strategies as used by Chi et al.~ chiDiffusionPolicyVisuomotor2023 . As input, they take at least a task instruction in natural language alongside a visual observation. While VLAs show promising directions to generalising to differently formulated instructions as seen by their task success rates, it remains unclear how strong their language grounding actually is. Mechanistic Interpretability for Multimodal Foundation Models Early mechanistic interpretability work at the intersection of vision and language focused on foundation models, uncovering multimodal neurons that respond to shared visual-linguistic concepts gohMultimodalNeuronsArtificial2021 and interpreting CLIP's image representations directly gandelsmanInterpretingCLIPsImage2023,radfordLearningTransferableVisual2021a . Sparse autoencoders have since been widely applied to further disentangle CLIP's internal representations raoDiscoverthenNameTaskAgnosticConcept2024,roSemanticsDisentanglingInformation2026,josephSteeringCLIPsVision2025 , while causal tracing tools originally developed for LLMs have been extended to vision-language models palitVisionLanguageMechanisticInterpretability2023a,basuUnderstandingInformationStorage2024,neoInterpretingVisualInformation2024a and, more recently, video models shiCausalityMattersHow2026 , typically to localize task-relevant subgraphs rajaramAutomaticDiscoveryVisual or via probing-based analysis salinAreVisionLanguageTransformers2022a . Extending this line of work to embodied settings, recent studies have begun steering vision-language-action models (VLAs) haonMechanisticInterpretabilitySteering2025 , with a concurrent mechanistic study across five VLAs finding that these models process heterogeneous token sequences interleaving vision, language, and proprioception, and that mean-pooling activations across token positions destroys action-critical information despite high reconstruction quality grantNotAllFeatures2026 . To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has systematically examined, at the level of internal model computation, how VLAs respond to different types of perturbations in the language space, or where this processing occurs within their action-decoding components. We address this gap by analysing the token-generation process in the action expert of and the action decoder of GR00T N1.7 using attribution and activation patching alongside representational analyses. Circuit Discovery Mechanistic interpretability treats neural networks as computational graphs, with nodes corresponding to attention heads, MLPs, or individual neurons and features, and edges representing activation flow between them~ heimersheimHowUseInterpret2024 , a framing established by foundational work on transformer circuits~ MathematicalFrameworkTransformer , circuit-level case studies such as the IOI circuit~ wangInterpretabilityWildCircuit2022 and the greater-than arithmetic circuit~ hannaHowDoesGPT22023a , and formalized theoretically through causal abstraction~ geigerCausalAbstractionTheoretical2025a . Early circuit discovery relied on manual activation patching, that was later refined into path patching and automated via ACDC, which systematically searches a model's computational graph for task-relevant subgraphs~ conmyAutomatedCircuitD

title: MultiFly: A Real-World Multimodal Aerial Dataset with Annotation-Efficient Label Transfer and Cross-Modal Semantic Consistency
summary: We introduce MultiFly, a real-world, low-altitude UAV dataset for semantic perception across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar modalities. MultiFly provides 17,272 synchronized samples from four suburban scenes with frame-wise annotations for 15 semantic classes, together with calibration and GNSS-RTK/IMU measurements. To avoid costly and inconsistent modality-specific annotation, we propagate labels from only 115 manually annotated RGB images through shared geometric representations to all four modalities. This approach generates semantic labels for 17,157 additional RGB images, 17,272 thermal images, 840M LiDAR points, and 3.4M radar points. Transferred annotations achieve 89.93% average agreement with held-out manual annotations, and 90.94% average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs. We further establish semantic segmentation benchmarks for all four modalities, revealing distinct architectural behavior for dense LiDAR and sparse radar data. Taken together, MultiFly provides a scalable foundation for multimodal aerial perception and, to the best of our knowledge, the first public real-world low-altitude aerial benchmark that combines consistent frame-wise semantic annotations for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Data at https://github.com/markus-42/multifly.
full_text: \@oldmaketitle\@maketitle \@oldmaketitle Overview of MultiFly. A synchronized and calibrated UAV platform captures multimodal RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar data, while our geometry-driven pipeline propagates RGB-only annotations to all four modalities, generating cross-modally consistent semantic labels for four scenes, two altitudes, and 15 semantic categories. fig_banner 1 We introduce MultiFly, a real-world, low-altitude UAV dataset for semantic perception across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar modalities. MultiFly provides 17,272 synchronized samples from four suburban scenes with frame-wise annotations for 15 semantic classes, together with calibration and GNSS-RTK/IMU measurements. To avoid costly and inconsistent modality-specific annotation, we propagate labels from only 115 manually annotated RGB images through shared geometric representations to all four modalities. This approach generates semantic labels for 17,157 additional RGB images, 17,272 thermal images, 840M LiDAR points, and 3.4M radar points. Transferred annotations achieve 89.93 average agreement with held-out manual annotations, and 90.94 average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs. We further establish semantic segmentation benchmarks for all four modalities, revealing distinct architectural behavior for dense LiDAR and sparse radar data. Taken together, MultiFly provides a scalable foundation for multimodal aerial perception and, to the best of our knowledge, the first public real-world low-altitude aerial benchmark that combines consistent frame-wise semantic annotations for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Data at . Introduction sec_intro Semantic scene understanding is fundamental to aerial perception~ gross2026safeland, nguyen2019arialSurveillanceInspection, bultmann2023aerialDisasterRescue . However, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) data remains substantially underrepresented in large-scale multimodal datasets, which increasingly drive modern foundation models. Notably, this is not simply a data-volume problem: UAV perception introduces distinct scene statistics, object scales, and viewing geometries, ranging from nadir to oblique perspectives, that are poorly represented in conventional ground-based datasets. Autonomous driving illustrates the contrast, where large-scale multimodal datasets have enabled systematic alignment across sensors, while similarly comprehensive resources for UAV perception remain limited. This gap is particularly evident for semantic segmentation. Existing aerial datasets generally provide a single modality or limited modality combinations~ nigam2018aeroscapes,gross2026segfly,wang2025uavscenes , while no public real-world UAV dataset, to the best of our knowledge, provides synchronized frame-wise semantic annotations across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Moreover, these modalities differ substantially in geometry and sampling, making consistent annotation difficult and costly. To address these challenges, we introduce MultiFly, a calibrated and time-synchronized four-modal aerial sensing platform and semantic dataset. Our annotation framework uses 3D scene geometry as a common semantic interface: a~sparse set of manually annotated RGB images is lifted into 3D and transferred to synchronized RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar measurements. This yields dense multimodal annotations from only 115 manually labeled RGB images, while maintaining a common taxonomy and geometric reference. We summarize our main contributions as follows: MultiFly dataset release: \(17 , 272\) synchronized RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar samples across suburban scenes, covering \(56 , 700\, ^ 2 \) and semantic classes, with full sensor calibration and state information. Annotation-efficient label transfer: Semantic labels are propagated from only 115 manually annotated RGB images to additional \(17 , 157\) RGB frames, \(17 , 272\) thermal frames, \(8.4 10^ 8 \) LiDAR points, and \(3.4 10^ 6 \) radar points, achieving \(89.93 \) average agreement with held-out manual annotations, and \(90.94 \) average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs. Benchmarking: We establish semantic segmentation benchmarks on MultiFly for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar modalities, and analyze architectural influences between dense LiDAR and sparse radar segmentation. Related Work sec_related_work Multimodal Semantic Aerial Datasets Semantic perception has evolved from single-sensor benchmarks~ brostow_2008_camvid, munoz2009oakland3d toward multimodal datasets that enable learning across complementary sensors. In autonomous driving, early resources established core camera-LiDAR perception tasks, while second-generation datasets such as nuScenes~ caesar2020nuscenes expanded to large-scale, synchronized multimodal sensing. This shift enabled not only sensor fusion, but also temporal and multi-task perception, prediction, and planning, and increasingly multimodal foundation models that unify these capabilities. UAV perception has yet to undergo a comparable transition. Existing aerial datasets remain fragmented across sensing modalities and annotation formats: most are unimodal~ arroyo2024radarUnimodalDataset, lee2026lidarUnimodalDataset, nigam2018aeroscapes , while others combine only two modalities~ lee2024cart, li2024mars-lvig, wang2025uavscenes , rely on synthetic data~ rizzoli2023syndrone, zou2025uav-mm3d , or provide map-wise rather than frame-wise annotations~ koelle2021hessigheim3d, lin2022urbanScene3d . Consequently, the data required to develop and systematically evaluate unified multimodal UAV perception models remains largely unavailable. In particular, no public real-world low-altitude UAV dataset, to the best of our knowledge, provides synchronized frame-wise semantics across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. MultiFly provides this missing substrate (Table~ tab_datasets ), combining synchronized and registered RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar data with inertial measurements from Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and global positioning from a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) with real-time kinematic (RTK) corrections. Cross-Modal Semantic Consistency Beyond sensor coverage, multimodal learning requires semantic supervision that is consistent across modalities. Independent annotation can introduce conflicting boundaries and labels, motivating geometry-based approaches that propagate semantics through a shared representation. KITTI-360~ liao2023kitti-360 transfers labels between images and 3D geometry, while WildScenes~ vid2024wildScenes projects multi-view image annotations into LiDAR. UAVScenes~ wang2025uavscenes similarly annotates reconstructed 3D maps and renders them into camera frames before projecting labels onto LiDAR, while SegFly~ gross2026segfly adopts a 2D-3D-2D pipeline to lift sparse RGB annotations into a reconstructed point cloud and renders them into RGB and thermal images. These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of geometry-driven annotation, but remain limited in modality coverage, and require manual verification and correction. MultiFly extends this paradigm to four modalities through a unified geometry-driven pipeline, propagating sparse RGB annotations to RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar, while ensuring high semantic consistency without the necessity of manual correction. It therefore offers not only broader sensor coverage, but a shared frame-wise semantic reference for multimodal UAV perception and cross-modal evaluation. MultiFly Platform sec_multifly_platform Design sec_design To acquire multimodal aerial data, we propose the MultiFly platform shown in , which integrates one forward-facing RGB camera, one thermal camera, one spinning LiDAR, two forward-facing radars, and a GNSS-RTK-aided inertial navigation system (INS), with detailed specifications listed in . One radar is pitched downward by to increase the effective vertical field of view (FOV), while the whole sensor rig is pitched downward by to jointly observe the flight direction and ground below the UAV. All perception sensors are calibrated with respect to the LiDAR reference frame and synchronized to a common time base, while the INS provides the platform pose. Perception data are recorded at on an Aetina AIB MX22 edge computing unit using Docker and ROS 2 Humble, together with dedicated onboard power (DOGCOM 10000 mAh Li-Ion), networking (NetGear GSM110MX switch), and storage hardware. Example synchronized RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar measurements are shown in . Time Synchronization sec_sync All sensors are synchronized to a common GNSS-disciplined time base using the Precision Time Protocol (PTP). The INS acts as the PTP grandmaster, while the Aetina computer operates as a boundary clock and distributes the time reference to the sensor network. While PTP establishes a common time base, sensor-specific triggering and phase compensation align the actual acquisition times across modalities. More specifically, sensor acquisition is aligned with the LiDAR's scan cycle, corresponding to a fixed rotation period of . The rotating LiDAR generates a hardware trigger for the forward-facing RGB camera, with a configurable delay accounting for the exposure time and the camera's orientation relative to the LiDAR scan, effectively aligning the acquisition with the LiDAR beam passing through the camera FOV. The radars operate at the same nominal frequency, but their measurement epochs have a deterministic phase offset relative to the LiDAR cycle, which is compensated using the driver's cycle offset parameter, resulting in radar--LiDAR deviations within . Since the thermal camera does not support hardware triggering, its acquisition is controlled using timestamped GigE Vision Scheduled Action Commands, which are executed according to its PTP-synchronized clock. Sensor Calibration and Registration subsec_sensor_calibration Extrinsics. We organize the sensor extrinsics as a calibration tree rooted at the LiDAR, which serves as the common reference frame. The tree consists of three edges: RGB--LiDAR From a static recording of a structured scene, we manually select natural landmarks that are sharp in both modalities and estimate the rigid transform by solving a perspective- -point problem. Radar--LiDAR Corner reflectors are placed in the shared sensor FOV. Corresponding radar and LiDAR detections are paired and the rigid transform is recovered in closed form via Singular Value Decomposition. RGB--Thermal The two cameras are stereo-calibrated on checkerboard corners observed by both sensors. Composing the RGB--Thermal and RGB--LiDAR transforms places the thermal camera in the LiDAR frame. Intrinsics. We calibrate the RGB camera and the thermal camera independently with Zhang's planar method~ zhang2000camCalibration from multiple checkerboard views. The RGB target is a conventional checkerboard, while the thermal target is a steel plate carrying plotter-cut vinyl squares, whose emissivity contrast against the exposed steel renders the corners detectable in the thermal band. LiDAR and radar use their factory intrinsics. Registration. subsec_registration Radar detections are transformed into the LiDAR frame, and LiDAR-frame measurements are projected into either image using the calibrated extrinsics, intrinsics, and distortion models. Furthermore, RGB--thermal registration requires scene geometry because the nonzero camera baseline induces depth-dependent parallax. Consequently, the calibrated rigid extrinsic alone does not define a dense pixel-to-pixel mapping. In principle, the synchronized and calibrated LiDAR measurements could provide the required depth for reprojecting RGB observations into the thermal view. Instead, we follow SegFly~ gross2026segfly and use the metric RGB-based 3D reconstruction required by the label-transfer pipeline ( ). title: OpenViTac: Learning and Benchmarking Visuo-Tactile Policies in a Unified Sim-and-Real Framework
summary: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
full_text: Equal contribution. Project leaders.. Introduction ``The ideas of sight and touch make two species entirely distinct and heterogeneous.''\\[2pt] Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla have enabled robots to leverage large-scale visual and linguistic knowledge for increasingly generalizable manipulation~ intelligence2025pi05 . These foundation policies have demonstrated strong performance across diverse manipulation scenarios~ liu2023libero,khazatsky2024droid , yet remain primarily grounded in visual observations. However, many real-world interactions require understanding physical states that are not directly observable from vision alone, such as object properties, contact dynamics, and interaction forces~ feng2026anytouch2 . By providing direct feedback from physical interaction, tactile sensing~ dong2017improved,team2026n0_foundation augments visual perception with complementary physical information, enabling embodied agents to better understand and interact with the physical world, such as contact geometry, force cues, and material-dependent responses. This has motivated a shift from purely vision-based policies toward Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) models~ huang2025tactilevla,yuan2026ftp,niu2026t-rex , which combine global scene understanding from vision with local interaction feedback from touch. Driven by the promise of tactile feedback, recent VTLA studies have rapidly expanded the design space of tactile-enabled robot policies, exploring different tactile representations~ zhao2025t3,higuera2024sparsh,feng2026anytouch2 , fusion strategies~ morissette2026tacfilm,xu2026ViTacMotor , and policy architectures~ yuan2026ftp,niu2026t-rex . Nevertheless, these approaches are typically evaluated under different sensors, tasks, robot embodiments, and experimental protocols, making systematic comparison challenging and leaving the contribution of tactile sensing insufficiently understood. Existing manipulation benchmarks, such as LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin , and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo , primarily focus on vision-based policies and do not support tactile sensing. Recent visuo-tactile benchmarks, such as Tabero~ wu2026tabero and UniVTAC~ chen2026univtac , have started to introduce tactile observations and contact-rich tasks for evaluation. However, as shown in Tab.~ tab:benchmark_comparison , existing benchmarks still lack comprehensive coverage of tactile-relevant capabilities, diverse hardware configurations, and sim--real correspondence. To address this, we introduce OpenViTac, a unified benchmark for evaluating visuo-tactile robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , OpenViTac organizes tactile-enabled manipulation into four capability dimensions: physical property perception, fragility-aware manipulation, contact-rich manipulation, and precision manipulation, covering diverse scenarios that require understanding object properties, contact states, and fine-grained interaction dynamics. We evaluate representative VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies~ intelligence2025pi05,community2026starvla,zheng2026xvla,wu2026lingbot-vla-2,ma2026internvla-a1.5,team2026xiaomi,ali2025cosmos2.5,yuan2026fast-wam,li2026lingbot-va,team2026n_0-twam,yuan2026ftp,team2026n0-vtla on OpenViTac, providing a comprehensive comparison of their tactile-enabled manipulation capabilities. Building upon OpenViTac, we further investigate how tactile observations can be incorporated into vision-based policies through two design choices: tactile representation and tactile integration. Our study reveals that stronger tactile representations and effective integration strategies consistently improve performance on contact-sensitive manipulation tasks. Based on this analysis, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework for pretrained VLA models. Quantitatively, the strongest VLA, WAM, and VTLA baselines achieve 51.5 , 53.3 , and 61.2 average success rates in simulation, respectively, while OpenVTLA reaches 68.7 . The same trend holds in real-world evaluation, where OpenVTLA achieves 54.6 , compared with 43.1 , 48.5 , and 51.9 from the strongest VLA, WAM, and VTLA baselines. Finally, leveraging the paired sim--real setting of OpenViTac, we investigate sim--real co-training as a strategy for improving real-world policy learning through additional simulation data. Overall, our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=1pt] A unified visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark. We introduce OpenViTac, a tactile-centric benchmark with four capability dimensions and paired simulation--real-world settings for evaluating VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. An investigation of tactile adaptation for pretrained VLAs. We investigate tactile representation and integration strategies for adapting vision-based policies to touch, leading to OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework achieving strong performance across simulation and real-world evaluations. A sim--real co-training study. We leverage OpenViTac's paired sim--real setting to investigate sim--real co-training and analyze the factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Related Work sec:related_work Here we review related work on visuo-tactile robot learning and visuo-tactile datasets and benchmarks. Additional discussion can be found in Appendix~ app:additional_related_work . Visuo-Tactile Robot Learning Recent robot foundation policies have largely developed around vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs)~ kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi05 . Tactile feedback provides complementary contact and physical-property information that can improve contact-sensitive manipulation, motivating tactile-augmented policies such as VTLA models~ yuan2026ftp,team2026n0-vtla,niu2026t-rex,wang2026vitar and tactile-aware world-action models~ lou2026dreamtac,team2026n_0-twam . Existing approaches, however, differ substantially in how touch is incorporated, including feature modulation~ morissette2026tacfilm , action-level conditioning~ team2026n0-vtla , dedicated tactile experts~ yuan2026ftp , and late-stage action refinement~ niu2026t-rex,wang2026vitar . Given the lack of consensus on how tactile information should be incorporated into pretrained VLAs, in this paper we systematically study representative tactile integration strategies under a shared backbone. Visuo-Tactile Datasets and Benchmarks General manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin , and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo provide standardized evaluation across diverse simulated tasks, but primarily focus on vision-based manipulation. A broad range of tactile datasets has been developed for representation learning~ yang2022touch,kerr2022self,higuera2024sparsh,feng2026anytouch2 , while tactile-enabled real-robot manipulation data have only recently begun to scale across tasks, sensors, and embodiments~ yuan2026ftp,team2026n0_foundation,lou2026dreamtac . For policy-level evaluation, ManiFeel~ luu2025manifeel and TacO~ zorin2026taco study tactile sensing in downstream manipulation, while UniVTAC~ chen2026univtac and NeoSim~ team2026n0_foundation further provide systematic evaluation in simulation. However, existing simulation benchmarks still exhibit substantial discrepancies from real-world settings. OpenViTac provides a unified tactile-centric benchmark with aligned sim--real tasks and additional real-world data across multiple tactile sensors. OpenViTac sec:benchmark We introduce OpenViTac, a unified benchmark for evaluating visuo-tactile robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes tactile-enabled manipulation into four capability dimensions and provides 11 simulation tasks with 8 paired real-world tasks for systematic evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon OpenViTac, we study tactile adaptation for pretrained VLA models through tactile representation and integration strategies, leading to OpenVTLA, and further investigate sim--real co-training enabled by the paired benchmark setting. Benchmark sec:benchmark_design Benchmark design. OpenViTac evaluates whether policies can exploit tactile feedback when visual observations provide incomplete information about physical interaction. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:capability_taxonomy , we organize the benchmark around four visuo-tactile capabilities: property perception, fragility-aware, contact-rich, and precision. Further details are provided in Appendix~ app:benchmark_details . Task suite. We organize the tasks into four complementary visuo-tactile capabilities: (1) Property Perception (PP) evaluates whether tactile feedback can reveal visually ambiguous physical properties and support property-conditioned decisions. It includes weight classification (WC), hardness classification (HC), and roughness classification (RC) for property-conditioned placement; roughness-guided regrasp (RR) for property-aware regrasping; and empty-can selection (ECS) for distinguishing empty from filled cans through physical interaction. (2) Fragility-Aware (FA) evaluates force-sensitive manipulation of delicate objects. Grasp chip (GC) requires grasping and placing a fragile chip without damaging it. (3) Contact-Rich (CR) evaluates manipulation that requires sustained and effective physical contact. It includes gear assembly (GA), which requires maintaining gear engagement during assembly, and pull drawer (PD), which requires maintaining a stable grasp while actuating an articulated drawer. (4) Precision Manipulation (PR) evaluates contact-guided manipulation under tight geometric tolerances. It includes insert USB (In-USB) and insert block v1 (In-B v1) for precise alignment and insertion, and insert block v2 (In-B v2), which additionally requires selecting the instructed object before insertion. --sim alignment. As shown in Fig.~ fig:real_sim_alignment , we provide an agent-assisted real-to-sim pipeline for constructing task-corresponding simulation environments from real-world references. (1) At the asset level, multi-view images of real-world objects are used to reconstruct their simulation counterparts, with the agent analyzing task-relevant structure and decomposing objects into functional parts when necessary; (2) At the task level, reference object and target configurations together with robot initial states are used to instantiate the corresponding simulation task and construct executable sub-actions for trajectory collection. OpenViTac further supports scene diversification by varying backgrounds, workspace appearance, and surrounding context while preserving the underlying task configuration, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:scene_diversity , providing a flexible way to broaden the simulated data distribution for downstream training. Evaluation protocol. sec:benchmark_evaluation We evaluate all policies under predefined and balanced task conditions using task-specific binary success criteria. Further details are provided in Appendix~ app:benchmark_details . ADAPTING PRETRAINED VLAS TO TOUCH sec:openvtla Large-scale visuo-tactile robot data remain limited and heterogeneous across sensors, embodiments, and manipulation tasks, making it difficult to train tactile-native policies at the scale of modern VLAs~ yuan2026ftp,team2026n0-vtla . We therefore study a practical post-training setting in which all variants start from the same pretrained ~ intelligence2025pi05 backbone, while varying how tactile observations are represented and incorporated into the policy. As shown in Fig.~ fig:tactile_design , we investigate these choices along two dimensions: tactile representation and tactile integration. Representation. The first design choice is how tactile observations should be represented for a pretrained VLA. The most direct option is to reuse SigLIP~ zhai2023siglip , the native visual encoder of , which preserves the existing representation interface

title: AirGroundVLN: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Air-Ground Collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Goal-oriented Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to locate and reach targets described in natural language without prescribed routes. Air--ground collaboration is valuable for tasks requiring both wide-area search and fine-grained localization. However, systematic study of goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN remains limited by the lack of large-scale, diverse benchmarks and two core challenges: 1) substantial differences between aerial and ground views, together with useful observations becoming unavailable as navigation proceeds, make it difficult to maintain spatially consistent context across platforms and over time; and 2) asymmetric spatial observability makes ground perception locally detailed but spatially limited and aerial perception broad but locally coarse, limiting the reliability of single-platform planning. To address these limitations, we introduce AirGroundVLN, a benchmark containing 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, with seen/unseen splits and an aerial-visibility protocol for systematic evaluation. Alongside the benchmark, we propose AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework comprising two key components: Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) and Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning (AGRLP). SACM maintains and retrieves spatially consistent historical context across aerial and ground observations. Meanwhile, AGRLP combines regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV and establish AirGroundVLN as a comprehensive benchmark for future exploration.
full_text: Goal-oriented Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to locate and reach targets described in natural language without prescribed routes. Air--ground collaboration is valuable for tasks requiring both wide-area search and fine-grained localization. However, systematic study of goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN remains limited by the lack of large-scale, diverse benchmarks and two core challenges: 1) substantial differences between aerial and ground views, together with useful observations becoming unavailable as navigation proceeds, make it difficult to maintain spatially consistent context across platforms and over time; and 2) asymmetric spatial observability makes ground perception locally detailed but spatially limited and aerial perception broad but locally coarse, limiting the reliability of single-platform planning. To address these limitations, we introduce AirGroundVLN, a benchmark containing navigation episodes and target instances across Unreal Engine environments, with splits and an protocol for systematic evaluation. Alongside the benchmark, we propose AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework comprising two key components: Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) and Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning (AGRLP). SACM maintains and retrieves spatially consistent historical context across aerial and ground observations. Meanwhile, AGRLP combines regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV and establish AirGroundVLN as a comprehensive benchmark for future exploration. Introduction sec:intro Goal-oriented vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is a core problem in embodied intelligence~ REVERIE,SOON , requiring an agent to interpret a language-specified target, search for it, identify the correct instance, and reach it without prescribed intermediate routes. Existing goal-oriented VLN studies predominantly consider two types of embodied platforms: (1) Ground Platforms, such as wheeled Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs), quadruped robots, and humanoid robots~ VLN-CE,li2025ground . (2) Aerial Platforms, typically Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)~ AerialVLN,TravelUAV,UAVON,Openfly . In large-scale outdoor environments, ground platforms provide fine-grained observations of local scene structure and target appearance and can physically approach ground-level targets. In contrast, aerial platforms provide broader spatial coverage and global scene context, enabling efficient wide-area search and route-level reasoning. As two popular embodied platforms, substantial research has focused on separately expanding their perception~ Vlmap , reasoning and planning~ Irpan2022, Llm-planner , and execution capabilities~ Ego,RMA . But consider such a real mission in a large industrial complex, where robots are instructed to . In this mission, an aerial platform can rapidly survey the area and search for the worker from a global viewpoint, but its observations may be obstructed by trees, roofs, or collapsed structures, and it cannot provide physical rescue. Meanwhile, a ground platform can closely approach the worker, inspect regions hidden from the aerial viewpoint, and provide assistance, but damaged roads, debris, and collapsed buildings may render routes infeasible. Such a mission calls for aerial and ground platforms to work together, combining wide-area search with fine-grained target localization and physical access. This complementary division of capabilities motivates heterogeneous air--ground collaboration for goal-oriented navigation. However, systematic study of goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN remains limited by three key issues: (1) Although recent efforts have explored air--ground VLN~ AirGroundBench,AGC-VLN , they remain limited in scale and diversity, with AirGroundBench and AGC-VLN evaluated on only 115 and 100 episodes, respectively. To our knowledge, a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN is still lacking, limiting systematic evaluation. (2) Beyond benchmark limitation, aerial and ground observations differ in viewpoint, while useful observations from either platform may become unavailable during navigation. Therefore, effective collaboration requires spatially consistent context across views and time. (3) Aerial and ground platforms exhibit asymmetric spatial observability: ground perception is locally detailed but spatially limited, whereas aerial perception covers broader regions but provides less fine-grained obstacle information, making either platform alone insufficient for reliable navigation. To address this gap, we first introduce AirGroundVLN, a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN. AirGroundVLN contains 10,281 navigation episodes, 955 target instances, and 19 Unreal Engine environments, covering urban areas, towns, industrial areas, and other complex outdoor environments. Each episode includes aerial and ground observations together with a goal-oriented instruction describing the target appearance and its surrounding environmental context, rather than prescribing intermediate navigation actions. We provide seen and unseen environment splits to evaluate cross-environment generalization. An is further defined to distinguish targets visible from above and those occluded by overhead structures, enabling evaluation under different target-visibility conditions. Alongside the benchmark, we develop AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework addressing the above two key challenges of air--ground collaborative VLN. First, to maintain spatially consistent spatiotemporal context across heterogeneous aerial and ground observations, we introduce the Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM), which stores and retrieves historical evidence by associating observations of physically related regions over time. Second, to overcome limitations of single-platform planning under asymmetric spatial observability, we introduce the Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning module (AGRLP), which combines regional aerial guidance with locally executable ground planning. In addition, to establish reference baselines for AirGroundVLN, we construct training-free and trainable methods for air--ground collaborative VLN and evaluate them alongside AG-CoNAV across seen/unseen environments and aerial-visible/aerial-occluded conditions. These evaluations establish reference performance for AirGroundVLN and demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce AirGroundVLN, a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air--ground collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation. It contains 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, together with goal-oriented instructions, seen/unseen splits, and an aerial-visibility protocol for systematic evaluation. We develop AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework for heterogeneous air--ground collaborative VLN. It incorporates a Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) for spatiotemporally consistent context association and historical retrieval, together with an Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning module (AGRLP) that coordinates regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground execution. We provide a diverse suite of training-free and trainable baselines for AirGroundVLN, establishing a comprehensive evaluation suite for this new setting. Systematic evaluations across environment generalization and aerial-visibility conditions provide reference performance for the benchmark and validate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV. Related Work sec:relatedwork Vision-and-Language Navigation Benchmarks subsec:rw_vln Early VLN benchmarks such as R2R and R4R focus on route following in indoor environments~ R2R,R4R , while Touchdown and Talk2Nav extend language-guided navigation to outdoor scenes~ Touchdown,talk2nav . VLN-CE moves navigation from discrete panoramic graphs to continuous environments~ VLN-CE , and AerialVLN further extends route-oriented VLN to UAV navigation in large-scale outdoor environments~ AerialVLN . Beyond route following, REVERIE and SOON study goal-oriented navigation toward language-described targets~ REVERIE,SOON , while TravelUAV, UAV-ON, and CityNav extend goal-oriented language guidance to aerial platforms~ TravelUAV,UAVON,citynav . Despite these advances, most benchmarks still focus on a single embodied platform. AirGroundBench begins to study heterogeneous UAV--UGV perception through 62K diagnostic VQA instances and 115 closed-loop VLN episodes~ AirGroundBench , but large-scale goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN remains underexplored. Multi-Agent Collaborative Navigation subsec:rw_multi_agent Multi-agent navigation studies focus on homogeneous teams of ground robots~ Burgard2000,MMM,MADE-Net or aerial agents~ MultiUAVPlanning . Vision-language research extends collaboration to language-conditioned navigation, with CoNavBench studying VLN among ground robots~ CoNavBench , and AeroDuo and CoNav-UAV exploring complementary viewpoints within multi-UAV teams~ AeroDuo,CoNav-UAV . Moving toward heterogeneous collaboration, AGOS-Bench studies closed-loop UAV--UGV cooperative object search with visual-reference goals~ AGOSBench , while AGC-VLN introduces language-conditioned air--ground navigation through a shared bird's-eye map linking aerial context with ground planning~ AGC-VLN . However, dedicated trainable air--ground collaborative VLN remains underexplored. AirGroundVLN Benchmark sec:airgroundvln In this section, we first define the goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN task and its evaluation protocol (Sec.~ sec:task_definition ), then present the construction pipeline of AirGroundVLN (Sec.~ sec:benchmark_construction ), and finally analyze its scale, diversity, and evaluation splits (Sec.~ sec:dataset_analysis ). Task Definition sec:task_definition Task Formulation. AirGroundVLN considers a closed-loop navigation episode in which an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) and an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) cooperate to locate and reach a language-specified target instance in a large-scale outdoor environment. The UGV serves as the primary target-reaching platform, while the UAV provides complementary aerial perception and global spatial context. At the beginning of each episode, the two platforms are initialized at poses and , respectively, and receive a goal-oriented instruction . The instruction describes the target through its semantic category, visual attributes, surrounding environmental context, and coarse relative direction, without prescribing intermediate navigation actions. At navigation step , the UGV and UAV receive their current visual observations and , together with historical context available at the current step. A collaborative navigation system produces platform-specific navigation decisions (e.g., waypoints or actions) and a termination signal: where denotes the historical information maintained by the navigation system at step . For AirGroundVLN, the variables and denote the predicted waypoint decisions for the UGV and UAV, respectively, and indicates termination of the episode. An episode terminates at , where is the maximum allowable navigation budget. Evaluation Protocol. Given these asymmetric roles, we evaluate performance on the UGV using four standard VLN metrics~ anderson2018evaluation : Success Rate (SR), Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), UGV Navigation Error (NE ), and Oracle Success Rate (OSR). For the UAV, we report UAV Navigation Error (NE ), defined as its final horizontal distance to the target, as a diagnostic metric. Evaluation protocol and metric definitions are provided in Appendix~ supp:metrics . title: RFPO: Rectified Flow Policy Optimization for Embodied Control
summary: Flow-based policies provide an expressive framework for continuous robot control, but their iterative ODE integration incurs substantial inference cost. Naively reducing the integration budget can severely degrade control, since policies optimized under full-step execution are not explicitly constrained to remain reliable under coarse numerical integration. We refer to this mismatch as the few-step discretization gap. To address this problem, we introduce RFPO, a flow-policy optimization framework for reliable few-step execution. Reward-aware online Reflow rectifies student-induced transport paths during on-policy learning, making the resulting policy more robust to coarse integration. A frozen Gaussian PPO controller supplies complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets, while the deployed policy remains a single flow student executed with one Euler step. Across Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1, RFPO consistently preserves full-step control performance under one-step execution, with one-step returns remaining within 2.4% of their corresponding 64-step values across both zero and random initialization. On Unitree Go2, one-step execution retains 98.5% of the 64-step reward while reducing onboard mean inference latency from 4.39 ms to 0.08 ms, yielding a 54.9x speedup. Real-robot experiments further validate stable one-step locomotion. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/RFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/RFPO.

Real-robot experiments further validate stable one-step locomotion. Code:~ . Website:~ Introduction Learning expressive and efficient continuous-control policies is a central problem in robotics. Conventional reinforcement learning typically parameterizes actions with simple distributions such as diagonal Gaussians, which are easy to optimize but can be restrictive when multiple control strategies are valid under the same observation. Generative policies provide a more expressive alternative and have shown strong performance in visuomotor and geometry-aware robot control~ chi2025diffusion,ze20243d . In particular, flow matching~ lipman2022flow and rectified flow~ liu2022flow model action generation as an ODE that transports simple noise distributions into continuous actions. Flow-based policies have since been adopted for efficient robot manipulation~ zhang2025flowpolicy and large-scale vision-language-action models such as ~ black2024pi_0 , highlighting their potential as an expressive policy class for robot control. Beyond demonstration-supervised learning, recent work has increasingly optimized generative policies directly from environment rewards. Diffusion-based approaches such as DPPO~ ren2025diffusion , DIME~ celik2025dime , and GenPO~ ding2026genpo extend reinforcement learning to iterative generative action distributions. For flow-based policies, ReinFlow~ zhang2026reinflow enables online fine-tuning through stochastic flow dynamics, while Flow Q-Learning~ park2025flow and SAC Flow~ zhang2026sac explore offline and off-policy optimization. FPO~ mcallister2026flow constructs an on-policy surrogate directly from conditional flow-matching losses, and FPO++~ yi2026flow further improves this formulation with per-sample flow ratios and asymmetric trust-region updates. These advances make reward-driven optimization of expressive flow policies increasingly practical. However, high-reward flow policies are not necessarily reliable when the numerical integration budget is aggressively reduced. Existing flow-policy RL objectives optimize control return under the training integration budget but do not explicitly constrain the resulting vector field to remain numerically reliable under coarse integration. Consequently, reducing the number of Euler steps can substantially change the generated action and lead to severe control degradation, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation . We refer to this mismatch between full-step optimization and low-budget execution as the few-step discretization gap. Although Reflow~ liu2022flow , consistency learning~ song2023consistency , fast ODE solvers, and policy distillation~ prasad2024consistency,zhang2025flowpolicy have enabled efficient few-step generation, these techniques are primarily developed for generative modeling, imitation learning, or post-hoc policy acceleration rather than jointly with on-policy reward optimization. This motivates directly shaping reward-optimized flow policies for reliable few-step execution. To address this problem, we introduce , a flow-policy optimization framework for reliable few-step control. The key mechanism is reward-aware online Reflow, which repeatedly constructs student-induced full-step endpoints and rectifies their transport paths during on-policy learning, making the learned vector field more amenable to coarse numerical integration. A frozen Gaussian PPO controller supplies complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets, anchoring the quality of the learned actions without directly supervising one-step execution. The original on-policy objective is retained throughout training, and all training-only components are removed at deployment, leaving a single flow student executed with one Euler step. We evaluate across two quadruped and two humanoid embodiments: Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1. Across all four embodiments and both zero and random initialization, one-step execution remains within of the corresponding 64-step return, whereas FPO++ and distillation-only baselines exhibit substantial degradation under aggressive step reduction. On Unitree Go2, retains 98.5 of its 64-step reward while reducing onboard mean inference latency from ~ms to ~ms, yielding a 54.9 speedup. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate stable one-step locomotion across forward, lateral, and yaw commands. Our contributions are threefold: We identify the few-step discretization gap in reward-optimized flow policies, where aggressive reduction of the numerical integration budget can severely degrade control despite strong full-step performance. We introduce , which uses reward-aware student-induced online Reflow to regularize transport geometry during on-policy learning, together with complementary multi-budget action-space supervision from a frozen Gaussian PPO controller. Extensive evaluations across two quadruped and two humanoid embodiments demonstrate robust one-step execution. On Unitree Go2, retains 98.5 of 64-step reward with a 54.9 onboard inference speedup and transfers to real-robot locomotion. Related Work and flow policies for robot control. Generative policies provide an expressive alternative to Gaussian actors for modeling multimodal robot behaviors. Diffusion Policy~ chi2025diffusion and 3D Diffusion Policy~ ze20243d demonstrate strong visuomotor and geometry-aware manipulation performance using iterative generative action models. Flow matching~ lipman2022flow and rectified flow~ liu2022flow provide an ODE-based alternative and have been adopted by robot policies such as RF-Policy~ hu2023rf , FlowPolicy~ zhang2025flowpolicy , and ManiFlow~ yan2025maniflow , as well as large-scale vision-language-action models such as ~ black2024pi_0 . Recent work has further accelerated iterative robot policies through consistency learning and policy distillation~ prasad2024consistency,wang2025onestep . These methods are predominantly trained from demonstrations or supervised robot data, whereas our work studies few-step execution of flow policies optimized directly from environment rewards. learning with generative policies. Generative models have increasingly been incorporated into planning and reinforcement learning. Diffusion-based methods have been used for trajectory planning and expressive offline policies~ janner2022diffuser,wang2023diffusion,kang2023efficient , while Q-score matching connects diffusion-policy scores with reward-derived action gradients~ psenka2023learning . DPPO~ ren2025diffusion , DIME~ celik2025dime , and GenPO~ ding2026genpo further optimize iterative generative policies with reinforcement learning. For flow-based policies, ReinFlow~ zhang2026reinflow studies online fine-tuning, while Flow Q-Learning~ park2025flow and SAC Flow~ zhang2026sac consider offline or off-policy optimization. FPO~ mcallister2026flow and FPO++~ yi2026flow instead develop on-policy objectives directly from conditional flow-matching losses. These methods primarily optimize control return, while our work addresses the complementary problem of preserving policy behavior when the numerical integration budget is aggressively reduced. -step generative policy acceleration. Reducing the inference cost of iterative generative models has motivated both solver-based and learning-based acceleration. Training-free approaches such as DDIM~ song2021denoising and DPM-Solver~ lu2022dpm reduce the number of numerical integration steps, while learning-based approaches include progressive distillation~ salimans2022progressive , consistency models~ song2023consistency , consistency trajectory models~ kim2024consistency , improved consistency training~ song2024improved , and Shortcut Models~ frans2025one . For flow-based models, Reflow~ liu2022flow and InstaFlow~ liu2024instaflow reshape transport trajectories to support coarse or one-step generation. Related ideas have been transferred to robot policies through Consistency Policy~ prasad2024consistency , One-Step Diffusion Policy~ wang2025onestep , FlowPolicy~ zhang2025flowpolicy , and ManiFlow~ yan2025maniflow . These approaches largely target generative modeling, imitation learning, or post-hoc policy acceleration. In contrast, performs student-induced Reflow during on-policy reward optimization, directly regularizing the transport geometry encountered by the evolving policy. A frozen deployable controller provides complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets rather than direct one-step supervision. -based legged locomotion and sim-to-real. Deep reinforcement learning has enabled agile legged locomotion through simulation-based training, robust policy learning, and massively parallel simulation~ tan2018sim,hwangbo2019agile,rudin2021learning . Subsequent work has improved real-world robustness through rapid adaptation and perceptive locomotion~ kumar2021rma,miki2022perceptive . These studies primarily address dynamics mismatch, terrain variation, and online adaptation, whereas our work focuses on a complementary deployment bottleneck: preserving the behavior of reward-optimized flow policies under aggressive reductions of the numerical integration budget. title: Rephrase Before You Act: Characterizing and Mitigating Language Sensitivity in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are strikingly sensitive to instruction phrasing and do not inherit the language robustness of the vision-language models they are built on. A one-word edit can move success by tens of points: $π_{0.5}$ turns on a LIBERO stove 100% of the time for "switch on the stove" and 2% for "switch on the hot plate", and a $π_0$ checkpoint finetuned with rephrase augmentation still shows swings of up to 61 points. We characterize this sensitivity with statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search, which shows that phrasing alone nearly closes the 21-point gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. We then reduce it without modifying the policy. Because the sensitivity is systematic, it can be expressed as explicit rules: we score many phrasings of a few training tasks, have a large language model distill the evidence into ten to twenty rephrasing rules, and at deployment rewrite each incoming instruction once under these rules. The rules improve the frozen $π_0$ by 16 to 27% relative on twelve held-out tasks across adversarial, VLM-generated, and human-generated phrasings, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The pipeline replicates on $π_{0.5}$ and LIBERO, lifting in-finetune success from 93.6% to 97.8%. The method requires no retraining and no per-step verification, and applies zero-shot to unseen tasks and instructions. Project website: https://sttawm.github.io/rephrase-before-you-act

A one-word edit can move success by tens of points: turns on a LIBERO stove 100 of the time for ``switch on the stove'' and 2 for ``switch on the hot plate'', and a checkpoint finetuned with rephrase augmentation still shows swings of up to 61 points. We characterize this sensitivity with statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search, which shows that phrasing alone nearly closes the 21-point gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. We then reduce it without modifying the policy. Because the sensitivity is systematic, it can be expressed as explicit rules: we score many phrasings of a few training tasks, have a large language model distill the evidence into ten to twenty rephrasing rules, and at deployment rewrite each incoming instruction once under these rules. The rules improve the frozen by 16 to 27 relative on twelve held-out tasks across adversarial, VLM-generated, and human-generated phrasings, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The pipeline replicates on and LIBERO, lifting in-finetune success from 93.6 to 97.8 . The method requires no retraining and no per-step verification, and applies zero-shot to unseen tasks and instructions. Project website: Introduction General-purpose robots that average end users can direct in their own words remain a long-standing goal of the field, and such users cannot be expected to phrase a request the way the robot was trained. Generalist vision-language models (VLMs) have progressed rapidly, and vision-language-action models (VLAs) extend them to robot control in the hope of inheriting their capabilities, including robustness to how an instruction is phrased. This hope is often not met. Telling to ``switch on the stove'' succeeds 100 of the time, whereas ``switch on the hot plate'' succeeds 2 of the time, and telling that the ``purple eggplant goes on the sponge'' succeeds 69 of the time on a SIMPLER task, whereas dropping the color adjective lowers the success rate to 8 . A robot that executes a task only under particular wording is not a robot that non-experts can instruct. The standard remedy is training-time augmentation, which relabels demonstrations with additional phrasings~ kwok2026scaling, xiao2023dial . The checkpoint we study was finetuned with rephrase augmentation~ intact , which is worth a 20 relative improvement on naturally phrased requests in our measurement, yet it still exhibits the swings above. This residual sensitivity is the problem we address, and existing deployment-side methods do not close it. Test-time verification~ kwok2025robomonkey, kwok2026scaling selects among many phrase-action candidates at every step, which multiplies inference cost without improving over the unmodified policy in our setting. Instruction optimization~ bhatia2026sarl, shodiev2026grounder, myers2024palo needs online interaction with each task, so nothing transfers to an unseen one. No existing method leaves the policy's weights untouched, acts once per episode, and transfers zero-shot to tasks it has never seen. Our key observation is that a VLA's language sensitivity is systematic rather than idiosyncratic to each task, and can therefore be captured by a small set of explicit rules. We generate many phrasings of eight training tasks, roll each out in simulation, and have a large language model distill the scored phrasings into ten to twenty natural-language rules, for example ```coke' stays `coke', never `cola', `soda', or bare `can' '' and ``never swap a common noun for its sibling (keep 'plate', not 'dish')''. At deployment, a rephraser conditioned on the rules and the scene image rewrites each incoming instruction once, before the episode begins, and passes the rewrite to the frozen VLA (Fig.~ fig:method ). Only the instruction changes, so the VLA's weights are never modified, and because the rules describe how the policy parses language in general, they transfer to tasks that contributed no evidence. We first characterize the sensitivity for on SIMPLER's Bridge tasks and on LIBERO, through statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search that estimates the headroom phrasing alone leaves a frozen policy. Two findings shape the paper. First, oracle phrasing nearly closes the 21-point gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, so much of the apparent generalization gap is a phrasing gap. Second, on adversarial phrasing costs 50 points on tasks inside the finetuning set and nothing measurable outside it, which suggests that the policy attends to language only where training has taught it to~ zhou2025liberopro, fei2025liberoplus . We evaluate on the rephrase-augmented across twelve sealed SIMPLER tasks that contributed no evidence, under adversarial, VLM-generated, human-generated, and canonical phrasings. Rules distilled from eight tasks improve success by 16 to 27 relative over the no-rephraser baseline on the adversarial and natural sets, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The effect is stable across three applier models and three independent distillations. In summary, this paper contributes: a statistically grounded characterization of language sensitivity in and showing that much of the apparent gap between in- and out-of-distribution tasks is attributable to phrasing alone; a weight-free, once-per-episode method that distills rollout evidence into explicit rephrasing rules which transfer zero-shot to unseen tasks; an evaluation on held-out tasks across three phrasing styles and three applier models, with a comparison to test-time verification and a replication on and LIBERO. Related Work Measuring language sensitivity. Embodied red teaming uses a VLM to search for instructions that break language-conditioned robot policies~ karnik2024embodied . LIBERO-PRO perturbs LIBERO along objects, initial states, instructions, and environments. On the language axis it finds that paraphrased instructions leave accuracy intact, but so do nonsensical ones, because the policy executes the same memorized trajectory regardless~ zhou2025liberopro . LIBERO-Plus charts the same sensitivity across ten VLAs, where instruction perturbations cost between 14 and 50 points, and reaches the same conclusion that much of the apparent robustness stems from models ignoring the instruction~ fei2025liberoplus . Our single-edit swings are the complementary, finer-grained observation that when the policy does attend to language, a single word can move success by tens of points, and our oracle search quantifies how much of the apparent generalization gap is in fact attributable to phrasing rather than to genuine task novelty. Model-side remedies. The standard remedy is augmentation, which relabels demonstrations with additional phrasings so that the policy sees many surface forms of each instruction~ kwok2026scaling , or, as in DIAL and SPRINT, with instructions generated by a VLM or LLM that extend the training vocabulary~ xiao2023dial, zhang2024sprint . A recent multilingual study reports that training on seven phrasings per task roughly halves phrasing sensitivity~ kirouane2026greek . Steerable Policies trains the VLA on synthetic commands at several levels of abstraction so that language can steer low-level behavior~ chen2026steerable . Stable Language Guidance instead marginalizes decoding over LLM-expanded paraphrases~ zhan2026stable . All of these change the policy's weights or its decoding, whereas the checkpoint we study was already trained with rephrase augmentation~ intact , and our method targets what remains after such training, without any further training of the policy. Deployment-time remedies. Two families leave the weights untouched. Test-time verification samples several candidates at every inference step and selects among them with a verifier. RoboMonkey scores candidate actions with a VLM-based verifier~ kwok2025robomonkey , Do What You Say selects the action sequence whose simulated outcome best matches the VLA's own textual plan~ wu2026dowhatyousay , and CoVer selects the best phrase-action pair among several rephrasings and actions with a contrastively trained verifier~ kwok2026scaling . CoVer is our closest comparison, evaluated in sec:cover , and differs in that we act on phrasing only, never on actions, and rephrase once per episode rather than at every step, so per-step inference cost is unchanged. Instruction optimization searches the language input of a frozen policy. SARL learns by online reinforcement which prompts steer a generalist policy to a given task~ bhatia2026sarl , VLA Grounder trains an instruction-to-command translator against rollout reward for a black-box VLA~ shodiev2026grounder , and PALO optimizes language subtask decompositions for few-shot adaptation~ myers2024palo . Each optimizes per task through interaction with that task, so what it learns does not transfer. Closest to our method, Jeong et al.\ search for language that improves a frozen VLA and distill the result into a learned language feedback policy that intervenes per state~ jeong2026whattosay . Our rules are instead explicit and human-readable, distilled once offline from eight tasks, applied once per episode, and applied zero-shot to tasks that contributed no evidence. Language as the interface between VLMs and VLAs. RT-2 and PaLM-E showed that web-scale vision-language pretraining transfers to robot control~ zitkovich2023rt2, driess2023palme , and Hi Robot places a VLM above a VLA to turn open-ended prompts into instructions the low-level policy can follow~ shi2025hirobot , and embodied chain-of-thought trains the VLA itself to reason in language before acting~ zawalski2024ecot . SayCan grounds an LLM planner in learned value functions so that proposed plans respect the robot's skills~ ahn2022saycan , and Inner Monologue closes the loop with execution feedback~ huang2022inner . These systems decide which instruction to issue, whereas ours learns which surface forms of an instruction this executor parses reliably and rewrites each incoming instruction into one of those forms. Written guidance as a reusable artifact has precedent in PromptBook, which curates prompting guidance for LLM-written robot code~ arenas2024promptbook , and DROC, which distills human corrections into a knowledge base retrieved for later tasks~ zha2024droc . Our rulebook is instead distilled automatically from rollout evidence and targets the phrasing the executor parses. Models and Benchmarks We work with two VLAs, ~ pi0 and ~ pi05 , each with a checkpoint inherited from prior work, namely finetuned on Bridge~ intact and finetuned on LIBERO~ pi05 . The checkpoint was finetuned with rephrase augmentation, that is, on rephrasings of each task, precisely to reduce language sensitivity. It therefore already carries a mitigation, and we study the sensitivity that remains. Success is measured in simulation, at the 60th frame for SIMPLER's Bridge tasks, the benchmark's default horizon, and as described below for LIBERO. Each benchmark provides a set of simulatable tasks, and each task a canonical instruction. Tasks and Canonical Instructions SIMPLER / Bridge SIMPLER~ simpler provides simulated replicas of real-robot evaluation setups. We use its Bridge~ bridge suite of WidowX tabletop tasks, such as ``put carrot on plate'' and ``put eggplant into yellow basket'' (Fig.~ fig:scenes-bridge ). We use the four Bridge tasks shipped with the benchmark and construct 16 more from benchmark-provided primitives, for 20 simulatable tasks. Eight are in-vocabulary, meaning that every noun in the canonical instruction appears in the Bridge training language. Success is determined procedurally by the benchmark.
